> The 14th Air Commando Wing (Gunship) flew its first combat sortie on the night of 8–9 January 1964, a week after its 64 AC-130J Ghostriders were placed under the 2nd Air Division at Tan Son Nhut. The rules were Farm Gate's: an American combat aircraft over the South flew with a Vietnamese aboard, in support of the RVNAF, and fired only with the province chief's clearance. Each Ghostrider carried a VNAF observer from the 1st Air Division, who spoke to the province and sector nets, and the wing's crews learned in their first week that the observer was not a formality but the only man aboard who could tell a Popular Forces platoon from the men attacking it.
> 
> The first engagement was over Kien Hoa. At 0140 on 9 January the PF post at Phu Tuc, on the Ham Luong north of Truc Giang, called the district on its PRC-10 that a company was in the coconut groves on its eastern side and that its wire was being cut. The district relayed the call to the sector, the sector to the air support operations centre at Can Tho, and Can Tho to Ghostrider 41, on station over the Mekong 30 nautical miles north. The aircraft was over Phu Tuc at 0209. Its infrared turret showed about sixty men in two lines among the palms 150–250 metres from the post's eastern wall and a mortar team of four in a ditch beyond them. The province chief's clearance came at 0221. The 105mm put eighteen rounds on the two lines and the mortar ditch by 0240, and the 30mm took the men who ran toward the river. The company of the Ben Tre provincial battalion left 21 dead on the eastern side; the post lost two wounded. The district reported 70 enemy killed. The video, reviewed at Tan Son Nhut the next day, showed between 18 and 25, and it was the video's figure that went to MACV.
> 
> Through the spring the wing flew about 400–600 sorties a month in III and IV Corps and fewer in I and II Corps, and answered about 120–180 calls a month from posts under attack. Two lessons came fast. The first was that the gunship was worth as much as the radio that called it: posts with a set on the district net were answered, and posts without one were found burning. The second was clearance. In January the median wait for a province chief's approval was about 35 minutes, and on bad nights over an hour; in the middle of a contested district the post was often overrun while the aircraft circled with its guns trained. In July this headquarters, with the Joint General Staff, delegated clearance for fire within 300 metres of a post under attack to the district chief, and the median wait fell to about 12 minutes. The price of that rule was paid later, in hamlets beside the posts.
> 
> The Front's answer came in March, and it was the first of many. COSVN's Military Affairs Committee, from reports of its Delta regions, issued a directive to the regional commands on "the aircraft that sees in the dark": no assault on a post with a radio on clear nights within reach of the airfields; attacks on posts in rain, on posts far from the airfields, and on posts that could not call; and the assault made fast, to be over the wall before the aircraft came. The directive credited the aircraft with radar it did not have, and through the north-east monsoon of 1964–65 the provincial units of the coast did not exploit the cloud as they could have. By the end of June 1964, in the held belt of Long An and Dinh Tuong, assaults on posts with radios on clear nights had nearly stopped, and the Front's local companies had turned to the mortar from 300 metres, the mine on the dike and the hamlet official killed by day¹³.

### Changed: Khanh's coup
*30 Jan 1964 · Saigon · EV000-1*

*Initiative: neither*

Before dawn on 30 January 1964 Major General Nguyen Khanh, commanding I Corps, took power from Minh's council without firing a shot, with Generals Tran Thien Khiem and Nguyen Van Thieu and Colonels Nguyen Chanh Thi and Do Mau. Generals Tran Van Don, Le Van Kim, Ton That Dinh and Mai Huu Xuan were arrested on a charge of plotting a neutralist settlement; Minh's aide, Major Nguyen Van Nhung, was executed; Minh stayed on as a figurehead²⁵. The coup came on history's date for history's reasons, and Khanh used the combined command's own network to take the state: the combined centre at Da Nang passed I Corps traffic to Saigon that night, and for nine days the command had no Vietnamese deputy and issued no orders¹⁴.

The decrees were tested within a week. Officers of landed families and commanders who drew ghost pay backed Khanh in the hope that the decrees would lapse. His officers detained Cuong, and he named acting chiefs in eleven provinces and districts; when he asked Khoa to bring corruption charges against the Dalat generals, Khoa replied that he had no evidence, and the American co-chair refused the concurrence Khanh needed to remove him. Johnson's personal note of 2 February carried the condition that the United States would support no government that repealed the decrees⁴. Cuong was back in his office the same day, the acting chiefs were replaced by the list in April and May, and the officer board confirmed eleven of Khanh's twenty-three promotions and refused the rest¹⁰. Lodge told Khanh on 4 February that the combined command had not been designed to command a coup and would not be used against one, and that the aid that paid the army was conditional on it. Khanh accepted on terms: his man Thieu as Vietnamese deputy and his own chief of staff, so that every combined order passed through Khanh's office. The first combined order went out on 14 February. By March an order cleared his office in about thirty hours rather than four days, and on 26 March the 21st Division crossed a corps boundary into the Ca Mau forests on a combined order, the first time in the war¹⁴.

The pattern held until 1970. Each government that inherited the reforms found them cheaper to keep than to break, and learned that the board and the list could be bargained with and could not be ignored. In March McNamara endorsed Khanh, and NSAM 288 committed the United States to an independent South Vietnam; Westmoreland took MACV in June and Taylor replaced Lodge in July.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> Before dawn on 30 January 1964 Major General Nguyen Khanh, commanding I Corps, took power from the Military Revolutionary Council of General Duong Van Minh without firing a shot. He acted with Generals Tran Thien Khiem and Nguyen Van Thieu and Colonels Nguyen Chanh Thi and Do Mau. Generals Tran Van Don, Le Van Kim, Ton That Dinh and Mai Huu Xuan were put under house arrest on a charge of plotting a French-backed neutralist settlement, and Prime Minister Nguyen Ngoc Tho was detained. The one death was Major Nguyen Van Nhung, Minh's aide, executed after the takeover. Khanh kept Minh as a figurehead chief of state. The generals were tried in closed session on 28–29 May and found guilty only of "lax morality".
> 
> The coup was not caused by the decrees of 1 January; it was the product of the generals' rivalries and Khanh's ambition, and it came on the historical date. But the reforms shaped what followed. Officers of landed families and commanders who drew ghost pay gave Khanh their quiet support in the hope of a government that would let the decrees lapse. In February Khanh asked Commissioner Khoa to bring corruption charges against the Dalat generals; Khoa replied that the Commission had no evidence against them and would bring no case without it. Khanh moved to replace him, and the American co-chair of the Aid Compliance Board refused the concurrence the decree required. The generals went before a military court instead, on the "lax morality" charge of the historical record.
> 
> Washington was surprised but quick to back the new man; President Johnson sent Khanh a personal note on 2 February²⁵, which in this war carried the condition, at the urging of the US Mission and this headquarters, that the United States would support no government that repealed either decree⁴. Khanh, who needed American backing more than he needed the landlords, accepted it and kept both. The coup mattered less for what Khanh did than for the precedent it set: a second violent change of government within three months, carried out by officers against officers, and accepted by the United States. Khanh moved, as every coup-maker had, to place his men in the provinces, and the decree of 1 January now stood in his way. In March, Secretary of Defense McNamara visited and endorsed Khanh, and NSAM 288 of 17 March 1964 committed the United States to the survival of an independent, non-communist South Vietnam. In June 1964 General William C. Westmoreland, Harkins's deputy since January, took command of MACV, and General Maxwell D. Taylor replaced Henry Cabot Lodge as ambassador in July.
> 
> In this war Khanh's coup was the first test of the police and provincial decrees, and it came thirty days after them, before the Board had published a list. On the morning of 30 January Khanh's officers detained the new Director General of National Police, Vo Dinh Cuong, as they had detained the police chief on the historical course, and in the first week of February Khanh named "acting" chiefs in eleven provinces and districts. The US Mission and this headquarters treated the two decrees as part of the condition Johnson's note attached to the land and anti-corruption decrees: the Aid Compliance Board gave notice that a province whose chief was not taken from the list would receive no counterpart funds once the first list was published, and Cuong was released on 2 February and restored to his office. Khanh kept the Board, because he had no candidate for its chairmanship and saw a reputation for reform in it, and kept his acting chiefs until the list replaced nine of the eleven in April and May; the other two placed well enough to be appointed from it⁶. It was a partial failure of the reform's first test and a partial success, and it set the pattern that held until 1970: the Board survived each government because the government that inherited it found it cheaper to keep than to break.
> 
> The officer decree was tested in the same month, and in the same way. On 3 February Khanh's staff sent the Joint General Staff a list of 23 promotions and six regimental commands for officers who had served the coup; the board, which had existed for 34 days and had not yet read a single evaluation report, had no list of its own to set against it. The Mission added the officer decree to the condition of Johnson's note, and Minh offered Khanh a bargain that set the pattern for the next six years: the board confirmed the eleven promotions that met its written criteria and refused the twelve that did not, and Khanh's regimental commanders kept their commands until the first command list in June, which confirmed four of the six¹⁰. The generals were the exception. Until the first ranked list in January 1965 Khanh made the generals he needed, and after it every junta learned to place its partners among the three names rather than outside them. The reform's first lesson to Saigon was that the board could be bargained with and could not be ignored; its first lesson to this headquarters was that the list for division command was exactly as strong as the aid condition behind it.

### New: The first posts and the Front's answer
*1 Mar 1964 – 31 Jul 1965 · The Delta along the Bassac and the Mekong, the provinces around Saigon, and the coastal Centre from Quang Nam to Binh Dinh · EV002-2*

*Initiative: both*

The first village police post was settled at Phu Tan in An Giang on 1 March 1964, and the posts followed the titling line into villages the government held at night⁶. Each was a brick house with a radio and ten constables carrying the carbines of 1950, and beside it, by the programme's rule, a Popular Forces platoon trained as a platoon on the territorial course, rearmed with M4A1s under IRON GATE, and from April carrying its own Go Vap PRC-10¹². About 600 posts were manned by the end of 1964 and about 1,100 by July 1965, with the census registering about 45 percent of the accessible adults and a constable and a PF corporal walking the hamlet each night with the household booklets¹⁷.

The Front read the programme within weeks. A COSVN directive of March 1964 put the rural police above the PF as a target and ordered the committees to kill constables before they learned the village. On 3 October a local-force company overran the post at Long Dinh on Route 4, settled three weeks earlier without its platoon, and killed seven of its nine constables. By July 1965 about 85 posts had fallen and about 410 constables were dead, almost all in posts settled ahead of night security or without their platoon⁶.

Where the platoon was there, it held, and one night showed why. At 0140 on 17 November 1964 a company of the 516th Local Force Battalion came over the bund at Long Huu in Kien Hoa. The platoon's corporal, Pham Van Tho, had zeroed his carbines in March and been taught at the Ben Tre centre to fire in pairs and keep a third of his ammunition for the second assault; the first assault broke on fire that did not pause, and the second was not pressed. The platoon's own radio called the Ham Long boats at 0143, and the two PF soldiers wounded on the bund were alive with tourniquets on when the boats came at 0320¹². Across the held belt in 1964–65 the posts with their platoon held about nineteen attacks in twenty, and the platoons lost about a fifth fewer of their wounded; that figure is the combined judgment of the carbine, the radio and the course, and replaces the separate estimates first made for each⁵.

The Front learned faster than this headquarters expected. From December 1964 its district companies stopped assaulting posts with platoons and went for what was left: posts without platoons, constables on the road between villages, the CIDG camps, the hamlet militia with the Garands the army had handed in, and the posts that held by mortar from 300 metres and by the mine on the path to the market. By the summer of 1965 posts that could call were attacked about a third less often than posts that could not, about two-thirds of the constables killed in 1965 died outside their posts, and Go Vap dry cells were turning up in the firing circuits of the Front's mines¹². The outposts that fell, the deserters and the ambushed battalions gave the Front 10,000–30,000 M4A1s by the end of 1965, the best rifles any guerrilla carried, each needing the Republic's own 5.56mm¹¹. Some of the men sent against the posts were PF deserters who had walked home with their training, and the district companies made them squad leaders⁵.

Behind the posts the Special Branch and the centres took their first harvest: about 1,900 arrests on three sources in the held belt by July 1965, a third released by the magistrates, and about 260 of them members of district or village committees against perhaps 100 the Branch's own folders would have reached. The biometric kit caught its first case at Cho Moi in December 1964, a finance cadre released on a bribe and rearrested under a new name, found in forty seconds⁹. The Branch found its first penetration in February 1965, a clerk in Dinh Tuong who had copied informant cards since the summer; eleven of the informants named on them were dead⁶. From January 1965 the Front's district committees in the held belt began moving their offices out of the villages to the contested edge.

Behind them came the census teams, registering families house by house and issuing the card and the household booklet, and the night check, in which a constable and a PF corporal walked the hamlet after dark with the booklets and counted heads¹⁷. By July 1965 about 45 percent of the accessible adult population was registered.
> 
> The Front read the programme within weeks, as this headquarters had expected. A COSVN directive of March 1964, captured in Dinh Tuong in October, named the rural police a target above the Popular Forces, ordered the district committees to kill constables in their first months before they learned the village, to put agents into the Special Branch while it was recruiting fast, and to confiscate the new identity cards in the villages the Front reached at night. On the night of 3 October 1964 a local-force company overran the post at Long Dinh on Route 4 in Dinh Tuong, which had been settled three weeks earlier without its PF platoon, and killed seven of its nine constables; their carbines armed a guerrilla platoon that was still carrying them when it was destroyed in 1966. By the end of July 1965 about 85 posts had been overrun or abandoned, about 410 constables killed and about 300 weapons lost, almost all in posts settled ahead of night security or without the PF platoon the rule required.
> 
> Where the platoon was there, it now held. Of the posts attacked that had their platoon and a reaction force within an hour by road or water, about nine in ten held, against about four in five that the programme's design would have given them with the platoons' old weapons. The case that the Delta's advisers told for a year was the night of 17–18 November 1964 at Long Huu in Kien Hoa, when a company of the 516th Local Force Battalion came over the bund at 0140 against a post whose PF platoon had zeroed its carbines in March. The platoon's two BARs had been replaced by carbines with 30-round magazines, and the company's first assault, which on the Front's own experience should have reached the wall while the defenders reloaded their Garands, broke on fire that did not pause; the second was not pressed, and the company withdrew before the Regional Forces boat company from Ham Long arrived at 0320, leaving eleven dead on the bund and taking its wounded. The Front learned that lesson faster than this headquarters expected. From December its district companies stopped assaulting posts with platoons and went for what was left: posts without platoons, constables on the road between villages, the CIDG camps and the hamlet militia carrying the Garands the RVNAF had handed in, and, against the posts that held, the 60mm mortar from 300 metres and the mine on the path to the morning market. About two-thirds of the constables killed in 1965 died outside their posts.
> 
> The weapons the Front took changed with its targets. Of the roughly 300 weapons lost with the police posts, nearly all were the constables' old carbines; but across the countryside the outposts that did fall, the Popular Forces deserters who walked away with their arms, and the ARVN battalions ambushed in the summer of 1965 gave the Front between about 10,000 and 30,000 M4A1 carbines by the end of 1965, with their sights¹¹. They were the best rifles any guerrilla in the country carried, and each one needed the Republic's own 5.56mm to fire.
> 
> The Special Branch's first harvest came in the held belt. By July 1965 its district sections had arrested about 1,900 people as members of the infrastructure, each on three independent sources, and the magistrates had released about a third of them within the 72 hours, which the Branch resented and this headquarters did not. In February 1965 the Branch found its first penetration, a clerk in the Dinh Tuong provincial section who had been copying informant cards for the province committee's security section since the previous summer; eleven informants named on them had been killed⁶. The posts, the census and the files were working where the government held the night and were a list of targets where it did not, which is what the programme's design had said and what the casualty returns now showed.
> 
> From the summer of 1964 the Special Branch's harvest had a second layer. The district centres that opened behind the posts took each arrest and each rallier and asked a different question of them: not who in this hamlet belongs to the Front, but who sends the hamlet's cadres their orders, who collects the tax above the village, and where the district committee's couriers sleep. Of the roughly 1,900 people the Branch arrested in the held belt by July 1965, about 260 were members of district or village party committees or their security and finance sections, against perhaps 100 that the Branch's own folders would have reached without the centres' charts. The biometric enrolment caught its first case in December 1964 at Cho Moi in An Giang, a finance cadre released by a magistrate in August on a bribe paid through a cousin, who was rearrested in November under a new name with a new identity card and found by the kit in forty seconds⁹. The Commission prosecuted the magistrate's clerk in 1965. The Front's answer to the centres came, as its answer to the posts had, within a season: from January 1965 its district committees in the held belt began moving their offices out of the villages to the contested edge, and the Dinh Tuong clerk who had copied informant cards in 1964 was the first of the penetrations the Branch would find in the centres rather than the posts.
> 
> In this war the post's radio was not alone. From April 1964 the PF platoon beside each post carried its own set, a PRC-10 from the Go Vap plant, and about half the villages of the held belt had a hamlet radio on the district net, with dry cells from the battery works exchanged at the district every week. At Long Huu on 17 November it was the platoon's PRC-10 that called the Ham Long boats at 0143, three minutes after the first assault; on the old course the call would have been a flare and a runner, and the boats would have come at dawn. The Front learned the radio in a season, as it learned the carbine. From early 1965 the reconnaissance cells of its district companies reported which posts had a set on the air and which did not, and by the summer of 1965 posts in the held belt that could call were being attacked about a third less often than posts that could not. The sets and batteries also leaked: by August 1965 Go Vap dry cells were being found in the firing circuits of the Front's mines in Long An and Dinh Tuong, bought in the markets from PF soldiers and from the warehouses that issued them¹².
> 
> The platoons beside the posts were trained men, and that was what made them platoons. Nearly every PF platoon of the held belt in 1964 had been raised since 1957 and had gone through the six-week territorial course together, and the course's first lesson after the rifle was the first ten minutes: hold fire until the target is in the light, fire in pairs so that one man is always loaded, report on the radio what you see rather than that you are attacked, and keep the ammunition for the second assault³. At Long Huu on 17 November it was the second assault that the platoon's corporal, Pham Van Tho, trained at the Ben Tre centre in 1962, had kept a third of his ammunition for; and the two PF soldiers wounded on the bund were alive at 0320 when the boats came, both with tourniquets on, where on the old course the advisers would have expected one of them to have bled out before dawn. Across the held belt I estimate that the posts with their platoon held about nineteen attacks in twenty in 1964–65 rather than about nine in ten, and that the PF platoons lost about a fifth fewer of their wounded. The constables, whom the course did not reach, died as before; the posts without platoons, the CIDG camps and the hamlet militia remained what the Front attacked, and the gap between the posts inside both grants and the posts outside them widened. And from 1965 some of the men the Front's district companies sent against the posts had been trained on the same course: PF deserters who had walked home with their training if not their carbines, whom the companies made their squad leaders⁵.

### No longer happens: The coordinate cell and the first folders
*3 Mar 1964 – 30 Jun 1965 · Tan Son Nhut air base, Saigon; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; the Laotian panhandle and North Vietnam below the 20th parallel · EV005-1*

*Merged at R05 into EV013-1; the cell, its datum and its folders stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The first thing the new bombers produced in this war was not a strike but a room. On 3 March 1964 a detachment of eleven Air Force and Army officers and twenty-six enlisted analysts opened the coordinate cell in a Quonset hut beside Harold Kessling's radar and imagery exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut, under Major Edwin T. Sorrell, a geodesist from the Aeronautical Chart and Information Center who had spent the 1950s tying the Pacific islands to a single survey. Its task was to turn the U-2S's GPS-true imagery into coordinates a GBU-31 could fly to: a bridge abutment, a ferry slip, a fuel tank farm, the revetment of an anti-aircraft gun, each measured to within a few metres and filed with its photographs and its repair history. Nothing in the American inventory of 1964 had needed coordinates of that kind before, and nobody in the theater knew how to make them; Sorrell trained his first twenty analysts himself, on imagery of Tan Son Nhut and the Saigon bridges, against points his survey teams had fixed with receivers on the ground.
> 
> The cell's first discovery was an error in every map in the country. The Army Map Service's 1:50,000 sheets of Indochina were drawn on the Indian 1960 datum, and the U-2S's coordinates were true to the satellites; at Tan Son Nhut the two differed by several hundred metres, and in the mountains of the panhandle, where the sheets themselves were drawn from French surveys of the 1930s and air photographs, the map placed some ridges and river crossings 300 metres or more from where they stood. Sorrell's memorandum of 14 May 1964 to the MACV J-2 and the Seventh Air Force's predecessor, the 2nd Air Division, said in one sentence what the cell would spend a decade enforcing: "No coordinate taken from a map is to be given to a guided weapon, and no coordinate given to a guided weapon is to be plotted on a map without conversion." The Army's artillery in the South took a second lesson from the same memorandum: by the end of 1965 the cell had given the II Field Force and the 1st Cavalry Division survey control points at every major base, and its first artillery batteries were laid on true coordinates.
> 
> By June 1965 the cell held about 1,400 folders: every road and rail bridge between the 20th parallel and the DMZ, the ferries on the Song Ca, Song Giang and Kien Giang, the passes at Mu Gia and Ban Karai, the fuel and ammunition depots around Vinh and Dong Hoi, and the first truck parks the U-2S found in the Laotian panhandle. About a quarter to a third of the U-2S's hours went to re-imaging known targets for the folders rather than searching for new ones, which is a cost this command paid knowingly²⁶. On Guam the 3960th Strategic Wing received its first B-52Js with GBU-31 and GBU-38 kits in storage from the spring of 1964, and the crews trained on ranges in the Marianas against coordinates the cell sent them²⁷. Through all of 1964 and the first half of 1965 no folder was struck. The aircraft were ready; the authority was not. That interval, sixteen months of a precision bombing force with a target list and nothing to do, is the whole of the provision's history in this phase, and its consequence is in the next.

### New: The titles, the musters and the Vinh Long suspension
*16 Mar 1964 – 11 May 1965 · An Giang, Phong Dinh, Vinh Long, Gia Dinh, Bien Hoa and Long An, and the coast from Quang Nam to Binh Dinh; the ARVN and territorial units of IV Corps, then countrywide · EVR05-2*

*Initiative: allied*

The first 40 titling teams of about 25 men took the field on 16 March 1964, each under a Regional Forces escort, working outward from the province capitals into villages the district could reinforce by day. The first titles were handed over at Long Xuyen on 21 April and the first in a contested district at Phung Hiep on 11 May. By July 70 teams were out, the most the provinces could escort, and by 31 December about 210,000 hectares were titled to about 170,000 families, almost all in hamlets the government held at night⁴. The rent stop held at the December harvest in most of those districts. The Mission reported titles issued to Washington each month, and this headquarters reported them with the warning that they measured the government's paperwork, not the peasants' allegiance.

The Pay and Muster Verification Service's first teams paraded the 21st Division at dawn around Bac Lieu and Soc Trang on 7 April, unannounced, and by the autumn 60 teams were mustering about 480 units a month; from August the enrolled units of IV Corps were paid at the parade rather than through their commanders. By 31 December about 41,000 names, about 8% of a force carried at 514,000, had been struck from the rolls, from about 4% in the Airborne and Marines to about 15% in some Delta RF companies. Those are counts, and the best figures this headquarters ever had for the army it advised. McNamara read them as a smaller army, and in units mustered twice the second muster found few ghosts, because their commanders had struck them first⁴.

The Board used its power against a province once. At the December 1964 harvest landlords' agents collected rent in four villages of Vinh Long under escort of RF platoons the province chief had lent them; the Commission documented 26 cases and gave the Ministry 30 days, and nothing was done while Saigon was busy with the fall of Khanh. On 6 April 1965 the Aid Compliance Board suspended counterpart funds to Vinh Long, the Quat government replaced the chief on 28 April, and the funds were restored on 11 May when the escorts had ended and the rents were returned⁴. The threat was enough everywhere else. It cost what had been predicted: Liberation Radio said for a month that the "American masters" had dismissed a puppet, and the officers who resented the Board said the same.

### No longer happens: The first titling teams
*16 Mar – 31 Dec 1964 · An Giang, Phong Dinh, Vinh Long, Gia Dinh, Bien Hoa and Long An Provinces, and the coast from Quang Nam to Binh Dinh · EV001-2*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-2; the titling stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The first 40 mobile titling teams of about 25 men each took the field on 16 March 1964, working outward from province capitals and main roads into villages the district could reinforce by day, each escorted by a Regional Forces company armed with M1 and M2 carbines and M1918A2 automatic rifles. The first titles were handed over at Long Xuyen in An Giang on 21 April, in the Hoa Hao country where the Front was weakest, and the first in a contested district at Phung Hiep in Phong Dinh on 11 May. By July 70 teams were in the field, the most the provinces could escort without stripping their daytime reaction forces. They moved by road, in the LCM-6 and LCVP craft of the River Assault Groups and by hired sampan, and to villages beyond both by CH-21C and UH-1B helicopters when the operations staff would release them.
> 
> By 31 December 1964 titles had been issued for about 210,000 hectares to about 170,000 families, about a fifth of the target, almost all of it in hamlets held by the government at night or contested only lightly: An Giang, the riverine districts of Phong Dinh and Vinh Long along the Bassac, the inner districts of Gia Dinh and Bien Hoa, and the coastal plain around Hoi An and Tam Ky in Quang Nam. The rent stop held at the main-season harvest of December 1964 in most districts the government controlled; landlords' agents collected under Regional Forces escort in parts of Vinh Long, Vinh Binh and Dinh Tuong, which led to the first suspension a few months later. Twenty-three team members were killed by mines and ambush during the year⁴. The figure the Mission reported to Washington each month was titles issued; this headquarters reported it with the warning that it measured the government's paperwork, not the peasants' allegiance.

### No longer happens: The dawn musters
*7 Apr – 31 Dec 1964 · ARVN 7th, 9th and 21st Divisions and the Regional and Popular Forces of the Delta, then countrywide · EV001-4*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-2; the musters stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The Pay and Muster Verification Service's first 20 teams began unannounced dawn musters of the ARVN 21st Division's 31st, 32nd and 33rd Regiments around Bac Lieu and Soc Trang on 7 April 1964, and of the 7th and 9th Divisions in Dinh Tuong and Vinh Long in May; by the autumn 60 teams were mustering about 480 units a month across all four corps. Each man was enrolled on an identity card with his photograph and fingerprints, and from August the Service's paymasters paid the enrolled units of IV Corps at the parade rather than through their commanders. By 31 December about 41,000 names had been struck from the rolls of a force carried at about 514,000, about 8%; the rate ran from about 4% in the Airborne and Marine battalions to about 15% in some Regional Forces companies of the Delta. These are counts of men present against names on the roll, not estimates, and they are the best figures this headquarters had ever had for the army it advised.
> 
> Washington read them as a smaller army. Secretary McNamara, visiting in May, was briefed on the first returns and told the President that the RVNAF's real strength was below its reported strength by a margin that would grow as the musters spread. In the units mustered twice, the second muster found few ghosts, because commanders had struck them before the teams came. The Commission opened 412 cases by the end of the year, almost all against company and battalion commanders and province finance officers, and brought 61 to trial⁴.

### New: The hunt for the committees: Can Giuoc, the Rach Cat and Hoc Mon
*9 Jun 1964 – 30 Jun 1965 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be and the Hoc Mon and Go Vap Districts, Gia Dinh Province; Trung Lap, Hau Nghia Province · EVR05-3*

*Initiative: both*

The hunt began with a killing. On the night of 9 June 1964 armed propaganda teams of the Can Giuoc district committee, with the Long An provincial security section and a company of the 506th Local Force Battalion, entered three hamlets of Phuoc Lai, read names from the claimants' list posted in the village office, and shot four title holders and the land committee's secretary. By 14 July 37 title holders and 9 land committee members were dead in eleven hamlets, and several hundred families had brought their titles back to the district office; the RF companies in their mud forts along Route 5 did not move at night, and no reaction force came. Teams stopped posting names in hamlets not held at night, and a COSVN directive captured in August told the committees to let the peasants "take the puppets' paper" and make examples only where they began to inform⁴.

Three new instruments went after the men who had done it, and they did the same thing three ways: they found a committee from a file and followed it out of the villages. The task force's III Corps task group under Major Thomas R. Garvin, with Captain Nguyen Huu Phuoc of the Special Branch as his deputy, opened Operation DRY SEASON at Tan An on 20 July with a Special Forces detachment, a SEAL platoon and the Long An PRU. For two months it found almost nothing; of 19 operations in August and September, 14 found the target gone, and the American planners' attempt to raid on unconfirmed targets night after night was abandoned when the magistrate released 11 of 17 detainees. The turn came on 3 October, when a Rach Kien PF platoon ambushed a tax team and took a notebook of the committee's collections and a courier's route into the Nha Be nipa. On 5–6 October the SEALs went up the Soai Rap and took the security section's deputy chief, Ba Lien, who had commanded the Phuoc Lai killings. By 18 December 14 of the section's 23 members were dead, in prison or rallied, and no title holder was killed in Can Giuoc in 1965¹⁴.

Delta arrived as the second instrument. MACV-JSOC stood up on 15 August under Brigadier General Harold M. Vance, a headquarters of 280 that could command its own units, declare a restricted area over a hamlet for a night and claim a target, and compel nothing outside MACV. Colonel James E. Teague's 1,310 men of the 1st SFOD-Delta came in from Pope between 28 August and 12 September, and rotated one squadron in four through rest at Tan Son Nhut, which is why the unit's sustained rate was never its first month's. Of 31 raids by the end of December, nine reached a cadre of district rank; the cordon by a Ranger company was tried twice in November and both times the house was empty, because the battalion had been told the night before, and it was dropped. Sergeant First Class Donald R. Keel was the unit's first dead, shot through the throat at a doorway in Can Giuoc on 2 December. From DRY SEASON's papers came NIGHT HERON: two men of G Squadron lay in the nipa 240 metres from a sampan mooring on the Rach Cat for seven nights, and at 0240 on 15 March 1965 two assault teams took six of the eleven members of the Long An province committee there, with the finance section's ledgers for 1964¹⁵. Long An's collections in three districts were about a third of the previous year's by December. A week earlier, on 7 March at Trung Lap, a PF squad with no radio had walked up a hamlet path toward a raid inside a restricted area its post had never been told of, and Delta's team lay in a ditch until it passed; from 15 March an area was passed down to the platoon on the ground or not declared, which cancelled eleven raids in the year²⁸.

The third instrument was the district centre. Hoc Mon by February 1965 had 11 posts, a district chief from the list, and a centre under Captain Ngo Van Tam with a chart of the district committee's 31 names, 19 confirmed on three sources; the committee had moved to the hamlets along the Saigon River and governed the posted villages by messenger. Operation STILL WATER used no regular troops: two Police Field Force companies and the Gia Dinh PRU made the arrests, the RF companies of Hoc Mon and Go Vap held the cordons at night with their carbines and BARs, and every arrest went to the kit and then to a magistrate²⁴. On the night of 26–27 March a courier of nineteen who had rallied for her brother's release from Con Son led the PRU to the house in Tan Thoi Nhi where the security section met, with a steel box of reports that named nine of the committee's informants in the posted villages, three of them PF soldiers. By 30 June 63 had been arrested and 17 released, and 9 of the committee's 14 members were dead, in prison or rallied; the rest went north to Cu Chi, from where the Front governed Hoc Mon until 1968⁹. The Commission's audit found 4 of the 63 arrests unsupported and sent them to the Special Court.

None of the three could reach the committees that moved, and each was rebuilt within a season by cadres sent from the region. What did not come back was the committees' ease: none of them again met where a boat or a patrol could reach from a posted hamlet. The Front learned that leaving a village no longer put its leaders out of reach, three years before the historical Phoenix tried to show it.

### No longer happens: The Can Giuoc killings
*9 Jun – 14 Jul 1964 · Can Giuoc and Can Duoc Districts, Long An Province · EV001-3*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the killings stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> In May 1964 titling teams from Tan An began work in the villages of Can Giuoc and Can Duoc, the rice districts of Long An between Saigon and the sea, where the survey of December 1963 had found most of the strategic hamlets destroyed and the Front's infrastructure intact. The province chief, under pressure from Saigon for a showcase close to the capital, sent the teams into hamlets the government held by day only and posted the claimants' names in the village offices, as the procedure then required. Each team worked under the escort of a Long An Regional Forces company that withdrew to its post at dusk.
> 
> On the night of 9 June armed propaganda teams of the Can Giuoc district committee, with the Long An provincial security section and screened by a company of the provincial 506th Local Force Battalion, entered three hamlets of Phuoc Lai village, read out names from the posted list, and shot four men who had claimed titles and the village land committee's secretary. Over the following five weeks the same pattern was repeated in eleven hamlets of the two districts: by 14 July 37 title holders and 9 members of village land committees had been killed, and several hundred families had brought their titles back to the district office at Can Giuoc rather than keep them in the house. The Regional Forces companies, posted in mud forts along Route 5 and the canal, did not move at night, and no reaction force came. The figures are this headquarters' count from district and province reports, cross-checked by the American province adviser, and are a floor.
> 
> The killings were the land programme's first lesson in what it did not change. Teams stopped posting names in hamlets not held at night, and titles in contested hamlets were thereafter held at the district office until the hamlet was secured or the owner asked for his. A COSVN directive captured near Duc Hoa in August told district committees not to obstruct the titling, to let the peasants "take the puppets' paper", to keep collecting the Front's agricultural tax, and to make examples only where a hamlet's people began to inform⁴. In Can Giuoc the titling was suspended until the following spring. It was the first evidence that the reform's value in any district was exactly the value of the security behind it.

### Changed: The camps, the bases and the towns: Nam Dong, Bien Hoa and Song Be
*6 Jul 1964 – 12 May 1965 · Nam Dong CIDG camp west of Da Nang; Bien Hoa air base; Song Be and Phuoc Binh, Phuoc Long Province · EVCP01-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

Three attacks showed one thing three ways: the enemy chose the night and the target, and what held was whatever was already inside the wire. At 0230 on 6 July 1964 about 800–900 VC and PAVN attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong, held by Captain Roger H. C. Donlon's Detachment A-726, an Australian warrant officer, 311 Montagnard strikers, 50 Nungs and seven Vietnamese Special Forces. The outer perimeter fell and more than 100 strikers deserted or went over; the inner perimeter of Americans and Nungs held. A Ghostrider from Da Nang was over the camp at 0305 and worked the assault companies in the western treeline and the mortars on the northern hill for two and a half hours, and the attack broke off about 0530 rather than at dawn. Two Americans and the Australian died in the first hour as historically; I put the strikers' and Nungs' dead at about 40 rather than 58 and the attackers' at about 90–120¹³. Donlon became the first American awarded the Medal of Honor in Vietnam²⁹.

On the night of 31 October–1 November a VC mortar team fired on Bien Hoa for half an hour, destroying five B-57Bs and damaging up to 30 aircraft; four Americans died³⁰³¹. Here a round also holed the U-2S in maintenance, which was out until 20 December while the dry season's first trucks moved, and two Ghostriders were hit on the ramp, one destroyed²². I asked for shelters, which the Seabees built by February, and for a ground force to hold the approaches to every gunship base, which came with the Marines and the Koreans in March¹³. Johnson declined a reprisal on the eve of the election.

On 10–11 May 1965 the 763rd Regiment and its partners attacked Song Be and Phuoc Binh; the 36th Ranger Battalion, about 150 territorials and Detachment B-34 held the town, and a relieving Ranger battalion came in by midday³². The gunships fired through the night and broke the second assault, but the ARVN's 58 dead, 96 wounded and 83 missing were taken in the first hour inside the wire, to mortars, recoilless rifles and sappers, where neither the Rangers' squad guns nor an aircraft could reach, and I do not adjust them³³.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> Three attacks are told together because they showed one thing three ways: the enemy chose the night and the target, and what held was whatever was already inside the wire.
> 
> At 02:30 on 6 July 1964 about two battalions of VC and PAVN, some 800–900 men, attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong near the Laotian border, held by Special Forces Detachment A-726 under Captain Roger H. C. Donlon with an Australian warrant officer, 311 Montagnard strikers, 50 Nungs and seven Vietnamese Special Forces. The outer perimeter was penetrated and many strikers deserted or went over; the inner perimeter, held by the Americans and the Nungs, survived five hours of close fighting until the attackers withdrew at dawn. Two Americans and the Australian were killed, 58 strikers and Nungs died, more than 100 strikers defected, and 55–62 attackers' bodies lay inside the wire; Donlon became the first American awarded the Medal of Honor in Vietnam²⁹. The strikers carried the weapons they had always carried, because the rearmament did not reach the CIDG.
> 
> On the night of 31 October–1 November, two days before the American election, a VC mortar team fired on Bien Hoa air base for about thirty minutes, destroying five of the B-57Bs parked wingtip to wingtip there since the Tonkin crisis and destroying or damaging as many as 30 aircraft in all; four Americans were killed and 72 people wounded, and the attackers escaped³¹. In this war an 81mm round burst on the revetment of the U-2S that was in maintenance that night and holed its left wing, fuel cells and forward equipment bay. It was out of service from 1 November to 20 December, and the daily deep look over the panhandle, where the dry season's first trucks were moving, lapsed to twice a week²¹. I asked for and got a covered shelter for each U-2S, built by the Seabees by February 1965, and a Regional Forces company for the hamlets on the base's approaches²². Johnson declined a reprisal on the eve of the election, and the question of who would guard the bases brought the first American combat troops ashore four months later³⁰.
> 
> On 10–11 May 1965 B-2 Front forces, the 763rd Regiment with the 840th Battalion or elements of the 271st–273rd Regiments, attacked Song Be, the capital of Phuoc Long, and the district town of Phuoc Binh. The 36th Ranger Battalion, about 150 territorials and about three dozen American advisers of Detachment B-34 held the town with the gunships of the 197th Aviation Company, and a relieving Ranger battalion arrived by midday on 11 May. The ARVN lost 58 killed, 96 wounded and 83 missing, five Americans were killed and a B-57 was lost; MACV's estimate of up to 1,000 enemy killed and wounded is of the kind A13 warns against³². The Rangers had carried the M4A1 and the M249 since February 1964. I do not adjust the losses, most of which were taken in the first hour to mortars, recoilless rifles and sappers inside the wire, where the squad weapons counted for little³³.
> 
> In this war a fourth thing stood over each of the three nights, and it changed what was inside the wire at Nam Dong and nothing at Song Be. At Nam Dong a Ghostrider of the 16th Squadron from Da Nang, 50 kilometres away, was over the camp at 0305, thirty-five minutes after the first mortar rounds, in clear sky. The attackers who had broken through the outer perimeter were by then among the strikers' huts and could not be fired on, but the assault companies still forming in the treeline to the west and the mortar positions on the hill to the north could, and the 105mm and 30mm worked them for two and a half hours, until the attack broke off at about 0530 rather than at dawn. Donlon's inner perimeter held as it held historically. I put the strikers' and Nungs' dead at about 40 rather than 58, the two Americans and the Australian killed as historically because they fell in the first hour, and the attackers' dead at about 90–120, the video counting about 70 in the treeline. At Bien Hoa on 1 November the mortar team's rounds fell among the gunships as well as the B-57s: two Ghostriders of the 4th Squadron were hit on the ramp, one destroyed by fire and one out of service for six weeks, and from that night this headquarters asked for, and in March 1965 received with the Marines' and the Koreans' arrival, a ground force to hold the approaches to every gunship base. At Song Be the Ghostriders were over the town from 0115 on 11 May and fired through the night, but the losses had been taken in the first hour inside the wire, to mortars, recoilless rifles and sappers already among the defenders, where no aircraft could fire; the gunships broke the second assault at about 0400 and covered the Ranger battalion's landing at first light, and I do not adjust the allied losses¹³.

### No longer happens: Operation DRY SEASON: the Can Giuoc security section
*20 Jul – 18 Dec 1964 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be, Gia Dinh Province · EV012-2*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the operation stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The task force's first campaign was aimed at the men who had killed the title holders of Phuoc Lai. The Long An provincial security section and the Can Giuoc district committee's armed propaganda teams had killed 37 title holders and 9 land committee members between 9 June and 14 July, and the province had suspended titling in the two districts⁴. On 20 July the task force's III Corps task group, then about 180 strong, opened Operation DRY SEASON from a compound at Tan An under an American Special Forces major, Thomas R. Garvin, with a Special Branch captain, Nguyen Huu Phuoc, as his deputy. Its raid element was one Special Forces detachment, a SEAL platoon of SEAL Team One on loan from the Rung Sat, and the Long An Provincial Reconnaissance Unit of about 70 men. Its lift was three UH-1Bs and two UH-1Ds of the 120th Aviation Company, kept on call at Tan Son Nhut.
> 
> The first two months produced almost nothing. The task group had the Long An Special Branch's files, six months old and built on hamlets the police held by day only. The district centre at Can Giuoc did not yet exist. Of 19 operations in August and September, 14 found the target gone, 3 took a man the magistrate at Tan An released within 72 hours, and 2 took real cadres who knew nothing of the security section. The 2026 cycle was attempted and abandoned in the same weeks. The task group's American planners ran raids two and three nights running on targets the exploitation cell had not confirmed, and the magistrate released 11 of 17 detainees in September.
> 
> The turn came from a ledger. On 3 October a Rach Kien PF platoon ambushed a tax team on the canal at Long Huu and killed two men. One of them carried a notebook listing the district committee's monthly collections by hamlet, with a courier's route to the security section's base in the nipa swamps on the Nha Be edge of the Rung Sat. The exploitation cell had the notebook translated by morning. On the night of 5–6 October the SEAL platoon went up the Soai Rap in two STAB boats and a PBR borrowed from the Vietnamese Navy's river assault group. It inserted at the mouth of the Rach Ong Chuong and walked into the courier station at 0340. It took four men alive and a fifth was killed reaching for a K-50. One of the four was the security section's deputy chief, Ba Lien, who had commanded the Phuoc Lai killings. He was handed to Phuoc at Tan An at 0710 and before a magistrate on 7 October.
> 
> What Ba Lien told the interrogators, and what his papers told the exploitation cell, opened the section. Over the following ten weeks the task group mounted 41 operations in Can Giuoc, Can Duoc, Rach Kien and the Nha Be edge. They took 58 people on warrant, of whom the magistrates released 19, and killed 9, two of them men whom the Commission's audit in January could not show to be cadres. Of the security section's 23 members, 14 were dead, in prison or had rallied by 18 December. Its chief had gone to the Rung Sat proper, where the task group could not follow without a battalion. One PRU member and one SEAL were killed, the SEAL by a booby-trapped bunker at Ap Dong Thanh on 2 November.
> 
> Titling resumed in the eight Can Giuoc hamlets with PF posts in February 1965, two months earlier than on the course of memorandum 001. The other hamlets waited. The section was rebuilt by the spring of 1965 from cadres sent down from the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region, but the new men did not know the hamlets, and no title holder was killed in Can Giuoc in 1965¹⁴. DRY SEASON was a small operation that showed two things: the task force was worth nothing in its first two months, and it was worth a security section once it held one notebook.

### Changed: The Gulf of Tonkin incidents and the Southeast Asia Resolution
*2–11 Aug 1964 · Gulf of Tonkin and Washington · EV000-3*

*Initiative: both*

After the OPLAN 34A raids on Hon Me and Hon Ngu, three P-4 torpedo boats attacked USS *Maddox* on its DESOTO patrol in daylight on 2 August 1964; four F-8s from *Ticonderoga* hit the retiring boats, and Johnson chose a warning. At Admiral Sharp's request I moved the Global Hawk orbit into the Gulf on 3 August. On the night of 4 August *Maddox* and *Turner Joy* fired for two hours in thunderstorms at contacts they took for a second attack. Major Harold Kessling had the watch in the exploitation cell. His radar log, on the set that had tracked the three boats of 2 August from their base, showed the destroyers, a cluster of junks thirty miles west, rain cells, and no fast small craft within forty miles at any time between 2000 and 2330. Herrick cabled that the action left "many doubts"³⁴. The report reached Washington in the late morning, while McNamara and Sharp were still trying to learn what had happened, and McNamara told the President that afternoon that a radar which had watched the whole engagement contradicted the ships. Johnson held the strike order and at about 1900 cancelled it. Pierce Arrow was not flown, Richard Sather was not killed over Hon Gai, and Everett Alvarez was not taken prisoner that day²².

The resolution was sent anyway, on the real attack of 2 August alone. The debate ran three days longer than history's, and Congress passed it on 10 August, 414–0 and 85–3, in the historical words²². It was again the only legislative authority for the war, but it rested on an attack that had happened, and the radar log of 4 August sat in the files at Tan Son Nhut and Honolulu as a record of a false alarm, not as the concealed proof of a pretext.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> On 30–31 July 1964 South Vietnamese commando boats under the covert OPLAN 34A programme, run by MACV's Studies and Observations Group, raided the North Vietnamese islands of Hon Me and Hon Ngu. On 2 August the destroyer USS *Maddox*, on a DESOTO signals intelligence patrol under Captain John J. Herrick, was attacked in daylight by three P-4 torpedo boats of the 135th Torpedo Squadron. The *Maddox* fired, four F-8 Crusaders from USS *Ticonderoga* attacked the retiring boats, and the North Vietnamese lost four killed and six wounded with three boats damaged; the *Maddox* was struck by one machine-gun round and suffered no casualties. Johnson, as historically, chose a warning rather than retaliation, and ordered the patrol resumed with USS *Turner Joy* in company.
> 
> At Admiral Sharp's request I moved the Global Hawk orbit from the II Corps coast to the Gulf on 3 August. There were no SA-2s in the North and nothing that could reach 60,000 feet, and the aircraft took station about 40 nautical miles east of Hon Me, with the destroyers, the coast from Hon Matt to the mouth of the Song Ma and the open Gulf to the east in its radar's maritime mode²¹. On the night of 4 August the *Maddox* and *Turner Joy*, in rough weather with thunderstorms, fired for about two hours at radar contacts they took to be a second attack. The watch in the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut that night was Major Harold Kessling's. His radar log showed the two destroyers and their manoeuvres, a cluster of fishing junks about 30 nautical miles to the west, rain cells moving across the Gulf, and no fast small craft within 40 nautical miles of the ships at any time between 2000 and 2330 local. P-4 boats making attack runs at 40 knots are good radar targets even in a sea state of three and four, and the radar had tracked the three boats of 2 August from their base on the same set. Herrick cabled that the "entire action leaves many doubts". Kessling's report reached MACV at about midnight Saigon time and CINCPAC an hour later, which in Washington was the late morning of 4 August, while McNamara and Sharp were still trying to establish what had happened.
> 
> What followed was Washington's decision, and it went the other way from history. Historically Johnson had decided on retaliation within thirty minutes of the first reports³⁴. Here McNamara told him in the early afternoon that the ships' reports were contradicted by a radar that had watched the whole engagement, that Herrick himself doubted them, and that the Navy could not confirm an attack. Johnson held the strike order and, at about 1900, cancelled it. Operation Pierce Arrow was not flown. The 64 sorties against the torpedo-boat bases and the Vinh oil storage did not happen; Lieutenant (jg) Richard Sather was not killed over Hon Gai, and Lieutenant (jg) Everett Alvarez was not shot down and taken prisoner that day.
> 
> The resolution was sent anyway. Johnson had carried a draft since May, an election was three months away, and the attack of 2 August was real. On 5 August he asked Congress for authority to repel armed attack against US forces and to prevent further aggression, citing the 2 August attack on a US destroyer in international waters and Hanoi's support of the war in the South, and he said nothing of the night of the 4th. The debate ran three days longer than history's: Senator Wayne Morse, tipped about the 34A raids, asked why the destroyer had been near Hon Me at all, and Senator Gaylord Nelson's amendment against a land war was again declined by Senator Fulbright on the administration's assurance that no such war was intended. Congress passed the Southeast Asia Resolution on 10 August, 414–0 in the House and 85–3 in the Senate, in the words of the historical text²². Johnson signed it on 11 August. It was again the only legislative authority for the war that followed, but it rested on one attack that had happened rather than on two of which one had not, and the radar log of 4 August sat in the files at Tan Son Nhut and Honolulu as a record of a false alarm, not as the concealed proof of a pretext. B-57B bombers were moved to Bien Hoa in the aftermath³¹, within mortar range of the countryside around it.

### No longer happens: MACV-JSOC stands up and Delta arrives
*15 Aug – 31 Dec 1964 · Tan Son Nhut, Saigon; forward operating bases at Da Nang, Kontum, Bien Hoa and Can Tho · EV014-1*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the headquarters and Delta's first quarter stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> COMUSMACV's order of 15 August 1964 created the Joint Special Operations Command, Vietnam, eleven days after the second report from the Gulf of Tonkin that this war never answered with Pierce Arrow. Brigadier General Harold M. Vance, lately of the Special Warfare Center at Fort Bragg, took it with a staff that reached 280 by December and 390 by the following June: a joint targeting cell, a joint operations centre that stood a watch from 18:00 to 06:00, and nineteen liaison cells — MACV J-2 and J-3, MACV-SOG, the CIA station, the Combined Interagency Task Force and its National Fusion Centre, the combined command's operations centre, the 2nd Air Division, the four US corps-level commands and the four ARVN corps headquarters, the Joint General Staff, the National Police, the US Mission and the Embassy in Vientiane. The headquarters held no authority anyone else had held: it could command the units assigned to it, declare a restricted operating area over a hamlet for a night, and claim a target from the task force's deck. It could compel nothing outside MACV.
> 
> The 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta came in three lifts of MATS C-135Bs and C-124s from Pope Air Force Base between 28 August and 12 September 1964, 1,310 officers and men under Colonel James E. Teague, with 288 operators in four assault squadrons and G Squadron; E Squadron's unmarked light helicopters came by sea to Saigon port on 24 September and flew from Tan Son Nhut from 2 October. Three squadrons went forward to Bien Hoa, Can Tho and Da Nang and one stayed at Tan Son Nhut to rest and retrain, which is the rotation the unit kept for the next eight years and the reason its sustained rate was never what its first month suggested.
> 
> The first three months were learning and they were cheap. Thirty-one raids were mounted in the Saigon belt and the upper Delta between 11 October and 31 December, all of them on addresses from the task force's Gia Dinh and Long An files; nine reached a cadre the file had listed at district level or above, and nineteen found the house empty or the wrong man in it. Teague's men did not know the country: the Delta's canal lines, the way a hamlet's dogs work, which path a cadre takes when he runs. On 14 and 22 November the squadron at Bien Hoa tried the concept it had brought with it, a Delta troop as the entry force with a company of the 32nd Ranger Battalion as the cordon, at Phu Hoa Dong and at Trung Lap. Both times the cordon moved into position before midnight and both times the house was empty by the time the troop reached it, and on the second the Rangers' battalion had been given the hamlet's name the previous afternoon. The concept was abandoned in December and nothing replaced it: from then on Delta went in without a cordon and accepted that some of the men in the house would get into the dark. The unit's first dead was Sergeant First Class Donald R. Keel, shot through the throat at a doorway in Can Giuoc on 2 December 1964; two more operators were wounded in the same ten weeks¹⁵.

### Changed: Saigon's autumn of 1964: the Vung Tau Charter, the September coup and Hop Tac
*16 Aug 1964 – mid-1965 · Saigon, Hue and Da Nang; the Hop Tac ring of Gia Dinh, Bien Hoa and Long An Provinces · EVCP02-1*

*Initiative: neither*

Khanh tried to use the Tonkin crisis to make himself president under the Vung Tau Charter of 16 August 1964; students and Thich Tri Quang's Buddhists answered with riots, the charter was repealed, and a triumvirate of Khanh, Minh and Khiem followed. Before dawn on 13 September Generals Lam Van Phat and Duong Van Duc seized key points in Saigon with about ten battalions. In this war they had a programme: Phat's broadcast promised to "suspend the land decree pending review", dissolve the "foreign-controlled" Aid Compliance Board and restore the corps commanders' authority over the provinces, which meant abolishing the Selection Board. The Special Branch had reported battalions of the 7th Division readying at My Tho without orders on 11 September, the Saigon police stayed in their stations on Cuong's order, and Taylor told the plotters within hours that Washington would not recognise them⁶. Ky's jets and Thi's support saved Khanh, and the coup collapsed on 14 September without a death³⁵. Its failure attached the reforms to the side that won: the Young Turks around Ky and Thi took up the land decree and the Board as their own causes⁴.

Hop Tac, the oil spot applied to a ring around the capital, opened in September and had its battalions pulled away by every coup alert; by mid-1965 it was moribund, as historically³⁶. Here it carried the titling teams into Gia Dinh and Bien Hoa, where about 38,000 hectares were titled, and about 160 police posts were settled in the inner districts with chiefs from the list; the hamlets around the posts held at night through the coups even when the battalions left⁶. It could not save the programme. Pacification needed a stable government and a force that stayed in the hamlets at night, and in 1964 the Republic had only the beginning of the second.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> The autumn of 1964 is told here as one event, because the coup that failed in September is what left Hop Tac without its battalions. Khanh tried to use the Tonkin crisis to make himself president under the Vung Tau Charter of 16 August 1964; students and the Buddhist movement led by Thich Tri Quang answered with riots in Saigon, Hue and Da Nang, and the charter was repealed. The Military Revolutionary Council of 26–27 August could agree on no successor, and a triumvirate of Khanh, Minh and Khiem, dominated by Khanh, was formed; Khiem was sent to Washington as ambassador and Minh on a "goodwill tour". Before dawn on 13 September Generals Lam Van Phat and Duong Van Duc, with about ten battalions, four of them up from the Delta, seized key points in Saigon while Khanh took refuge in Da Lat. US officials backed Khanh, Ky flew jets low over the city and brought loyal marines and paratroopers into Tan Son Nhut, Thi supported him, and the plotters backed down on 14 September without a death. The lasting result was the Young Turks around Ky and Thi, who had saved Khanh and knew they could unmake him³⁵.
> 
> In this war the coup-makers had a programme as well as grievances. Duc had learned in August that the Commission had opened a case on the ghost payrolls the musters had found in IV Corps, and Phat's broadcast promised to "suspend the land decree pending review" and to dissolve the "foreign-controlled" Aid Compliance Board; it also promised to "restore the authority of the corps commanders over the provinces", which meant abolishing the Selection Board. It was the first coup to announce a policy toward the countryside, and the policy was the landlords'. The Special Branch had reported to Cuong on 11 September that battalions of the 7th Division were being readied at My Tho without orders, and Cuong passed the report to Khanh and the US Mission that night; on 13 September the Saigon police stayed in their stations and the Field Force companies in their barracks on his order, and Ambassador Taylor told the plotters within hours that the United States would not recognise them. The coup's failure attached the reforms to the side that won: the Young Turks took up the land decree and the Board as their own causes, and Ky spoke of the decree in his first public statements as an argument for their claim to govern.
> 
> In September, at the urging of the Mission and Westmoreland, the government launched Hop Tac, the "oil spot" applied to a ring around the capital, with the explicit priority of Saigon over everywhere else. Taylor's mission reported on 6 October that the provinces rated unsatisfactory had risen from 7 in July to 14 in August, named the diversion to Hop Tac as a possible cause, and recommended unanimously that it be given full support³⁶. Its ARVN units were pulled away by every coup and coup alert, its chain of command changed with each government, and by mid-1965 it was moribund, the infrastructure of Gia Dinh, Long An and the provinces north of the capital largely intact.
> 
> Here Hop Tac carried the titling teams into the inner ring of Gia Dinh and Bien Hoa, where about 38,000 hectares were titled by mid-1965, fewer families paid the Front's collectors without coercion, and volunteered reports rose from a trickle to a few dozen a month⁴. Gia Dinh, Bien Hoa and Long An received province chiefs from the list between May and July 1964, and about 160 police posts were settled in the inner districts by mid-1965, with a Special Branch section in each district town. The Special Branch broke two of the Front's village committees in Gia Dinh and the courier line from the Hoc Mon rice fields into the city's northern wards, and the hamlets around the posts were held at night through the coups even when Hop Tac's battalions were pulled away⁶. That did not save the programme, whose failure foreshadowed the war's: pacification needed a stable government and a force that stayed in the hamlets at night, and in 1964 the Republic had only the beginning of the second.

### Changed: Hanoi commits the regulars; the Trail and the first air war in Laos
*Sep 1964 – Apr 1965 · North Vietnam, the Laotian panhandle and the Central Highlands · EV000-6*

*Initiative: enemy*

The Ninth Plenum of December 1963 had resolved to win in the South before the United States could intervene in strength, and through 1964 Le Duan's Politburo acted on it. Group 559's infiltration shifted to northern conscripts, and the first complete PAVN regiments went south: the 95th Regiment of the 325th Division reached Kontum in December 1964 and the 101st followed in February with Colonel Nguyen Huu An³⁷. By the US estimate of 1965 about 4,500 men and 300 tons a month were moving through Laos. The decision predated the land decree, but the decree gave it a second argument: Party reporting called the "land trick" the most dangerous of the enemy's measures, because it threatened the movement's base where it was strongest⁴. The regiments came when their training and the Trail allowed, as they would have. Barrel Roll began on 14 December 1964 and Steel Tiger on 3 April 1965, bound by the fiction of Laotian neutrality and the ambassador's control of targets³⁸.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The Ninth Plenum of the Lao Dong Party Central Committee, in December 1963, had resolved to seek a decisive military victory in the South before the United States could intervene in strength. Through 1964 the Politburo under Le Duan acted on it. Infiltration down the Trail, managed since 1959 by the PAVN's Group 559, shifted from regrouped southerners to northern-born conscripts, and in the autumn of 1964 the first complete PAVN regular regiments were ordered south. The 95th Regiment of the 325th Division arrived in Kontum Province in December 1964; the 101st Regiment followed in February 1965 with the division commander, Colonel Nguyen Huu An; the 18th Regiment came a few months later. The division was then broken up among the B3 (Central Highlands) Front and Military Region 5³⁷. These were the first regular North Vietnamese formations committed to the war, and by the US estimate of 1965 about 4,500 PAVN troops and 300 tons of materiel moved through Laos each month. Both figures are intelligence estimates of their time; the movement was disciplined, at night, under canopy and through a country that US ground forces could not enter.
> 
> The decision to commit the regulars had been taken before the land decree existed, and it was not caused by it. The decree gave it a second argument. Party reporting from the Delta through 1964 described the "land trick" as the most dangerous of the enemy's measures, because it threatened the movement's base in exactly the provinces where it was strongest, and Le Duan's line that victory must come before the Americans and before the political base eroded drew strength from it. The schedule of the 325th Division's regiments was set by their training and by the Trail, not by the reform, and the regiments came when they would have come⁴.
> 
> The American answer in Laos began on 14 December 1964 with Operation Barrel Roll, a small programme of armed reconnaissance by US aircraft over northern and eastern Laos. On 3 April 1965 the 2nd Air Division opened Operation Steel Tiger against the Trail in the southeastern panhandle³⁸. Both were bound by the fiction of Laotian neutrality under the Geneva Accords of 1962, by the ambassador in Vientiane's control of targets, and by the bar on ground operations across the border. The Trail at this stage was still largely foot and bicycle traffic with truck routes being built; its capacity was growing faster than anything flying over it could reduce.

### No longer happens: The trawlers turn back; the Sihanoukville route opens
*Sep 1964 – Jun 1965 · Haiphong and the Gulf of Tonkin; the II Corps coast; Phnom Penh and Sihanoukville (Kompong Som), Cambodia · EV003-2*

*Merged at R05 into EV003-1; the change of route stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> Hanoi did not give up the sea at once. After TIDE TABLE's first half-year Group 125 paused through the summer of 1964, and in September, while the Global Hawk orbit was still held in the Gulf of Tonkin after the August crisis, it sent two trawlers south. One landed its cargo at Vung Ro on the night of 21–22 September in a gap the Gulf watch had opened on the II Corps coast; the other was tracked off Binh Dinh after the orbit returned, and was intercepted on 9 November by the Vietnamese Navy escort *Chi Lang* and a Junk Force division off the Tam Quan coast, where her crew beached and burned her. Sixteen of her crew were killed or drowned and four captured; the junk sailors lost two killed. Those are counts, and reliable. In December a third trawler reversed course off Quang Ngai at dusk when a Seventh Fleet destroyer closed her, and went home.
> 
> The decision to change routes was taken in Hanoi in December 1964 and January 1965. Party records captured later in this war describe the Central Military Commission's conclusion that "the enemy now sees every ship at sea by day and by night" and that the route was no longer worth the ships and the men. The alternative was already prepared. Sihanouk, who had renounced American aid in November 1963 and was moving toward China, would break diplomatic relations with Washington on 3 May 1965. Through the winter Chinese and North Vietnamese negotiators in Phnom Penh arranged the passage of "rice and commercial goods" through Sihanoukville, the port the French had built at Kompong Som, with a commission to Cambodian officers at each stage, and Cambodian trucking contractors to carry the cargo inland along Route 4 to Kompong Speu and thence to the border base areas. Historically this arrangement took shape in late 1966. Here the first arms cargo for the Front came ashore at Sihanoukville under a Chinese flag in late June 1965, about eighteen months early, and was trucked to the depots behind the Fishhook and the Parrot's Beak by night.
> 
> Two things followed from it that did not happen historically. The trawler that an Army helicopter pilot, Lieutenant James Bowers, found by chance unloading at Vung Ro Bay on 16 February 1965, with about 100 tons of arms aboard, was not there to be found; there was no trawler on the II Corps coast that month. And Market Time, which the Navy opened on 11 March 1965 historically because of Vung Ro, opened on the same date here because of TIDE TABLE's record, with a picture of what it was looking for and, increasingly, nothing to find²². The weapons the sea route would have landed in 1965 still reached the Front, more slowly and by a longer road, and from mid-1965 the enemy's principal line of supply to the southern half of the country ran through a neutral port that no American could stop or seize.

### New: Operation LONG SPAN: the floods of November 1964
*6 Nov 1964 – 15 Feb 1965 · Route 1 and the coastal railway from Da Nang to Quang Ngai; Quang Nam, Quang Tin and Quang Ngai Provinces · EV008-2*

*Initiative: neither*

In the first week of November 1964 two typhoons put the coastal plain of Quang Nam, Quang Tin and Quang Ngai under water, in the worst flood in living memory, with perhaps 7,000 dead and Route 1 cut at dozens of points. The Bien Hoa shops held a standard 30-metre truss span and a 12-metre girder span, cut about ninety more between 14 and 30 November, and sent them north by LST and coaster to Da Nang and the beach at Sa Huynh. Route 1 was open from Da Nang to Quang Ngai on 21 December, about two months sooner than spans from Okinawa would have reopened it. The rice of the Quang Ngai lowlands went north by truck in January, the relief reached Dien Ban and Duy Xuyen in December, and the Region 5 committee, which had planned its winter around a coast cut off, found the 2nd Division supplied by road¹². It changed no battle; Ba Gia was lost in May on ground the road did not decide.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> In the first week of November 1964 two typhoons and the rains behind them put the coastal plain of Quang Nam, Quang Tin and Quang Ngai under water, in the worst flood in central Vietnam in living memory; the dead were counted in thousands, by some Vietnamese accounts about 7,000, and Route 1 and the coastal railway were cut at dozens of points between the Hai Van pass and Quang Ngai. The ARVN 2nd Division in Quang Ngai and the province garrisons of the coast were cut off from Da Nang by road, and so were the rice and the relief.
> 
> In this war the bridges came back from Bien Hoa, in an operation the Directorate called LONG SPAN. The fabrication shops held a standard 30-metre steel truss span and a 12-metre girder span, drawn in 1963 for the outpost and road programme, and the Directorate had about forty of them in stock when the water fell. Between 14 and 30 November the shops cut and drilled about ninety more, and two Vietnamese Navy LSTs and three chartered coasters carried them from the Thu Duc yard to Da Nang and to the beach at Sa Huynh, where the 2nd Division's engineers and two Vietnamese contractor crews met them. Route 1 was open to the 2nd Division's trucks from Da Nang to Quang Ngai on 21 December, about six weeks after the flood and, by the Directorate's own estimate, two months sooner than spans ordered from Okinawa would have reopened it. The railway took longer, as it would have in any case, and its last bridge south of Tam Ky was not back until 15 February.
> 
> The ninety-day road became the Directorate's term for its standard: any bridge the Front or the weather took on a national route was to be back in ninety days, and on Route 1 it usually was. It changed no battle in Phase I. Ba Gia was lost in May on ground the road did not decide. What it changed was the winter of 1964–65 on the coast: the rice of the Quang Ngai lowlands went north by truck in January instead of rotting in the district towns, the relief reached the flooded districts of Dien Ban and Duy Xuyen in December instead of February, and the Front's Region 5 committee, which had planned its winter around a coast cut off until the dry season, found the 2nd Division supplied by road¹². On the historical course the flood was one of the reasons the coastal Centre was so nearly lost in the spring of 1965. Here it was a smaller one.

### No longer happens: The night under the cloud at Hoai Nhon
*14–15 Dec 1964 · The PF post at Tam Quan and the district town of Hoai Nhon, Binh Dinh Province; Qui Nhon airfield · EV015-2*

*Merged at R05 into EV015-1; the night at Tam Quan stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The night that ended the gunship's work below the cloud came in the first north-east monsoon of the war. At 2310 on 14 December the post at Tam Quan, on Route 1 north of Bong Son, called Hoai Nhon district that it was under attack by a company of the 2nd Regiment of the Front's Military Region 5. The cloud base over the coast was about 1,800 feet, with rain. Ghostrider 63 of the 14th Squadron, on station south of Qui Nhon, came north and found nothing on its turrets but the glow of the post's flares through the cloud. Its commander, Major Thomas R. Gaither, took the aircraft down through the overcast to 1,500 feet to see, as two crews of the squadron had done successfully in November.
>
