> He found the attack at once and it found him. The company had two 12.7mm machine guns sited on the paddy dikes south of the post, and they opened on the aircraft's first turn. The Ghostrider fired for about six minutes and broke the assault on the southern wall; in those minutes it took about thirty rounds of 12.7mm through the left wing and the fuel tanks, lost an engine and a hydraulic system, and was flown back to Qui Nhon on three engines with a fire in the wing that the fuel-tank protection kept from spreading. Two crewmen were wounded. The post at Tam Quan held until 0400, when the attack was renewed in the rain with no aircraft overhead, and fell; nineteen of its thirty men were killed or taken.
> 
> On 16 December the wing forbade attacks below 3,500 feet. From then on, on monsoon nights over the coast, the Ghostrider could give the posts of Binh Dinh, Quang Ngai and Quang Nam nothing but a GPS weapon on a coordinate the posts could not give it, and the Front's provincial units, which had believed since March that the aircraft saw through cloud, learned over the winter that it did not¹³. It was the provision's limit (D14), found in a night.

### Changed: Saigon's governments and the war in the city
*19 Dec 1964 – 19 Jun 1965 · Saigon · EVCP01-1*

*Initiative: both*

Six months of Saigon's politics were one process: the generals unmaking every government they made, while the Front's city teams struck where they chose. The Young Turks dissolved the High National Council before Christmas and Taylor dressed them down; on 24 December a car bomb under the Brink BOQ killed two Americans, and Johnson refused a reprisal³⁹. On 27 January 1965 Huong was removed, Quat became prime minister on 16 February, and after the failed coup of Phat and the communist agent Pham Ngoc Thao the council voted Khanh out; he left the country on 25 February³⁵. On 30 March a car bomb outside the embassy killed 22 people⁴⁰. On 12 June Quat gave power back to the generals, and Thieu became chief of state and Ky prime minister⁴¹. Each government that inherited the decrees of 1 January 1964 kept them, because Johnson's condition and the Board made repeal dearer than survival⁴.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> Six months of Saigon's politics are told here as one event, because they were one process: the generals unmaking every government they made, while the Front's city teams showed they could strike anywhere in the capital. In the week before Christmas 1964 the Young Turks, with Khanh's acquiescence, dissolved the High National Council and arrested several of its members; Taylor dressed the officers down, Khanh attacked him publicly, and the Mission's relations with the junta reached their lowest point. At 17:45 on 24 December a car bomb of about 90 kg under the Brink Bachelor Officers' Quarters killed two Americans and wounded about 60–100 people; Johnson refused a reprisal, saying he had "never felt that this war will be won from the air", and changed his mind within six weeks³⁹.
> 
> On 27 January 1965 Khanh and the Armed Forces Council removed Huong. On 16 February the council appointed Dr Phan Huy Quat prime minister, and on 19–20 February, in the confusion of a failed coup by General Lam Van Phat and Colonel Pham Ngoc Thao, who was a communist agent, it voted Khanh out; he left the country on 25 February³⁵. On 30 March a car carrying about 300 pounds of plastic explosive blew up outside the US embassy; 22 people were killed, among them two Americans, and 183 wounded. Rolling Thunder was already running, and there was no reprisal⁴⁰. On 12 June Quat, deadlocked with the chief of state Phan Khac Suu, handed power back to the generals; on 14 June Major General Nguyen Van Thieu became chief of state, and on 19 June Air Vice Marshal Nguyen Cao Ky prime minister⁴¹.
> 
> In this war the sequence ran on its historical dates and for its historical reasons. One thing in it was different: each government that inherited the decrees of 1 January 1964 kept them, because Johnson's condition of February 1964 and the Aid Compliance Board had made repeal dearer than survival, and the September plotters' promise to repeal them had attached the reforms to the Young Turks who defeated them⁴.

### Changed: The battle of Binh Gia
*28 Dec 1964 – 1 Jan 1965 · Binh Gia, Phuoc Tuy Province · EV000-9*

*Initiative: enemy*

The 271st and 272nd Regiments, the nucleus of the forming 9th Division, about 1,800 men, took the Catholic refugee village of Binh Gia on 28 December 1964 and waited for the relief. The ARVN fed in four Ranger battalions and the 4th Marine Battalion of the general reserve piecemeal, with artillery badly placed and air support thin, as historically. The new rifles did not change the generals' plan, and the plan was the problem. On 31 December the 4th Marines, going to recover the crew of a downed gunship, were ambushed in the rubber at 20 to 40 metres and lost their commander, Major Nguyen Van Nho, in the first minutes⁴².

What followed was different. Two of the four company commanders fell in the same minutes, and their first sergeants, schooled to count their men, build a base of fire and report before moving, took the companies; Master Sergeant Nguyen Van Thuoc put the 2nd Company's three squad guns on the trees and moved his platoons back by bounds⁷. The battalion closed into two perimeters within a quarter of an hour, the second held the 271st's assault at 1640, and the Marines fought out of the rubber at dusk carrying most of their wounded¹¹. Captain Donald Cook, their adviser, was captured going back for a wounded Marine, as historically⁴².

The battalion lost about 50–60 killed and 100 wounded, against 122 killed and 71 wounded historically; most of the difference is the squad guns that held the trees, and the rest is wounded men who came out because a sergeant counted them⁷. I put allied losses for the battle at about 130 killed against history's 201, and the enemy's dead at about 120–200⁴³. The form did not change: a Viet Cong formation held ground for four days against armour, artillery and helicopters, chose the field, ambushed the general reserve on the road it had to use and withdrew intact, and the 271st took the name "Binh Gia Regiment"⁴². The 4th Marines were back in the line in February.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> Binh Gia, a Catholic village of northern refugees in Phuoc Tuy Province east of Saigon, was the site of the Viet Cong's first large set-piece battle. The attackers were the 271st and 272nd Regiments (then called the 1st and 2nd), the nucleus of the forming 9th Division, with the 80th Artillery Detachment and local battalions of the B-2 Front, an estimated 1,800 men. They took the village on 28 December and then waited for the relief. The ARVN committed the 30th, 33rd, 35th and 38th Ranger Battalions and the 4th Marine Battalion of the general reserve, with two artillery platoons and a section of M24 tanks, about 4,300 men, lifted and supported by the US 118th Aviation Company and the gunships of the 68th Assault Helicopter Company. Every one of those battalions had carried the M4A1, the M249 and the M110A2 since the spring; the attackers carried Type 56 and SKS rifles, RPD guns and recoilless rifles.
> 
> The relieving battalions were fed in piecemeal, the artillery badly positioned and air support thin, as they were historically. The rifles did not change the generals' plan, and the plan was the problem. On 30 December a 68th Company gunship was shot down near Quang Giao and its four crewmen killed. On 31 December the 4th Marine Battalion, going to recover the bodies, was ambushed in the rubber by the 271st at a range of 20 to 40 metres, as it was historically, and its commander, Major Nguyen Van Nho, was killed in the first minutes. What followed was different. The battalion's squad guns, three to a company platoon, put a base of fire into the trees that the Marines' BARs could not have sustained, and the companies, instead of being cut apart in the order they had marched, closed into two perimeters within about a quarter of an hour and fought out of the rubber at dusk carrying most of their wounded. The battalion lost about 60–70 killed and 90 wounded, against 122 killed and 71 wounded on the historical course¹¹. Captain Donald Cook, the Marine adviser, was wounded and captured going back for a wounded Marine, as he was historically, and died in captivity. MACV counted allied losses from 28 December to 6 January at about 140 killed, 220 wounded and 45 missing⁴⁴. MACV reported four helicopters shot down. The VC claim of 1,783 killed and captured is no more credible here than it was historically; their own dead, of whom at least 32 were confirmed historically, I put at about 120–200, because the Marines' marksmen and squad guns killed men in the rubber whom the 271st could not carry away⁴⁵.
> 
> The significance was still the form. A Viet Cong formation had held ground for four days against armour, artillery and helicopters, chosen the field, ambushed the general reserve on the road it had to use, and withdrawn intact. The 271st took the honorific "Binh Gia Regiment"⁴². US observers concluded, as they did historically, that the ARVN could not defeat main-force units of this kind without American firepower; what they could not say, as they said historically, was that a Marine battalion of the general reserve had been destroyed. The 4th Marines were back in the line in February.
> 
> The sergeants did the rest. The 4th Marine Battalion's NCOs had all passed the courses for their grades at Nha Trang since 1957, and its platoon sergeants the senior course; when Major Nho fell, two of the four company commanders were hit in the same minutes, and the companies were taken over by their first sergeants, who had been taught in the leader's course to count their men, establish a base of fire and report before they moved. Master Sergeant Nguyen Van Thuoc of the 2nd Company put his three squad guns on the trees and moved his platoons back by bounds; the companies closed into their two perimeters about five minutes faster than they would have done, and the second perimeter held the 271st's assault at 1640 without falling back into the first. I put the battalion's loss at about 50–60 killed and 100 wounded, against the 60–70 killed and 90 wounded of the earlier course, and MACV's allied losses for the battle at about 130 killed rather than about 140; the difference is wounded men who came out because a sergeant counted them⁷. The battle's form, which the 271st chose, did not change.

### New: The red cards: Seoul, Canberra and the combined command
*8 Jan – 30 Jul 1965 · Seoul; Canberra; Saigon; Bien Hoa air base; Di An, Bien Hoa Province · EV012-3*

*Initiative: allied*

The allies' consent to combined command was tested when their troops arrived. In Seoul in January 1965 the defence minister told the National Assembly that the Dove Force would serve under the combined commander "for the tasks agreed between the governments and no others", which was the red card stated in public. Canberra gave Brigadier O. D. Jackson three conditions for the 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment: not broken up below company level, not employed in the Delta, and any operation expected to cost more than a stated number of casualties referred to Canberra. On 28 June, when the 173rd went into War Zone D, the battalion's casualty estimate went to Canberra overnight and came back approved by 0600; nothing required the delay, but the precedent did. On 23 July Lieutenant General Chae Myung-shin signed a combined agreement placing the Korean field forces under operational control within an agreed area of the II Corps coast, with every order to a Korean formation countersigned by a Korean officer, and told Westmoreland he would carry out every order he countersigned and countersign only the ones he would carry out. It was a Korean veto in practice, and still better than the historical arrangement for one reason: the seam between the Korean area and the 22nd Division's was planned by one staff instead of negotiated by two¹⁴.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The Korean and Australian governments' consent to combined command, stipulated by this headquarters' instructions, was tested when their troops arrived. In Seoul the National Assembly debated the dispatch of the Dove Force of engineers and a security battalion in January 1965. The opposition asked whether Korean soldiers would be commanded by Americans abroad as they had refused to be commanded at home in matters of domestic order. President Park's defence minister, Kim Sung-eun, answered that they would be under the combined commander's operational control "for the tasks agreed between the governments and no others". That was the red card, stated in public. The Dove Force reached Di An in March under a Korean brigadier, and it took combined orders for its construction tasks without dispute, because it had no others to take²⁰.
> 
> The Australians had already given their consent at a price. When 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment arrived at Bien Hoa in June 1965 and joined the 173rd Airborne Brigade, Canberra's instructions to Brigadier O. D. Jackson, commanding Australian Army Force Vietnam, set three conditions on the combined command. The battalion would not be broken up below company level. It would not be employed in the Delta. And any operation expected to cost it more than a stated number of casualties would be referred to Canberra. The third condition was the one the combined staff had not expected. It meant that a combined order to the Australian battalion carried a casualty estimate, and that the estimate went to a capital. On 28 June, when the 173rd went into War Zone D, the combined staff's estimate for the battalion's part was sent to Canberra overnight and approved by 0600. Nothing in the operation required the delay. The precedent did.
> 
> The Koreans' combat consent was the larger question, and it was settled on paper in July. The working arrangement that historically gave the Koreans MACV's support without American command (6 September 1965) was replaced here by a combined agreement of 23 July²⁰. It placed the Korean field forces under the combined commander's operational control within an agreed area of responsibility on the II Corps coast, gave the Korean commander a right to refer any order outside that area to Seoul, and required a Korean officer to countersign any combined order to a Korean formation. Lieutenant General Chae Myung-shin signed it in Saigon. He told the combined commander, General William C. Westmoreland, that he would carry out every order he countersigned and countersign only the ones he would carry out.
> 
> That sentence defined the Korean contingent for the rest of the war. It was operational control in name and a Korean veto in practice. The combined staff learned to write orders for the Korean divisions that the Korean commander had already agreed to. It was, I judge, a better arrangement than the historical one for exactly one reason: the Koreans' orders and the ARVN's now came from the same plan, so that the seam between the Korean area and the ARVN 22nd Division's was planned by one staff instead of negotiated by two¹⁴.

### Changed: The American escalation: Flaming Dart, the opening strike, the Marines and the July decision
*7 Feb – 28 Jul 1965 · Pleiku and Qui Nhon; North Vietnam; Da Nang; Washington · EVCP01-2*

*Initiative: both*

Each step of the six months made the next one. At 0150 on 7 February 1965 the 409th Sapper Battalion hit Camp Holloway and the Pleiku advisers' compound, killing seven Americans; Flaming Dart struck Dong Hoi within twelve hours, and again after the Qui Nhon billet was blown up on 10 February with 23 Americans dead⁴⁶. What the President approved on 13 February was not history's "measured and limited air action". The theater's plan had been on his desk since the autumn: the Joint Chiefs' 94 targets extended by the Combined Targeting Cell with the North's command centres, radars, power and bulk fuel, run from Saigon without zones or pauses, with a 15-mile buffer on the Chinese border and one strike on Haiphong's port. Johnson kept the decision whether to bomb and its date, and gave the rest. Rolling Thunder opened on 2 March with HAMMER FALL, and the targets in every route package came from Tan Son Nhut rather than the Tuesday lunch⁸.

On 8 March the 9th Marine Expeditionary Brigade landed at Da Nang to guard the air base; on 1 April the President allowed it into combat, and on 6 May it became the III Marine Amphibious Force⁴⁷⁴⁸. On 7 June Westmoreland asked for a major reinforcement, and on 28 July Johnson announced, at a midday press conference, that US strength would rise from 75,000 to 125,000, the draft would double, and the Airmobile Division would deploy, without the reserves or new taxes⁴⁹. The ground war's steps came on their historical dates for their historical reasons. The July decision rested on Ba Gia and Dong Xoai, not on anything in the North, which by then had already lost what history spent two and a half years taking from it⁸.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> The six months in which the United States went from an advisory war to a war of its own are told here as one event, because each step made the next one. At 01:50 on 7 February 1965, while McGeorge Bundy was in Saigon and Kosygin in Hanoi, about 300 men of the 30th Company of the VC 409th Sapper Battalion attacked Camp Holloway and the advisers' compound at Pleiku, killing seven Americans and wounding 104 and destroying 10 aircraft. About twelve hours later 49 aircraft from the *Coral Sea* and the *Hancock* struck the barracks at Dong Hoi, the first strike of Flaming Dart; after the VC blew up the enlisted billet at Qui Nhon on 10 February and killed 23 Americans, about 160 aircraft struck Chanh Hoa and Chap Le⁴⁶. Bundy's report of 7 February argued for "sustained reprisal", and the administration accepted it.
> 
> What the President approved on 13 February was not history's "measured and limited air action" south of the 19th parallel. In this war the theater's plan had been on his desk since the autumn: the Joint Chiefs' list of 94 targets of August 1964, extended by the MACV Combined Targeting Cell with the North's command centres, radars, power plants and bulk fuel, and a request that the campaign be run from Saigon, without zones around Hanoi and Haiphong and without pauses, with a buffer of 15 miles along the Chinese border and one strike on Haiphong's port. Johnson kept two things: the decision whether the bombing would happen at all, and its date. He gave the rest. Rolling Thunder opened on 2 March, history's date, with the opening strike of Operation HAMMER FALL on the whole list in place of history's 104 USAF aircraft at Xom Bang; the 19 VNAF A-1s still struck the naval base at Quang Khe that day, as they had historically⁵⁰. The route packages divided the North between the services from the spring, as historically, but the targets in every package came from Tan Son Nhut, not from the President's Tuesday lunch.
> 
> On 8 March Battalion Landing Team 3/9 came ashore at Da Nang and BLT 1/3 flew in from Okinawa, the nearly 5,000 men of the 9th Marine Expeditionary Brigade under Brigadier General Frederick J. Karch, to guard the air base that Rolling Thunder needed and the Bien Hoa attack had shown to be vulnerable. Their orders, that they "will not, repeat will not, engage in day-to-day actions against the Viet Cong", lasted three weeks: on 1 April the President approved their use in active combat and 18,000–20,000 more support troops, and on 6 May the brigade became the III Marine Amphibious Force⁴⁷⁴⁸.
> 
> On 7 June Westmoreland asked for a major reinforcement and by 22 July the President had authorized 44 battalions⁵¹. On 28 July, at a midday press conference rather than before Congress, Johnson announced that US strength would rise at once from 75,000 to 125,000, with more as requested, that monthly draft calls would rise from 17,000 to 35,000, and that the Airmobile Division would deploy; the reserves were not called and no new taxes were sought⁴⁹. Westmoreland's concept behind it, to halt the losing trend in 1965, take the offensive in 1966 and then destroy the enemy's main forces and base areas, committed the United States to attrition against an enemy who controlled his losses by deciding when to fight.
> 
> The ground war's steps came on their historical dates for their historical reasons. The air war over the North did not. Its opening came on history's day and its shape was the theater's, and by the July decision the North had already lost what history spent two and a half years taking from it. Nothing in that loss changed the decision of 28 July, which was driven by the ARVN's defeats of May and June at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and not by anything in the North⁸.

### No longer happens: Operation NIGHT HERON: the Long An province committee
*9 Feb – 18 Apr 1965 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be, Gia Dinh Province · EV014-2*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the operation stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> NIGHT HERON was the first operation that showed what the unit was for, and it was built on a file three other provisions had made. The task force's DRY SEASON campaign had broken the Can Giuoc security section from a notebook in December 1964; the section's papers named a courier, the courier's family was in the Special Branch's census, and the land register said whose house he slept in. What none of that could do was reach the eleven men of the Long An province committee, who met every third or fourth week at a sampan mooring on the Rach Cat where no police patrol had been since 1962.
> 
> Two men of G Squadron lay in the nipa palm 240 metres from the mooring for four nights between 9 and 23 February and for three more in March, counted the arrivals, and photographed six of them at ranges under 300 metres with a starlight-assisted camera. On the night of 14–15 March 1965 two assault teams and a Special Branch inspector came in by three of E Squadron's helicopters to a paddy 900 metres east, walked in on goggles, and took the mooring at 02:40. Six of the eleven committee members were there, with the province finance section's ledgers for 1964 and a list of the collectors in nineteen villages; two cadre who reached for weapons were killed, the committee's secretary got into the Rung Sat with the political officer, and one Delta operator was shot through the forearm. The task force's exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut read the ledgers by 06:00 and the arrests ran for nine days: twenty-three collectors and two village committees taken on Special Branch warrants, with magistrate review in each case inside 72 hours under the 1964 statute.
> 
> Long An's collections from the posted villages of the three districts fell by about two-thirds through the summer of 1965 and were about a third of the previous year's by December, which cost the Front both money and the rice it bought with it in a province where the titling had already ended rent¹⁵. The secretary rebuilt the committee from the Rung Sat by August with cadres sent down from the region, as the Can Giuoc section had been rebuilt before it. What did not come back was the mooring: the committee never again met in a place a boat could reach from a hamlet with a post.

### New: Operation HAMMER FALL: the opening strike on the North
*2–9 Mar 1965 · Phuc Yen airfield, Hanoi (Bach Mai, the Citadel, Yen Phu, Duc Giang and the Paul Doumer bridge), Haiphong port and Thuong Ly, Nam Dinh, the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa, Vinh; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; Yankee Station; Korat and Takhli, Thailand · EV013-1*

*Initiative: allied*

The strike was a year in the making, and it began in a Quonset hut. On 3 March 1964 Major Edwin T. Sorrell, a geodesist, opened a coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut to turn the U-2S's GPS-true imagery into points a GBU-31 could fly to, each measured to a few metres and filed with its photographs. Its first discovery was that every map in the country was wrong: the 1:50,000 sheets were drawn on the Indian 1960 datum, and in the panhandle's mountains some crossings lay 300 metres or more from where the map put them. Sorrell's memorandum of 14 May 1964 said what the cell would enforce for a decade: "No coordinate taken from a map is to be given to a guided weapon, and no coordinate given to a guided weapon is to be plotted on a map without conversion"²⁷. By June 1965 the cell held about 1,400 folders on the panhandle and the North below the 20th parallel, at the cost of a quarter to a third of the U-2S's hours²⁶. The B-52Js of the 3960th Strategic Wing trained on Guam from the spring of 1964 against coordinates the cell sent them, and for sixteen months struck nothing; the aircraft were ready and the authority was not.

After the false alarm of 4 August the cell was given the North above the 20th parallel, and Brigadier General Walter E. Pruitt built a Combined Targeting Cell around it with Captain Harlan J. Reese for the Navy. To the Joint Chiefs' 94 targets it added the air defence command at Bach Mai, the Ministry of Defence in the Citadel, the transmitters, the radars, the power plants and the bulk fuel, about 760 aim points in all by February 1965. On the night of 2–3 March the crachin sat at 800–1,500 feet and nothing but the bombers could strike. Twenty-four B-52Js left Andersen in cells of three and released from 36,000–40,000 feet between 2340 and 0115. The first cells put GBU-38s on Phuc Yen's runways and revetments and wrecked 22–26 of the 921st Fighter Regiment's 36 MiG-17Fs; then the radars; then the penetrators on Bach Mai, the Citadel and Me Tri; then the Yen Phu and Haiphong power stations, the tank farms at Duc Giang and Thuong Ly, two spans of the Paul Doumer bridge, and the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa. The last target was Haiphong's port, its one strike: about forty cranes destroyed and none of the fourteen ships alongside struck, and Hanoi gave the International Control Commission a figure of 214 port workers killed⁸.

No B-52J was lost or hit; the guns fired blind into cloud at aircraft five miles above them. When the cloud lifted on 4 and 7 March the carriers and the F-105Ds from Thailand struck Kep, the rail yards and Thai Nguyen and lost seven aircraft to the guns, and two more cells restruck the Doumer bridge and the Haiphong power plant on 6 March, the first orders of the restrike watch. By 9 March the North had lost about 70–80 percent of its generating capacity, most of its bulk fuel, its great bridges, its only jet base and most of its fighters, its warning net and the cranes of its only deepwater port; its air defence command worked from provincial switchboards for three weeks. No member of the Politburo was hurt, because General Van Tien Dung's staff had worked from Hoa Lac since February, and the North's civilian dead were 800–1,500 by this command's estimate⁸. The trucks of Group 559, the porters in the panhandle and the regiments in the South noticed nothing at all.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The plan began on 5 August 1964, the morning after the false alarm in the Gulf that this war never answered with Pierce Arrow. Major Edwin T. Sorrell's coordinate cell at Tan Son Nhut, which had measured the panhandle since March, was given the North above the 20th parallel, and Brigadier General Walter E. Pruitt of the 2nd Air Division was sent to build a MACV Combined Targeting Cell around it, with Captain Harlan J. Reese of CINCPAC's staff as his deputy for the Navy. The Joint Chiefs' study of 24 August gave them 94 targets in five categories, airfields, lines of communication, military installations, industry and the routes of armed reconnaissance. The cell added what the list held thinly: the Air Defence–Air Force Command and its operations centre at Bach Mai, the Ministry of Defence and General Staff in the Citadel, the national radio transmitters at Me Tri, the long-haul exchanges, the early-warning radars, the Yen Phu and Haiphong power plants and the transformer stations between them, and the bulk fuel at Duc Giang, Thuong Ly, Nam Dinh and Vinh. By February 1965 the U-2S had imaged every one of them under the standing condition's satellite link, and the cell held about 760 desired points of impact, each measured to a few metres.
> 
> The President's order of 13 February set the day as 2 March. The crachin set the hour. On the night of 2–3 March the cloud over the Red River delta sat at about 800–1,500 feet with drizzle, and nothing but the bombers could strike (§1.1 D4 of memorandum 013). Twenty-four B-52Js of the 7th and 320th Bombardment Wings left Andersen in cells of three from 15:00 local time, flew about 2,200 nautical miles to entry points over the Gulf of Tonkin, and released from 36,000–40,000 feet between 23:40 and 01:15, from up to fifteen miles out. The order of the night was fixed by what could fight back. The first two cells put 70 GBU-38s on Phuc Yen's runway intersections and its 38 revetments, and destroyed or wrecked 22–26 of the 921st Fighter Regiment's 36 MiG-17Fs on the ground; eight that were on alert in the northern dispersal survived, and two of them flew to Kep at first light. The third cell struck the early-warning radars at Bach Mai, Phu Ly and Kep and the four fire-control radars the cell had located, all with GBU-38. Then the penetrators: twelve GBU-31(V)3/Bs on the Bach Mai operations centre, sixteen on the Ministry of Defence buildings in the Citadel, eight on the Me Tri transmitters. Then the fixed economy: the Yen Phu power station and Haiphong's, the transformer yards at Dong Anh and Thai Binh, the tank farms at Duc Giang and Thuong Ly, two spans of the Paul Doumer bridge over the Red River, the Ham Rong bridge at Thanh Hoa with twenty penetrators on its abutments and central pier, and the rail and road bridges at Nam Dinh, Ninh Binh and Phu Ly.
> 
> The last target of the night was Haiphong's port, its one strike. At dusk the Gulf watch had counted fourteen ships in the port, among them three Soviet, two Polish and one British freighter alongside the main quay. Six Js put 120 GBU-31(V)1/Bs on the gantry and portal cranes, the transit sheds and warehouses behind the coal quay, the port's substation and the lighter basin, and none on the berths with ships alongside. The British *Dartford* lost her gangway and a lifeboat to blast; no seaman of any flag died. The port's cranes, about forty of them, were destroyed or toppled; the North's own figures, given to the Polish member of the International Control Commission, were 214 port workers killed.
> 
> No J was lost or hit. The guns of the delta, about 1,500–2,100 of them, 37mm and 57mm, fired blind into cloud at aircraft five miles above their reach. The second wave flew on the first days the cloud lifted, 4 and 7 March: alpha strikes of 30–40 aircraft from the *Hancock* and the *Ranger* on Kep, Gia Lam and the guns around the struck bridges, and F-105D packages from Korat and Takhli with F-100D flak suppression on the Hanoi and Haiphong rail yards, Thai Nguyen's blast furnace under construction and the Viet Tri chemical works. The MiG-17s that had reached Kep rose on 7 March and lost two to F-8Es; the guns, now firing at aircraft under the cloud, shot down four F-105Ds, two A-4Cs and an F-8E in the week, with three pilots killed, two captured and two recovered at sea. Two more cells of Js restruck the Doumer bridge and the Haiphong power plant on 6 March on the U-2S's imagery of the 5th, the first orders of the restrike watch.
> 
> By 9 March the North had lost, on this command's count checked against the U-2S, about 70–80 percent of its generating capacity, most of its bulk fuel in storage, the Doumer, Ham Rong and Nam Dinh bridges, its only jet base and most of its jet fighters, its warning net, and the cranes of its only deepwater port. Hanoi radio was off the air for nine hours and its air defence command was in the provincial switchboards for three weeks. No member of the Politburo or the Central Military Commission was killed or, as far as anyone in Saigon could tell, inconvenienced; the Ministry's buildings had been empty but for duty officers, and General Van Tien Dung's staff had worked from Hoa Lac since February. The North's civilian dead of the week, by Hanoi's count given in Geneva in April, were about 1,700; this command's own estimate was 800–1,500, most in Hanoi and Haiphong. The trucks of Group 559, the porters in the panhandle and the Front's regiments in the South noticed nothing at all⁸.

### No longer happens: The restricted area over Trung Lap
*7 March 1965 · Trung Lap and Phu Hoa Dong, Hau Nghia Province · EV014-9*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the incident and the rule it produced stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The provision's first near-disaster was procedural and it is worth one event, because the procedure is most of what the new headquarters was for. On the night of 7 March 1965 an assault team raided a house at Trung Lap on a Hau Nghia file. MACV-JSOC's operations centre declared a restricted operating area of two kilometres' radius for four hours and passed it, as its standing procedure required, to the ARVN 25th Division, the province chief, the sector adviser and the combined command's III Corps centre. It did not reach the Popular Forces platoon at the post 1,400 metres away, because the sector's night net closed at 22:00 and the platoon, at a post outside the held belt whose platoons had carried their own PRC-10s since April 1964, had no radio of its own until the Go Vap sets arrived later that year²⁸. The platoon heard helicopters and small-arms fire at 01:50 inside its own village, stood to, and its leader took a squad up the hamlet path toward the noise. Delta's team, coming out with a prisoner, identified the squad at about 120 metres through goggles and went flat in a ditch until it passed; nobody fired.
> 
> Vance changed the procedure within the week: from 15 March a restricted area was passed down to the platoon holding the ground or it was not declared, which in the first year cancelled eleven raids outright¹⁵. The incident is the clearest statement in the record of what the headquarters' deconfliction duty costs and buys. It buys the lives of the men on both ends of a hamlet path. It costs eleven targets in a year, and it is the reason a provision that needs a secret needs a joint headquarters more than it needs another squadron.

### No longer happens: Operation STILL WATER
*8 Mar – 30 Jun 1965 · Hoc Mon and Go Vap Districts, Gia Dinh Province, inside the Hop Tac ring northwest of Saigon · EV006-2*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-3; the operation stands as told there, with R04's correction kept.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> STILL WATER was the first operation in the war aimed at a district committee rather than at the hamlets beneath it, and it was the case for the method. By February 1965 Hoc Mon had 11 village posts settled under the police decree, a Popular Forces platoon in each, about 70 percent of its families on the census, and a district chief from the first list, Major Pham Van Truc; the Front's hamlet cells in the posted villages had mostly been arrested or had left. What remained was the Hoc Mon district committee of the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region, about 14 members with a security section, a finance section and about 40 couriers, which had moved in January into the hamlets along the Saigon River at the district's northern edge, toward the Ben Cat and Cu Chi base areas, and governed the posted villages from there by messenger. The DIOCC at Hoc Mon, opened in July 1964 under Captain Ngo Van Tam of the Special Branch with 12 staff and two American advisers, had by February a chart of that committee with 31 names, 19 of them confirmed on three sources, built from 44 arrests, 23 ralliers and a cache of finance-section receipts found by a PF patrol in December.
> 
> The operation was Tam's plan, approved by Truc and by the Gia Dinh province chief on 1 March. It used no regular troops. Two Police Field Force companies and the Gia Dinh PRU of about 80 men made the arrests; the Regional Forces companies of Hoc Mon and Go Vap, with M4A1 carbines and the BARs that the territorials kept as their automatic rifles, held the cordons at night²⁴; a reaction platoon of the Gia Dinh sector and two UH-1Bs of the 120th Aviation Company stood by at Tan Son Nhut for the reaction; and every arrest went first to the biometric kit and then to a magistrate within 72 hours. Captain Whitcomb's counterpart in the next province was not involved; the American subsector adviser at Hoc Mon, Captain Luis Arredondo, was, and by the rule of the decree he did not go on the raids (EC006-13 abandoned).
> 
> The turn came on the night of 26–27 March. A finance-section courier arrested on 19 March, a woman of 19 who carried tax receipts in the hem of a conical hat, rallied on the 24th after the Chieu Hoi officer offered her brother's release from a prison on Con Son, to which he had been sent in 1962 under Diem without trial, and named the house in Tan Thoi Nhi where the committee's security section met twice a month. The PRU went in at 0300 under a moon nearly full with two Police Field Force platoons in the cordon. Four men were taken alive in the house, including the section's deputy chief, with a steel box of informant reports on the posts of four villages; a fifth was killed in the paddy behind it after firing on the cordon with a K-50 sub-machine gun; one PRU member died. The box named nine of the committee's own informants inside the posted villages, three of them PF soldiers.
> 
> By 30 June the operation had arrested 63 people on warrant, of whom the magistrates released 17; 9 of the committee's 14 members were dead, in prison or had rallied, 2 of them killed resisting arrest; the remaining five had moved north into Cu Chi. The Commission's first audit sample, drawn in July from STILL WATER's files, found 4 of the 63 arrests unsupported and the release of one man already paid for, and sent both cases to the Special Court. The Front did not rebuild the Hoc Mon committee inside the district; it governed Hoc Mon from Cu Chi until 1968, and the tax receipts captured in 1966 showed collections in the district's posted villages at about a fifth of 1964's⁹. In this war STILL WATER was a small operation, 63 arrests and three deaths in four months, and it changed the war in one particular: it showed the Front that the government could follow its leaders out of the villages it had cleared, three years before the historical Phoenix tried to.

### No longer happens: Moscow, Beijing and the rebuilt sky
*10 Mar – 31 Jul 1965 · Moscow; Beijing; Hanoi; the frontier crossing at Pingxiang and Dong Dang; the airfields of Mengzi and Ningming in Yunnan and Guangxi · EV013-2*

*Merged at R05 into EVCP02-2; the answer of the three capitals stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The answer to HAMMER FALL was decided in three capitals, and each decided for its own reasons. In Hanoi the Politburo under Le Duan, at its meeting of 25–27 March, ordered the North onto a war footing, the dispersal of every factory, depot and fuel store that could be moved, and a militia of the whole people for air defence and repair; and, reading the strike as the preparation for a landing, held the 308th and 312th Divisions and two regiments of the 320th in the delta and on the coast through the summer instead of preparing them for the South. In Moscow, Brezhnev and Kosygin, whose premier had left Hanoi on 10 February promising help, accelerated the air-defence package: SA-2 equipment for four battalions instead of two by July, about 1,000 advisers and technicians, MiG-21F-13s for the autumn, and diesel generators, pumps and trucks in place of the heavy plant the North had asked for in 1964. In Beijing, Mao and Zhou Enlai sent Chinese railway, engineer and anti-aircraft troops into the North from June, earlier and in larger numbers than they had historically, and placed three anti-aircraft divisions along the northeast and northwest railways, some inside the 15-mile buffer the Americans had left.
> 
> <!-- initiative -->Beijing's own decision, taken for its own reasons, slowed Moscow's. In April Moscow asked for an air corridor across China for Antonov transports carrying SA-2 equipment and its crews, and for the use of two airfields in Yunnan; the Chinese leadership refused both, as it did historically, and required every Soviet shipment to cross China by rail under Chinese escort and at Chinese pace. The refusal had nothing to do with the opening strike. It came from Beijing's quarrel with Moscow over the leadership of the communist world, and from Mao's suspicion that a Soviet presence in Yunnan was a Soviet presence on China's frontier. Its effect was that the first Soviet battalions of SA-2 reached Hanoi in late April and May by train through Pingxiang, three to five weeks later than Moscow had promised and with about a fifth of their equipment held at the border for inspection. The VPAF was given what Moscow could not use: its surviving MiG-17s and their pilots were moved to Mengzi and Ningming in China to train and re-form, and from the autumn its regiments flew into the North from Chinese fields to fight and back to rest.
> 
> By the end of July the North had about 2,500–3,000 guns rather than history's rising count, four SA-2 battalions in the Hanoi area rotating among about twenty prepared sites, and a fighter force that lived in China. Its fuel was in drums under the trees, its power in about 700 village diesels from the Soviet shipments, and its bridges were pontoons by night. It had begun to pay for the war in labour: perhaps 300,000–400,000 people were repairing, carrying and manning guns full time by July, a year before history's figure reached that size. Its rice imports from China were promised for the autumn, about 200,000 tons for 1966⁸.

### Changed: The air war of 1965: the rebuilt sky, the Thanh Hoa Bridge, the missiles and the first Arc Light
*10 Mar – 27 Jul 1965 · Hanoi, Moscow and Beijing; Pingxiang and the airfields of Mengzi and Ningming; Thanh Hoa (Ham Rong) and the Hanoi region; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; Ben Cat, Binh Duong Province · EVCP02-2*

*Initiative: both*

The answer to HAMMER FALL was decided in three capitals, each for its own reasons. On 25–27 March the Politburo put the North on a war footing, dispersed every factory, depot and fuel store it could move, raised a militia of the whole people for air defence and repair, and, reading the strike as the preparation for a landing, held the 308th and 312th Divisions and two regiments of the 320th at home through the summer. Moscow doubled the SA-2 package and sent diesels, pumps and trucks; Beijing sent railway, engineer and anti-aircraft troops earlier and in greater numbers than historically⁸.

<!-- initiative -->Beijing's own decision, taken for its own reasons, slowed Moscow's. In April it refused the Soviets an air corridor and two Yunnan airfields, as it did historically, and made every Soviet shipment cross China by rail at Chinese pace. The refusal had nothing to do with the strike; it came from the quarrel over the leadership of the communist world and Mao's suspicion of a Soviet presence on his frontier. The first SA-2 battalions reached Hanoi through Pingxiang three to five weeks late, with a fifth of their equipment held at the border, and the VPAF's surviving MiG-17s re-formed at Mengzi and Ningming, to fight from Chinese fields that autumn⁸.

The Ham Rong bridge, which history's 79-aircraft package under Lieutenant Colonel Robinson Risner failed to drop on 3 April, had been in the river since March; Risner's wing flew instead against the pontoons upstream, and the U-2S's dawn pass found each new pontoon for a strike within a day or two⁵². The first SA-2 site was imaged on 22 March and the first Fan Song heard on 18 April; each site was struck within 24–48 hours of its first image, and the North answered by preparing three or four sites for every battalion, history's answer brought forward a year. The first American aircraft lost to an SA-2 fell on 22 August rather than 24 July. Over the five months about 60–75 American aircraft were lost over the North, against perhaps 85–100 in history's same months, nearly all to guns at low level⁵³. By the end of July the North had 2,500–3,000 guns, four SA-2 battalions rotating among about twenty sites, its fighters in China, its fuel in drums, its power in about 700 village diesels, its bridges in pontoons by night, and 300,000–400,000 people repairing and carrying full time, a year before history's figure reached that size⁸.

The first Arc Light, on 18 June, was flown by thirty B-52Js from Andersen without tankers, so the collision that killed eight crewmen historically did not happen. Two aircraft put twenty GBU-31s each on four structures the U-2S had imaged near Ben Cat and found huts empty for days, and the rest found what history found²⁷. The press called it a sledgehammer swung at flies, now accurate to a few metres. It was the find-and-fix problem in its purest form, and the J changed none of it. By July the B-52's war had two halves: over the North a bomber that had destroyed in a week what history's fighter-bombers spent years on, and over the South a bomber that found nothing under the canopy⁸.

### No longer happens: The Vinh Long suspension
*6 Apr – 11 May 1965 · Vinh Long Province · EV001-5*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-2; the suspension stands as told there.*

The Commission documented 26 cases from the tenants' complaints to the land court on circuit and from the American province adviser's reports, and on 2 February 1965 sent them to the Ministry of the Interior with 30 days to act. Nothing was done; Saigon was occupied with the fall of Khanh. On 6 April the Aid Compliance Board suspended the release of counterpart piasters to Vinh Long Province. >

### Changed: The battle of Ba Gia
*28–31 May 1965 · Ba Gia, Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province · EV000-17*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 29 May 1965 the VC 1st Regiment of the forming 2nd Division, directed by Major General Chu Huy Man, overran the outpost at Loc Tho near Ba Gia and ambushed the 1st Battalion, 51st Regiment as it came to help⁵¹. Historically the battalion was destroyed. Here it was cut in two on the road and lost its headquarters in the first half hour, and its company commanders, lieutenants and captains of the educated classes of 1959–62, brought the other three companies onto the ridge north of the road, set the squad guns and called the battalion's mortars onto the paddy below; about 280 men came back to Quang Ngai over two days. I Corps sent a task force forward piecemeal. The 2nd Battalion, 51st, under Major Le Van Tri, one of the board's first selections, moved to Phuoc Loc with a company on the high ground each side of the road and was hit in the flank rather than in column¹⁰. On the night of 30–31 May the 3rd Marines held a moat line with nine M249s firing under illumination while their marksmen took the 40th Battalion's machine-gun teams at 300–400 metres¹¹. The VC withdrew at dawn.

I put the ARVN's losses at about 75 killed, 110 wounded and 190 captured or missing, against 107, 123 and 367 historically, and its weapons lost at about 230 rather than 384, most of them carbines that the 2nd Division's local battalions were firing within the month⁵⁷. The squad guns and the officers who placed them share the difference, and it is counted once. Ba Gia was still a defeat. The decisions that lost it were taken above both battalions by men who had never been before a board, the corps pulled its task force back to Quang Ngai, and by 3 June the VC held much of the north of the province; on 5 July they took Ba Gia again⁵¹.

### Changed: The battle of Dong Xoai
*9–13 Jun 1965 · Dong Xoai district town and CIDG camp, Phuoc Long Province · EV000-18*

*Initiative: enemy*

Late on 9 June 1965 the VC 272nd Regiment, with a battalion of the 273rd and heavy weapons companies, attacked the district headquarters and CIDG camp at Dong Xoai, with the 271st in reserve in the Thuan Loi rubber. The CIDG companies, which neither the rearmament nor the courses reached, broke first, and the camp was overrun from their sectors inward. The 111th RF Company, trained as a company in 1961 and led by schooled platoon sergeants, fell back to the district headquarters a platoon at a time with its wounded⁷. Three Ghostriders from Bien Hoa were over the camp from 0010 in broken cloud; they could not fire into the camp, but they found the 272nd's second wave forming in the open at 0200 and broke it before it reached the headquarters, and silenced the recoilless rifles on the edge of the rubber one by one¹³. The headquarters held until the 118th Aviation Company lifted its defenders out⁵⁸.

The two days after were daylight fights the gunships did not touch. On 10 June the 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment, was landed on the division's plan on an open zone beside the rubber where the 271st was known to wait, and lost about half its men; no private's training reaches a landing zone chosen for him⁵. In August the officer board relieved its commander and the division operations officer who wrote the plan, the first reliefs for cause in the ARVN's history that were not punishments for disloyalty¹⁰. On 12 June the 271st ambushed the 7th Airborne Battalion in the rubber. Its lead company was lost in the opening fire; the three behind it turned their squad guns into the trees and, after their captains were hit, were held together by first sergeants who had passed the leader's course. About 290 of the 470 reached Thuan Loi against about 150 historically, bringing about 60 wounded, of whom about 50 were alive the next morning with tourniquets put on in the rubber⁷.

I put the allied dead at about 230–240, against 416 killed, 174 wounded and 233 missing historically, with 18 Americans killed as historically. The difference is made of the carbines and squad guns, about 115 lives; the basic course's tourniquets and steadier companies, about 30; the sergeants, about 15; and the gunships in the night, about 15–25¹³. The enemy's dead I put at about 450–500, with the caution that applies to every count made at night. Second Lieutenant Charles Q. Williams and Construction Mechanic Third Class Marvin G. Shields received the Medal of Honor⁵⁸. After Dong Xoai the ARVN in III Corps had about two reserve battalions left rather than one¹¹. That did not change Westmoreland's request of 7 June, which rested on the PAVN regiments entering the Highlands as much as on the battalions lost.

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### Overview (changed)

Phase II is the American war at full stride. US strength rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967¹. The big operations win their battles and do not change the war: the Ia Drang, Masher/White Wing, Hastings, Attleboro, Cedar Falls and Junction City each kill men the reports exaggerate and are followed by the enemy's return, because he decides when to fight and withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. In Saigon the junta survives the Buddhist uprising and wins an election with a third of the vote; pacification is reorganised under CORDS in May 1967; and in Hanoi the militants around Le Duan plan a general offensive for Tet.

Beneath the main-force war runs the one the provisions changed most, the war for the held belt. The land programme leaves the phase with about 820,000 hectares titled to about 640,000 families⁴. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages, chiefs who stay, district centres everywhere and Delta's raids, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it, and the committees go to govern from the base areas and from across the border by courier. The Front answers by killing the best chiefs and moving its legal cadres into the towns, and where the method is pushed into villages the government does not hold at night it becomes the historical Phoenix, three years early. None of this alters the main-force war, fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live. It alters what that war is fought over.

The enemy's rear is now counted rather than guessed. The panhandle watch, the gunships and Delta's road teams count the Trail's trucks from December 1965, and the B-52J cuts every bridge it can measure from April 1966; the enemy answers with fords and pontoons no bomb can close, and by the autumn more is moving than before. Sihanoukville is measured by March 1967 as the source of most of the arms for III and IV Corps. The northern campaign is the theater's own: the restrike watch keeps the Red River crossings closed more days than not while the cell's monthly kills fall from about 140 to 35, there is no Christmas pause and no POL strike, and this command reports in October 1966 that the North's war in the South needs none of what is being destroyed⁸.

The armies are better in the fights the enemy grants and get no more of them. Every infantryman carries a modern carbine and every squad a belt-fed gun; the Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and no Marine on 881 South dies beside a jammed rifle. The ARVN's battalions are filled from the board's list, its sergeants schooled and its privates trained, and the enemy does what he does against every better unit: he declines to fight it and lays his ambush for the one beside it. He moves his war in the lowlands south of Da Nang to the mine, which no course teaches against, and the devaluation of 1966 sends trained privates home to families their pay no longer feeds. The radio puts every post on the district net, and the Front answers by ambushing the company that answers the call, until the districts learn to answer with guns and gunships rather than trucks.

> Phase II is the American war at full stride. US military strength in Vietnam rises from about 184,000 at the end of 1965 to 385,000 at the end of 1966 and 486,000 at the end of 1967, and American deaths by hostile action from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 and 9,378 in 1967¹. The strategy is Westmoreland's: US divisions and brigades, with airmobility and almost unlimited firepower, seek out and destroy the enemy's main-force regiments and base areas, while the ARVN is turned increasingly to territorial security and pacification. The measure of success becomes attrition, the "crossover point" at which the enemy loses men faster than he can replace them through recruitment in the South and infiltration from the North. The instrument of measurement becomes the body count, which inflates at every level of reporting and never once establishes that the crossover has been reached.
> 
> The shape of the phase is a series of large operations that win their battles and do not change the war. At the Ia Drang in November 1965 the 1st Cavalry Division meets PAVN regulars in the Central Highlands and both sides draw the lessons they want. In 1966 the operations grow (Masher/White Wing on the Bong Son plain, Hastings below the DMZ, Attleboro in War Zone C) and in 1967 they culminate in the corps-sized sweeps of Cedar Falls and Junction City. Each kills enemy soldiers in numbers the reports exaggerate, captures rice and documents, empties villages, and is followed by the enemy's return when the Americans leave. The enemy decides when to fight; most of the large engagements begin with his attack or his ambush, and he withdraws into Cambodia, Laos and the DMZ when the cost is too high. Along the DMZ the war becomes positional: the Marines are drawn from pacification in the coastal hamlets to strongpoints at Con Thien, Gio Linh and Khe Sanh under PAVN artillery fired from the North.
> 
> Behind the main-force war, three other wars run. Rolling Thunder, run from Saigon on a restrike list without zones or pauses, grows into the largest bombing campaign since 1945 against a North that owns less to bomb each month and whose air defences, rebuilt by Moscow and Beijing, grow with it; it does not stop the flow south. In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta survives the Buddhist uprising of 1966, writes a constitution and wins an election in 1967 with a third of the vote. And the pacification effort, neglected while the divisions fight, is reorganized under a single American manager, CORDS, in May 1967. In Hanoi, meanwhile, the militants around Le Duan conclude that the war of attrition is not being won either, and in the second half of 1967 they plan a general offensive to break it.
> 
> In this war a fourth runs beneath the other three, and it is the one the provisions of 1964 changed most. The land programme enters the phase with about 330,000 hectares titled and leaves it with about 820,000 titled to about 640,000 families⁴. GOLDEN SHEAF, its first clearing operation in the western Delta, shows what it can do and where it stops: at the edge of what the Regional and Popular Forces can hold after dark. The Commission survives the Buddhist crisis and the election behind the Aid Compliance Board, and in 1967 convicts its first general. With a Special Branch that owns the files, a constable in about 1,500 villages and chiefs who stay, the government's own belt is cleared of resident infrastructure before 1968 rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN in Long An is the case. The Front answers by killing the best chiefs and moving its cadres into the towns, and the police serves Ky against the Buddhists in 1966 as it served every government before. None of this alters the main-force war, which is fought on the borders and in the Highlands where few tenant farmers live. It alters what the main-force war is fought over.
> 
> The war of the enemy's rear is now counted rather than guessed. The panhandle watch counts the Trail's trucks from December 1965; the U-2S photographs the dispersed fuel drums before the POL strikes fly; and by March 1967 MACV and the CIA agree, from the radar's count of convoys out of Kompong Speu, that Sihanoukville supplies most of the arms for III and IV Corps. The counts show the bombing raising the toll on the transit without lowering what arrives, and change no rule in Washington.
> 
> Every American and South Vietnamese infantryman carries a modern carbine, and every squad a belt-fed gun and a marksman. The Ia Drang and the Hill Fights cost fewer American lives, and no Marine on 881 South dies beside a jammed rifle. The rearmed Regional Forces are good enough to be borrowed by the corps, and the districts they leave pay for it. None of it changes who chooses the battle.
> 
> Above the Trail the B-52J is allowed against fixed crossings in the panhandle from April 1966 and cuts every bridge it can measure; the enemy answers with fords, causeways and pontoons no bomb can close, and by the autumn more is moving than before. At Con Thien in September 1967 the siege is measured every night and lifts three weeks early at a heavy price to the PAVN. It is the first siege the enemy loses badly, and Westmoreland draws a lesson from it that will cost the coastal hamlets.
> 
> Three changes of 1964 run through the phase without altering its battles. Phung Hoang's centres cover every district by the end of 1965 and break the Front's district administration in the held belt before Tet rather than after it; NIGHT LANTERN takes the Can Giuoc committee itself, not only its security chief. The method spreads by its own success into the contested belt, where it becomes the historical Phoenix, and a PRU raid at Mo Duc in February 1967 makes "the American Phoenix" a press story three years early. The American battalions arrive and leave as units for twelve-month tours, trained together and commanded for the whole of them; they fight better in the contacts the enemy grants and get no more of them, and the enemy learns to aim at the week each one changes over, as it did at Dien Ban in August 1966. And the field advisers, now chosen and trained and on eighteen-month tours, are the men who carry what the American battalions forget each year.
> 
> The officer reforms change the ARVN in this phase more than any provision before them. From the board's second season in 1965 the battalions are filled from its command list, their commanders serve eighteen months and are relieved when they fail, and by the end of 1966 about three in four of the army's battalion commanders are men a board chose, against about one in two competent commanders on the historical course¹⁰. The enemy notices within a season and does what he does against every better unit: he declines to fight it, and lays his ambush for the battalion beside it, as the 272nd Regiment does on Route 13 in May 1966. The Buddhist uprising finds the board's commanders in I Corps on neither side, and in 1967 the ranked list gives the 25th Division its first commander chosen for competence, under the aid condition, while an agent in the board's secretariat gives COSVN every list it publishes. Above the battalions nothing moves: the corps are commanded by the same men, Westmoreland's strategy turns the ARVN to pacification as it did historically, and the generals still decide where the battalions go.
> 
> A fifth war runs under the fourth, in the factories. The steelworks at Bien Hoa rolls the pickets, wire and bridge spans of the countryside, at a fifth to a tenth below its rating because the Front has learned to drop the towers of the Da Nhim line. The radio plant puts a PRC-25 in every post of the held belt from 1966, and the Front answers the radio as it answered the carbine: it attacks the posts that cannot call, and at My Phuoc Tay in March 1967 it attacks a post in order to ambush the company that answers the call. The district chiefs answer with guns instead of trucks, and their platoons stay inside their wire. In Chuong Thien the posts call and nobody comes, because the corps has borrowed the companies. And at Phu Cat in August 1967 a bad lot of shell bodies teaches the army what an arsenal is worth without honest acceptance. None of it changes who chooses the main-force battle.
> 
> Under all of it, the private soldier of both armies is trained. Every ARVN recruit of the phase passes ten weeks at Quang Trung or a division centre before he joins his battalion, every territorial six weeks at his province's centre, and every American his service's 2026 course; from 1966 the drill-sergeant corps begins to return its sergeants to the battalions as platoon sergeants³. The effect is the one the officer reforms found: the better unit is attacked less, and the attack that is not made leaves nothing to count. The 272nd Regiment's ambush of the Bau Bang convoy breaks on trained Regional Force soldiers who cannot be trained out of riding their trucks. At the Ia Drang the troopers keep more of their wounded alive through the night at Albany. And the enemy answers the trained soldier as he answered the rifle, by moving his war to the weapon the course does not teach: in the lowlands south of Da Nang the mine and the booby trap become the principal killers of the Marines. The devaluation of June 1966 then shows what training does not buy: a trained private whose pay no longer feeds his family goes home with his training, and some of it reaches the Front.
> 
> Between the private and the officer, the sergeant is schooled too. Every ARVN and territorial NCO of the phase has passed the course for his grade at the academy at Nha Trang, a division school or his province's centre, and every empty squad in a regular battalion can be given to a corporal first class who has passed the leader's course; every American sergeant who wants a staff sergeant's rocker passes the Basic Leader Course first, at home or at MACV's academy at Bien Hoa. The squads hold their base of fire when their officers fall, as the 7th Division's did in the rice fields of Cai Be in November 1966, and the posts of the held belt keep their listening posts out at night⁷. The enemy reads all of it from the academy's own manuals and fights the posts and the battalions that keep the routine less often.
> 
> In this war the northern campaign is the theater's own, and so is its verdict. The restrike watch keeps the Red River crossings at Hanoi closed to rail more days than not, at the cost of about 2,000 men a night and a Chinese engineer regiment, and the cell's count of targets destroyed falls from about 140 a month to about 35 as the North stops owning anything worth a GBU-31⁸. There is no Christmas pause and no POL strike in June 1966, because there is no pause to offer and no bulk fuel left. The Chinese guns on the northeast railway take an American pilot inside the buffer in May 1966, and the President keeps the buffer at 15 miles.

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 men in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 killed in the year¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on the North⁵⁰, the Trail carries more than ever, and MACV and the CIA dispute whether the enemy numbers 300,000 or 430,000, a dispute over whether the guerrillas and the infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all. Westmoreland tells the National Press Club on 21 November that "the end begins to come into view"⁵⁹. McNamara is leaving. Saigon has an elected government under Thieu, and in Hanoi the Politburo has set Tet for the General Offensive and General Uprising. Each side is certain the other is weaker than it is.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts, and its committees govern from the Ho Bo woods, the Rung Sat and Memot by courier, with collections at a sixth to an eighth of 1964's; its legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less⁶. About 820,000 hectares are titled, rent has ended wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general⁴. Phung Hoang has an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, a fifth of them committee members, and the word Phoenix has been a press story since March⁹. The infrastructure is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, which is still most of the contested countryside.

The enemy's supply is measured, the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count and the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what his forces in the South need²². The bombers have learned that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. Over the North the theater has had the campaign it asked for and the result it predicted, about 40–90 fewer American aircraft lost than historically, and no hearings on restrictions that were never drawn⁸.

The armies enter 1968 better in the fights they are given. The American army has had no rifle crisis and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights and in the nights after them; its battalions rotate as units with staggered reliefs that cost 15,000–25,000 spaces in theater, and about 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps⁹. The ARVN has about four in five battalions under officers the board chose, its NCOs schooled and its privates trained, and the drill sergeants returning 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year⁵. **About two-fifths to a half of history's ARVN battalions broken in 1966–67 were not broken in this war. The judgment is low-confidence, and the true figure is more likely near two-fifths than a half**, because the officer reforms, the basic course and the NCO schooling each claimed a share from overlapping cases and none checked its cases against the others'²⁸. None of it shows in a return. The enemy declined the fights that would have shown it, attacked less what kept its routine, and moved his war to the mine in the lowlands and to the unit that still rode. The corps and the generals are what they were, and the palace has a file on the board's officers while COSVN has had every list the board published.

The factories produce what the domestic share buys, short of power and, after Phu Cat, short of their gunners' trust. Every post in the held belt has a radio, and where the guns reach, the first call is for fire, and the post holds itself better than the hamlet around it¹². The gunships have taken the clear night over the posts of the held belt; the coast's monsoon nights are still the Front's, and the first Vietnamese gunship squadron is flying. The combined command has one corps under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies, moving at the speed of the generals the palace chooses¹⁴. The population of the South, the object of the war, is still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

> At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year¹. Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December⁵⁰, and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.
> 
> On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"⁵⁹. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside⁴.
> 
> In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.
> 
> In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest⁶. The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.
> 
> The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North²². That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.
> 
> The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.
> 
> The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.
> 
> Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁹. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it¹⁰. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.
> 
> The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire¹². The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁵. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁷. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.
> 
> The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's¹⁴. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.
> 
> Over the North the phase ends with the campaign the theater asked for and the result it predicted. In October 1966 this command reported that the northern campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed and that the North's war in the South needed none of it, and the barrier began from that report. The air defence that history's gradualism let the North build under sanctuary was built instead under fire and from China: about 120 MiGs fighting from Chinese fields, and SA-2 battalions three sites to a launcher. About 40–90 fewer American aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67 than historically, and the Stennis hearings on the restrictions were never held⁸.
> 
> Delta ends the phase with its rate found and its limit found with it. Thirty-eight raids a month in 1966 and 44 in 1967, 297 listed cadre at district level or above in the two years, 61 of them province or region committee members, and nine finance sections taken with their ledgers; four in five of the raids in III and IV Corps, because that is where the file is. Ninety-four reconnaissance missions into the Laotian panhandle under the ambassador's limits produced the first measured coordinates under canopy in this war and changed what arrives in the South by one to four points, inside the width the phase already holds¹⁵. Fourteen operators are dead, four missing near the Ban Laboy ford, fifty-one wounded, and about a quarter of the men in the assault troops were selected after the war began, because the unit was committed whole and has nowhere to rotate to. And in the upper Delta the enemy has answered the whole provision with three sentences in a COSVN circular: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet, committees meet across the border, couriers carry nothing written. The committees of Dinh Tuong now govern their districts from Memot at two months' remove, their collections at about a sixth of 1964's, and the raid yield that measures this success is falling.
> 
> The gunships end 1967 with the clear night over the posts of the held belt taken from the Front, the monsoon night on the coast still its own, a hunter on every truck track in the panhandle that tonnage arriving barely notices, and the first Vietnamese gunship squadron flying.
