The ambush of the relief on the canal road is answered from the air.

### New: The war on the district chiefs
*Aug 1965 – Jun 1966 · The Delta, the provinces around Saigon and the coastal Centre · EV002-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

By the summer of 1965 the Front's provincial committees reported that the list-appointed chiefs had stayed through three governments, and COSVN concluded in August that the chiefs who kept their Popular Forces in the hamlets at night were its most dangerous enemies and were to be killed. Between August 1965 and June 1966 nineteen district chiefs and two province chiefs died, sixteen of them from the list. On 14 November Major Tran Van Sang of Mo Cay, whom the Kien Hoa committee called "the most harmful of the puppet district chiefs in the province", was killed by a command-detonated mine on the road to Ben Tre. The killings did not empty the districts, and that was the reform's quiet gain: a dead chief's deputy acted at once, the Board sent a ranked list for the vacancy within about three weeks, and Mo Cay had a new chief on 6 December. The chiefs learned to travel with escorts and vary their roads, the Special Branch traced five of the twenty-one attacks within the year, and the Front never killed chiefs at that rate again⁶.

**Before:**

> For its first year the Front read the Provincial Administration Reform as one more reshuffle of the puppet's officials, and it took until the summer of 1965, when the list-appointed chiefs had stayed through the fall of Khanh, the Quat government and the arrival of Thieu and Ky, for the provincial committees to report that the new chiefs were not changing. The conclusion COSVN drew in August 1965 was the one that hurt: the chiefs who kept their Popular Forces in the hamlets at night and directed the police were the enemy's most dangerous officials, and the district committees were to kill them. Between August 1965 and June 1966 nineteen district chiefs and two province chiefs were killed by mines, ambush and assassination, sixteen of them appointed from the list. On 14 November 1965 Major Tran Van Sang, district chief of Mo Cay in Kien Hoa since June 1964, was killed with his driver and two bodyguards by a command-detonated mine on the road from Mo Cay to Ben Tre; the provincial committee's own report, captured in 1966, called him "the most harmful of the puppet district chiefs in the province" because the hamlets of his district no longer sheltered its cadres at night.
> 
> The killings did not empty the districts, and that was the reform's quiet gain. A dead chief's deputy for administration acted at once, and the Board sent a ranked list for the vacancy within an average of about three weeks; Mo Cay had a new chief, a captain who had served as the district's deputy for security, on 6 December. Under the patronage system a vacant district had waited months for a patron's choice, and the Popular Forces had drifted back to the district town while it waited¹⁷. Each killing cost the Front a security cell's best men, because the chiefs now travelled with Field Force escorts and varied their roads, and five of the twenty-one attacks were traced and their teams taken by the Special Branch within the year⁶. The Front went on killing chiefs for the rest of the war. It never again did so at the rate of 1965–66, because the chiefs it could kill easily had been killed and the rest had learned.

### New: The restrike watch on the Red River
*1 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1966 · The Paul Doumer, Long Bien and Chuong Duong crossings at Hanoi; the Canal des Rapides and Bac Giang bridges on the northeast railway; the ferries at Phu Ly and Ninh Binh; the MACV Combined Targeting Cell, Tan Son Nhut · EV013-3*

*Initiative: both*

From August 1965 the Combined Targeting Cell ran the northern campaign on one list of about 300 targets and a daily repair list, and the Red River crossings at Hanoi were its pattern. The North did not rebuild the Paul Doumer bridge under the watch; by June the Hanoi bridge company and the Chinese 1st Railway Engineer Division had a pontoon bridge 3 km downstream, floated by night and broken up by day, and a rail ferry at Chuong Duong. The U-2S's dawn pass found each crossing in use and each repair, the cell's midday list ordered a J cell for the night or an F-105D package for the morning, and between August 1965 and December 1966 the crossings were struck 61 times and impassable to rail on about 290 of 517 days⁸. The pontoons were what the J could not solve, because they were targets only for the hours they were assembled, and the North kept three sets for every one in the river.

What the watch measured was the North spending labour to keep moving: about 2,000 men a night and a Chinese engineer regiment to carry 40–60 percent of the trains of February 1965. The cell's monthly count of targets destroyed rose to about 140 in the summer of 1965 and fell to about 35 by December 1966, as the North stopped owning anything else worth a GBU-31. In October 1966 J-2 sent Washington, beside those figures, the Gulf watch's count of coastal traffic south of Thanh Hoa and the CIA's estimate of the North's imports; neither had fallen. Westmoreland's covering note said that the campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed, and that the North's war in the South needed none of it⁸.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> This event is told at length because it shows what the provision did once the opening strike was over, and why its measure of success fell as its success grew. From August 1965 the Combined Targeting Cell ran the northern campaign on a single list of about 300 targets and a daily repair list, and the Red River crossings at Hanoi were its pattern. The Paul Doumer bridge, 1,680 metres on 19 spans, had lost two spans on 2–3 March and a third on 6 March. The North did not try to rebuild it while the restrike watch stood over it. By June the Hanoi Bridge and Road Company and the Chinese railway engineers of the 1st Railway Engineer Division had built a pontoon bridge 3 km downstream, floated by night and broken into sections along the bank by day, and a rail ferry at Chuong Duong.
> 
> Pruitt's cell answered with the rhythm that became its law. The U-2S's dawn pass, read at Bien Hoa by 07:30, found each crossing in use and each repair; the cell's midday list ordered a J cell for the night or an F-105D package for the next morning; the Gulf watch and the U-2S's evening pass showed whether the trains moved. Between August 1965 and December 1966 the Red River crossings at Hanoi were struck 61 times, 28 of them by Js with GBU-31s, and were impassable to rail on about 290 of the 517 days. The pontoons were the problem the J could not solve: a 200-metre bridge of steel sections is a target only for the hours it is assembled, and the U-2S saw it at dawn after it had been taken apart. The cell learned to strike the pontoon parks on the banks with GBU-38s by day and the approaches by night, and Captain Reese's carriers took the ferries; the North learned to keep three pontoon sets for every one in the river.
> 
> What the watch measured was the North spending labour to keep moving. By the autumn of 1966 about 2,000 men of the Hanoi crossings' repair and pontoon units were working the river at night, beside a Chinese railway engineer regiment, to carry about 40–60 percent of the trains the bridge had carried in February 1965. The cell's own monthly count of targets destroyed rose through the summer of 1965 to about 140 a month, and fell month by month thereafter to about 35 by December 1966, as the North stopped owning anything else worth a GBU-31. In October 1966 J-2 sent Washington, beside the cell's figures, the Gulf watch's count of the coastal traffic south of Thanh Hoa and the CIA's estimate of the North's imports: neither had fallen since the spring of 1965. General Westmoreland signed the covering note: the campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed, and the North's war in the South needed none of it⁸.

### No longer happens: The rhythm of the raid, 1965–1967
*1 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The Saigon belt (Gia Dinh, Long An, Hau Nghia, Bien Hoa), the upper Delta (Dinh Tuong, Kien Hoa, Vinh Long, Phong Dinh) and the coastal lowlands of Binh Dinh and Quang Ngai · EV014-3*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-4; Delta's rate, yield and losses stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> By the spring of 1966 the unit had found its rate, and the rate was not the one the first months had promised. Three assault squadrons forward gave six assault troops, and six troops with six to twenty-four hours of planning behind each raid produced 38 raids a month on average in 1966 and 44 in 1967 — with one month, March 1966, at 104 after the Dinh Tuong finance section's courier book fell into the task force's hands, and April at 19 while the squadrons that had flown it stood down. Reconnaissance ran at nine to twelve teams in the field at once, each out three to six days, and the two could not be run at full stretch together: a squadron raiding in Kien Hoa was not watching a trail junction in the Do Xa.
> 
> The yield was concentrated and it was real. Of about 1,000 raids in the thirty months, 171 reached a listed cadre at district level or above in 1966 and 126 in 1967, with 61 province or region committee members among them over the two years and nine finance sections taken with their ledgers. Four in five of those raids were in III and IV Corps, where the files were thick, and the squadron at Da Nang spent most of 1966 and 1967 on reconnaissance rather than raiding because the coastal hamlets of Quang Ngai had no file worth raiding on and the Front held them at night. In the Highlands the unit worked only as reconnaissance in the tri-border, where it had no file, no language and no Montagnard source it could use without an interpreter the enemy might own.
> 
> The price was paid in the one currency the unit could not print. Between August 1965 and December 1967 Delta lost fourteen operators killed, four missing in Laos and fifty-one wounded, with two of E Squadron's helicopters shot down over the Rung Sat and the Plain of Reeds¹⁵. Fort Bragg returned thirty to fifty operators a year from a selection course run by a cadre that was itself in Vietnam, so the unit held its numbers and spent its experience: by the end of 1967 about a quarter of the men in the assault troops had been selected and trained after the war began.

### New: The committees driven out: FOLLOW THROUGH, NIGHT LANTERN and the empty beds
*2 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · Hoc Mon, Cu Chi and Trang Bang; Can Giuoc and Can Duoc, Long An; Cai Lay, Cai Be and Giao Duc, Dinh Tuong; Memot, Cambodia; the towns of the Delta · EVR05-4*

*Initiative: both*

Three operations in the held belt, by the task force, the province and Delta, did the same thing in three places, and together they are the story of what happened to the Front's district government before Tet: it was driven out of the villages it governed and went on governing them from further away. The first followed the Hoc Mon committee to Cu Chi. On 2 August 1965 the task force's III Corps task group, now about 420 strong under Major Garvin and Lieutenant Colonel Phuoc, opened FOLLOW THROUGH against the committee's survivors and the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region's finance section in the hamlets along the Saigon River. For two months it took only couriers, each of whom knew only the next courier's name. On 14 October a cashier of twenty-three was arrested at a Hoc Mon market stall with 41,000 piasters in a rice sack and rallied against a named offer that her mother would not be detained. On the night of 19–20 October two SEAL platoons and the Gia Dinh PRU took the section's deputy chief in a tunnel under a family altar in Phu Hoa Dong, with the ledger for nine months of 1965, while a 25th Division company tasked against its division's plan held the land side. The ledger named the collectors of four districts: 64 arrests followed by March 1966, and 17 killed in raids, four of whom the Commission's audit could not show to be cadres. The committee's secretary, Nguyen Van Tu, went to the Ho Bo woods in January as the US 25th Division arrived at Cu Chi, and the region's collections from the posted villages of Hoc Mon and Go Vap in 1966 were about an eighth of 1964's¹⁴.

The second was Long An's own. Eighteen months after the Can Giuoc killings, about 400 families' titles were still held at the district office. Lieutenant Colonel Ha Thuc Lan, the province chief, and Major Le Cong Phuong, the district chief, both from the list, built NIGHT LANTERN in the 14 villages between Route 5 and the Vam Co around the settled post, the census and the folder, with eight RF companies, 26 PF platoons raised in the villages, two Police Field Force companies, 140 constables, a gunship on call at night, and Lan's rule that no post was settled until its platoon slept in the hamlet and a reaction force could reach it by water within the hour. The posts went in from 15 November. On 19 January 1966 two companies of the 506th attacked the new post at Phuoc Lai, where the killings had begun; the platoon and the constables held for three hours under the gunship until an RF company came down the canal, and the 506th left 38 dead. On 4 February a night check found a young man whose card did not match his booklet, and within a week his courier route had led to the chief of the district committee's security section, whose notebook the district centre matched against the census, 17 of 22 courier stations to their households. On 24–25 February the PRU took the committee's deputy secretary and finance chief at the Rung Sat's edge, where the committee had moved believing itself beyond the posts; the deputy secretary rallied and drew the chart of the province committee above him. By 30 April all 14 posts held, 212 had been arrested and 71 released, 64 had rallied to the police posts, the committee's first-quarter collections were a third of 1965's, and the 400 titles were handed to their families in their hamlets⁶. Captain Whitcomb, at the end of his eighteen months, reported that the committee's arrest and not a battalion's sweep had broken the tax, and that the families had asked him, not the district chief, whether the arrests would last⁹.

Delta was the third. By 1966 it had found its rate: 38 raids a month in 1966 and 44 in 1967, 171 and then 126 listed cadre of district rank or above taken, 61 of them province or region committee members, and nine finance sections with their ledgers, four raids in five in III and IV Corps, because that is where the files were. It paid in the currency it could not print: fourteen operators killed, four missing and fifty-one wounded by the end of 1967, and a quarter of its assault troops selected after the war began. In September 1967 the National Fusion Centre gave the Can Tho squadron twenty-six addresses in upper Dinh Tuong, the best file in the Delta. Twenty-three raids between 4 September and 14 November took two people. The other twenty-one found a bed that had been slept in and a family that said, truthfully, that the man had not been there for months. The courier taken on 19 September told why. The province committee had lived since March at Memot, across the Cambodian border, and came into the province for four or five nights every second month under a COSVN circular of April 1967 in three sentences: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet; committees meet in the base areas or across the border; couriers carry nothing written¹⁵.

The raid yield fell by two-fifths, and so did the Special Branch's arrests in the held belt, to about 40 percent of their 1966 peak, with the district centres' neutralizations of district cadre falling from about 140 a quarter to about 50⁹. Komer proposed monthly arrest targets in February 1967; this headquarters answered on 3 April that the count was falling because the programme was working, Khoa and Hieu opposed the targets on the record, and no centre was given one in 1967. The measures the enemy could not fake agreed. The committees of the held belt were running their districts by courier from the Ho Bo woods, the Rung Sat and Memot at two months' remove, with collections at a sixth to an eighth of 1964's, and the falling yield was the measure of that success¹⁵. The Front did not pay in people. It paid in walking time, which against the best three hundred operators of the American army was the cheapest answer any provision drew from it. And the legal cadres who left the villages settled in Can Tho, My Tho, Vinh Long and the edges of Saigon among the refugees, where a constable in a ward of 10,000 knew far less than one in a village of 2,000⁶.

### No longer happens: Operation FOLLOW THROUGH
*2 Aug 1965 – 30 Jun 1966 · Cu Chi and Trang Bang Districts, Hau Nghia Province; Hoc Mon District, Gia Dinh Province; the Ho Bo and Boi Loi woods and the Filhol rubber, Binh Duong Province · EV012-4*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-4; the operation stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> FOLLOW THROUGH was the task force's answer to the district committee that STILL WATER had driven out of Hoc Mon. Five of the Hoc Mon committee's 14 members had escaped STILL WATER and governed the district's posted villages from Cu Chi by courier⁹. With them in the Cu Chi hamlets along the Saigon River sat the Saigon–Gia Dinh Region's finance and economy section, which collected taxes from the market gardens of Hoc Mon and Go Vap and the rubber workers of the Filhol plantation. On 2 August 1965 the III Corps task group opened the operation from Hoc Mon district town, with Major Garvin commanding and Lieutenant Colonel Phuoc of the Special Branch as his deputy. The task group was now about 420 strong, with a Special Forces detachment, two SEAL platoons, the Gia Dinh and Hau Nghia PRUs and four UH-1Ds and two UH-1B gunships of its own.
> 
> The operation ran on the cycle the task force had learned in Long An: an arrest or a rallier, exploitation the same morning, the follow-on that night. Its first two months took eleven of the region finance section's couriers and none of its members, because every courier carried only the next courier's name. The break was a woman again, as it had been in STILL WATER. On 14 October a 23-year-old cashier of the finance section, arrested at a market stall in Hoc Mon with 41,000 piasters in a rice sack, rallied on the 16th against a named offer that her mother would not be detained. She described the section's three meeting houses in An Nhon Tay and Phu Hoa Dong.
> 
> The raid on Phu Hoa Dong on the night of 19–20 October was the task force's first contested-belt operation at full scale. Two SEAL platoons and the Gia Dinh PRU inserted by helicopter at 0230 into a paddy east of the hamlet. A Regional Forces company of Cu Chi district held a cordon on the river side, and a company of the ARVN 25th Division's 49th Regiment closed the land side. The III Corps combined centre had tasked that company at 1500 the previous afternoon on the task group's request, against the division's own plan for the night. The team took the section's deputy chief and two cadres alive in a tunnel entrance under a family altar, with the section's ledger for the first nine months of 1965. One SEAL was killed by a grenade thrown from a second tunnel mouth. The PRU killed three men in the paddy who had fired on the cordon. One of them was the deputy chief's 16-year-old son, carrying a K-44 rifle.
> 
> The ledger was the most valuable document the task force had yet taken. It recorded the region's tax collections hamlet by hamlet across Hoc Mon, Go Vap, Cu Chi and Trang Bang, and it named the collectors. Between November 1965 and March 1966 the task group made 64 arrests on warrants drawn from it, of which the magistrates released 21. It killed 17 people in raids, of whom the Commission's audit of May 1966 could show 13 to be cadres and could not show 4. Of the Hoc Mon committee's five surviving members, three were taken and one rallied. The fifth, the committee's secretary, Nguyen Van Tu, left Cu Chi for the Ho Bo woods in January 1966 with the finance section's remaining members, as the American 25th Infantry Division arrived at Cu Chi and began clearing the plantation edge. The task group could not follow him there. The woods were the 165th VC Regiment's base area and a main-force problem.
> 
> What FOLLOW THROUGH achieved shows in the Front's own accounts. The region finance section's collections from the posted villages of Hoc Mon and Go Vap in the first half of 1966 were about one-eighth of the first half of 1964's, against about one-fifth on the course of memorandum 006. Its collections from Cu Chi's contested hamlets fell by about two-fifths, where on that course they had grown. Nobody governed Hoc Mon from Cu Chi after March 1966. The Front governed it from the Ho Bo woods, eighteen kilometres further out, by couriers who now took two nights rather than one, and it never re-established a tax collector who lived in a Hoc Mon hamlet before 1968¹⁴. The operation cost the task force two SEALs, four PRU members and a Regional Forces soldier killed. It cost the Front the region's tax administration west of Saigon for about a year. It cost the families of the four men the audit could not clear a reason to hate the government, and the census told the Front which families they were.

### Changed: The big-unit war: Starlite, A Shau, Hastings, Long Tan, Attleboro, Cedar Falls and Junction City
*18 Aug 1965 – 14 May 1967 · The Van Tuong peninsula and the DMZ in I Corps; the A Shau valley; Phuoc Tuy; War Zone C and the Iron Triangle in III Corps · EVCP01-4*

*Initiative: both*

The big-unit battles of 1965–67 were each won on the ground, each followed by the enemy's return, and none changed the war. On 9–10 March 1966 the 95B Regiment overran the A Shau camp under cloud, and the valley became a PAVN base for the rest of the war⁶⁰. In Hastings in July the 3rd Marine Division and Ngo Quang Truong's 1st Division drove the 324B Division back across the DMZ, and drew the Marines north, away from the coastal hamlets⁶¹. On 18 August D Company, 6th Royal Australian Regiment held the Long Tan rubber for three hours against the 275th Regiment with the guns of Nui Dat behind it, losing 18 killed⁶². Attleboro grew from a brigade's shakedown into a corps battle against the 9th Division at a cost of 155 American dead⁶³. In 1967 Cedar Falls emptied Ben Suc and the Iron Triangle, which was a staging area again a year later, and Junction City sent two divisions and three brigades into War Zone C, where the enemy attacked American firebases five times at night or at dawn, at Prek Klok, Ap Bau Bang, Suoi Tre and Ap Gu, and lost heavily each time; the Americans lost 282 killed, COSVN moved, and the 9th Division withdrew into Cambodia⁶⁴⁶⁵.

The American battalions here, and the ARVN 1st Division at Hastings, carried the M4A1 and the M249; the Australians did not. In Junction City the Ghostriders of the 4th Squadron were over the night attacks, as they were over every allied position attacked at night in III Corps from 1964: at Suoi Tre and Ap Gu they lit the treelines and fired on the assault waves forming beyond the wire, and at Prek Klok they found the mortar positions⁶⁶. I do not adjust the historical returns for the rifles or the gunships. In each of these battles the fight was decided at the wire and by who attacked whom, where and when, and the enemy's losses were never counted closely enough for the difference to show³³. What they proved here is what they proved historically: the enemy lost heavily when he attacked an American position, and he decided for himself whether to do so.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> The big-unit battles of 1965–67 are told here together, because together they are the shape of the phase: each won on the ground, each followed by the enemy's return, none changing the war. On 18–24 August 1965, on a deserter's information, the 7th Marines under Colonel Oscar F. Peatross attacked the VC 1st Regiment on the Van Tuong peninsula south of Chu Lai by sea and helicopter in Operation Starlite, the first regimental-sized American battle of the war. The Marines lost 45 killed and 203 wounded and reported 614 VC killed but only 109 weapons taken, the first clear instance of a count inflated by its counters; the regiment was back in the field within months⁶⁷. On 9–10 March 1966, under cloud that kept most air support away, four battalions of the PAVN 325th Division's 95B Regiment overran the Special Forces camp in the A Shau valley; Major Bernard F. Fisher landed his A-1E on the strip under fire to rescue a downed pilot and received the Medal of Honor, and the valley became a PAVN base area and a terminus of the Trail for the rest of the war⁶⁰.
> 
> In July 1966 the PAVN 324B Division crossed the DMZ, and Task Force Delta of the 3rd Marine Division, with the ARVN 1st Division under Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong, drove it back in Operation Hastings for 126 American and 21 South Vietnamese killed against about 700 PAVN claimed. Its lasting effect was to draw the Marines north to the DMZ, away from the coastal hamlets III MAF had wanted to secure⁶¹. On 18 August, in monsoon rain in the Long Tan rubber, D Company, 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 108 men under Major Harry Smith, held for three hours against the VC 275th Regiment and the D445 Battalion with the guns of Nui Dat behind it, losing 18 killed and counting 245 enemy dead on the field⁶². From September to November Operation Attleboro grew from a brigade's shakedown northwest of Dau Tieng into a corps battle against the VC 9th Division and the PAVN 101st Regiment, costing 155 American dead against a claimed 1,016 enemy, of whom about 500 is the better estimate⁶³.
> 
> In 1967 the sweeps reached their largest size. In Cedar Falls, from 8 January, the 1st and 25th Divisions with brigades and armoured cavalry sealed the Iron Triangle, moved about 6,000 people from Ben Suc to a camp at Phu Loi and destroyed the village; the VC were back within days, and a year later the Triangle was a staging area for Tet⁶⁴. In Junction City, from 22 February to 14 May, II Field Force sent two divisions and three brigades into War Zone C to destroy the 9th Division and find COSVN, with the war's only major American parachute assault at Katum. The enemy attacked American firebases five times at night or at dawn, at Prek Klok, Ap Bau Bang, Suoi Tre and Ap Gu, and lost heavily each time; the Americans lost 282 killed and claimed 2,728 enemy dead, COSVN moved, and the 9th Division withdrew into Cambodia⁶⁵.
> 
> The figures above are the historical returns. In this war the American battalions in these fights, and the ARVN 1st Division at Hastings, carried the M4A1 and the M249; the Australians at Long Tan did not, because the provision did not cover them. I do not adjust these returns. In each of these battles who attacked whom, where and when decided the losses far more than the squad weapons did, and the enemy's own losses were never counted closely enough for a difference in rifles to show in them³³. What the phase's big-unit battles proved here is what they proved historically: that the enemy lost heavily when he attacked an American position, and that he decided for himself whether to do so.

### New: The command lists and the thirty-day reviews
*1 Sep 1965 – 30 Jun 1966 · The Joint General Staff, Saigon; the corps and division headquarters; the Command and General Staff College at Dalat · EV007-2*

*Initiative: allied*

The board's second season changed the army's battalions faster than anything since 1955. Its panels selected about 230 battalion and regimental commanders, and by June 1966 about three-quarters of the battalions were under officers the board had chosen, mostly majors of the classes of 1957–59, for eighteen-month commands against a historical median under a year; the captain-commanded battalion fell from a third of the army to about one in ten by the end of 1966. The board relieved 27 battalion and 3 regimental commanders for cause after thirty-day reviews, mostly for what the courses taught against: a convoy moved without route security, a night position without listening posts, a fire plan never made. Each finding went to every battalion commander in a monthly digest called Lessons of Command¹⁰. About 600 sergeants were commissioned in 1966, most of them farmers' sons who would never have passed the diploma bar. Major Bui Quang Trieu took the 2nd Battalion, 9th Regiment from the September list.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The board's second season was the first in which it had two years of evaluation reports to read, and it changed the army's battalions faster than anything since 1955. Between September 1965 and June 1966 the panels selected about 230 battalion and regimental commanders, most of the army's manoeuvre commands, and by the end of June 1966 about three-quarters of the army's battalions were commanded by an officer the board had chosen, about two-thirds of them majors and lieutenant colonels of the classes of 1957–59 who had passed the career course and the first Dalat staff year. Every command was for eighteen months, against a median of under a year on the historical course². The captain-commanded battalion, about a third of the army in 1965, fell to about one in ten by the end of 1966.
> 
> The thirty-day reviews were the part the army felt. In the season the board relieved 27 battalion commanders and three regimental commanders for cause, each after a review that heard the officer, his raters and his American adviser's written statement, and each review's finding was sent to every battalion commander in the army in a monthly digest the Central Training Command called Lessons of Command. Most of the reliefs were for what the courses taught against: a convoy moved without route security, a night defensive position without listening posts, a fire plan never made, a company sent forward without the battalion knowing where the others were. Two were for the sale of rice rations, and the Commission Against Corruption prosecuted both. The digest was read, as such things are read, mostly by officers who wished to know what the board punished; that was the point of it.
> 
> The board's own sale of commands ended and patronage moved to where the board did not reach. In the corps headquarters the price of a command fell to nothing, and the price of an assignment rose: the generals could no longer give a man a battalion, but they could still give him a division staff post, a province's sector headquarters, a seat on the career course ahead of his turn, or a battalion in the Delta rather than one on the Cambodian border. Lindqvist estimated in June 1966 that about half of what had been sold in 1964 was no longer for sale, and that the other half had changed its name.
> 
> The field commissions began in the same season. About 600 sergeants with a combat record and a commander's recommendation were commissioned in 1966 after a twelve-week course at Thu Duc and the branch basic course, most of them sons of farmers from the Delta and the coastal Centre, men who would never have passed the diploma bar the decree had abolished¹⁰. They went to the platoons of their own regiments, and in the PF and RF training camps it was noticed within the year that the new lieutenants spoke to the recruits in the recruits' own accent. Major Bui Quang Trieu took command of the 2nd Battalion, 9th Regiment, 5th Division from the September list.

### New: The Da Nhim line
*3 Oct 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The 230 kV line from the Da Nhim station at Don Duong, Tuyen Duc Province, through Di Linh in Lam Dong and Long Khanh to the Thu Duc and Bien Hoa substations · EV008-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

The Bien Hoa melt shop drew about half its power down 250 kilometres of line from the Da Nhim hydro station, and on the night of 3 October 1965 sappers of the Front's Region 6 dropped two of its towers east of Di Linh; the region had chosen the line because it was the one target whose loss was felt in Saigon and which could be reached without fighting anybody. The Bien Hoa shops built replacement towers in sets of four a week, and a dropped tower was back in four to ten days rather than the six to eight weeks of one shipped from Japan. The power company paid the Koho villages along the line a wage to watch it and gave each a hamlet radio, the first government wage or radio those hamlets had had. The Front dropped about forty towers in 1966 and twenty-five in 1967, and the steelworks lost a fifth and then a tenth of its hours, rolling 180,000 and 220,000 tonnes against a rated 200,000–300,000; the arsenal, on the Thu Duc station, lost nothing¹². The Republic got from the line, without meaning to, thirty Koho villages that took its wage, carried its radios and told the sector when the Front came through.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The steelworks ran on electricity it did not make, and the Front found that out in its second year. The melt shop drew 70–100 MW at peak, about half from the line that brought the Da Nhim hydro station's power 250 kilometres down from the Lang Biang plateau to Thu Duc and the rest from the 66 MW thermal station at Thu Duc¹⁹. On the night of 3 October 1965 a sapper team of the Front's Region 6 dropped two towers of the line in the hills east of Di Linh with charges of TNT in Bien Hoa-made ammunition boxes, and by the end of the year it had dropped eleven more. The Region 6 committee, which commanded the Front's war in the southern Highlands and the provinces east of Saigon, had chosen the line for its own reasons: it was the one target in its region whose loss was felt in Saigon, and it could be reached from the forest without fighting anybody.
> 
> The line was harder to cut than to mend, and the Directorate made it so. The fabrication shops at Bien Hoa built replacement towers to the Japanese drawing, a set of four in a week, and the line crews had a dropped tower back in four to ten days, against the six to eight weeks that a tower shipped from Japan would have taken. The power company and the Directorate paid the Koho villages along the line, between Don Duong and Di Linh, a monthly wage to watch it, and gave each line-watch village a hamlet radio on the Tuyen Duc sector's net. They were the first Montagnard hamlets in the province with either a government wage or a radio. The watch reported the sappers more often than it stopped them, because the villagers were not armed and were not asked to be.
> 
> The cost to the works was real and bounded. In 1966 the Front dropped about forty towers and the steelworks lost about a fifth of its hours; in 1967, with the watch, about twenty-five and a tenth. Bien Hoa rolled about 180,000 tonnes in 1966 and 220,000 in 1967 against a rated 200,000–300,000, and the shortfall fell on construction steel, not on the arsenal, whose lines ran on the Thu Duc station. The FULRO risings of these years were in Darlac, Quang Duc and Phu Bon, among the Rhade and Jarai, outside the country the line crossed; the base did nothing for them and they did nothing to it¹². The Front got from the line a cheap and lasting target, and the Republic got from it, without meaning to, thirty Koho villages that took its wage, carried its radios, and told the sector when the Front came through.

### Changed: Plei Me and the Ia Drang
*19 Oct – 18 Nov 1965 · Plei Me CIDG camp and the Ia Drang valley below the Chu Pong massif, Pleiku Province · EV000-23*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 19 October 1965 Major General Chu Huy Man's B3 Front attacked the camp at Plei Me and ambushed the relief by day; the 33rd Regiment's night assaults on the camp were met by Ghostriders from Nha Trang within about forty minutes, and its third, on the southern wall, was broken in the open. The PAVN withdrew toward the Chu Pong, and the newly arrived 1st Cavalry Division followed. On 14 November Lieutenant Colonel Harold G. Moore's 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry landed at X-Ray, in the 66th Regiment's assembly area, and held for three days with massed artillery, tactical air and the first tactical B-52 strikes⁶⁸. The troopers carried M4A1s with two M249s in each squad; two gunships held the night of 14–15 November over the perimeter, and the 7th Battalion, 66th Regiment, found forming on the slope at 0400, came in thinner at dawn¹³.

On 17 November Lieutenant Colonel Robert McDade's 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry, marching in column through tall grass to Albany, was ambushed by the 8th Battalion, 66th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 33rd, who grabbed the column by the belt where artillery and air could not reach⁶⁸. The head of the column formed a perimeter in the trees within minutes and held all afternoon. Behind it the companies broke into knots of men who could not see each other at 20 metres, except two whose captains, of the educated classes of 1959–62, had put flank security into the grass on their own authority when the column halted; their men were found in perimeters rather than knots¹⁰. Through the night the troopers in the grass put tourniquets on each other and on themselves, as the basic course had taught them, while the gunship overhead lit the field and fired on the PAVN search parties wherever the strobes in American helmets showed them more than 100 metres from any trooper¹³.

The campaign's American dead were about 165–170 against 237 historically. The squad guns account for about 30 of the difference, the companies that kept their security about 15, the tourniquets about 10–15 and the gunships about 10–20, most of them at Albany, which remained the worst American loss of a single day so far. Moore's count of 634 PAVN dead and the estimate of 1,215 remain the figures of record, with the same caution⁶⁸. Both commands judged the Ia Drang a success and drew the lesson that confirmed their strategy. The B3 Front's study added what the historical one did not need: the American squads now carried "a light machine gun in every cell", and the aircraft "that sees in the dark" made the night assault as costly as the day, so the belt-grabbing attack must be made at closer range, under cloud or in the forest, or not at all¹³. McNamara advised the President at the end of November that even doubling US forces might produce only a stalemate at a higher level.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> On 19 October 1965 the PAVN B3 Front under Major General Chu Huy Man attacked the Special Forces camp at Plei Me, south of Pleiku, and the next day ambushed the ARVN relief column; the relief reached the camp at dusk on 25 October and the PAVN withdrew west towards the Chu Pong massif on the Cambodian border. The 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), newly arrived, was turned loose in pursuit. On 14 November the 1st Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Harold G. Moore air-assaulted into Landing Zone X-Ray at the foot of the Chu Pong, into the assembly area of the 66th Regiment. For three days the 7th and 9th Battalions of the 66th, with elements of the 33rd, assaulted a perimeter held with the help of the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert Tully, massed tube artillery, tactical air and, from 15 November, B-52s striking about 7 km to the west, the first tactical use of the bombers, in five missions and 96 sorties over the campaign. The troopers carried M4A1s, with two M249s in each squad and an M110A2 marksman in most, where historically they carried the M16 and had the M60 at platoon; the perimeter held as it held historically, and I put American losses at X-Ray at about 70 killed and 115 wounded against 79 and 121. Moore's count of PAVN dead, 634 after his own reduction, and the estimate of 1,215 remain the figures of record and the same caution applies to them.
> 
> On 17 November the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Robert McDade, marching overland to Landing Zone Albany, was ambushed in column in tall grass by the 8th Battalion, 66th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 33rd Regiment. The PAVN, following Colonel Nguyen Huu An's order to "grab them by the belt", fought inside the column where American artillery and air could not reach them, for about sixteen hours. This is the kind of fight the squad gun was built for, and it helped less than it should have. Two belt-fed guns in every squad meant that the platoons which kept their cohesion, Alpha Company's and the battalion command group's at the head of the column, formed a perimeter in the clump of trees at Albany within minutes and held it all afternoon; but the companies strung out behind in the grass were broken into knots of men who could not see each other at 20 metres, and a machine gun is no use to a squad that cannot find its targets or its friends. The battalion lost about 125 killed, 130 wounded and 4 missing, against 155 killed, 124 wounded and 4 missing on the historical course, still the worst American loss of a single day so far. Over the campaign the United States counted about 205 dead, against 237 historically, and claimed a kill ratio of about ten to one; a PAVN report of 1966 gives 559 killed and 669 wounded. Both sides inflated the other's losses.
> 
> Both commands judged the Ia Drang a success, and each drew the lesson that confirmed its strategy: Westmoreland that airmobile forces with heavy fire support could destroy PAVN regulars at a favourable rate; the PAVN that by closing to close quarters and choosing when to fight they could neutralize American firepower and withdraw across the Cambodian border to rebuild. The B3 Front's after-action study added one sentence that the historical one did not need: that the American squads now carried "a light machine gun in every cell", and that the belt-grabbing assault must therefore be made from closer still, at night, or not at all¹¹. McNamara, visiting after the battle, advised the President at the end of November that even a doubling of US forces in 1966 might produce only a military stalemate at a higher level.
> 
> The officer education changed Albany in the companies and not in the column's order. Moore and McDade had been commissioned long before 1957 and the decision to march overland in column through the grass was McDade's; but the company commanders of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry were captains of the classes of 1959–62, and they had been through the branch course and the career course, which taught the movement to contact in close country as a drill. Two of them put flank security out into the grass on their own authority when the column halted at about midday, and their companies were the ones whose men were found in perimeters rather than in knots; two did not, because the column was moving and the battalion had given no order. I put the battalion's loss at about 105–115 killed rather than about 125, a judgment on two companies' conduct that I hold loosely, and the campaign's American dead at about 190¹⁰. It remains the worst American loss of a single day so far.
> 
> The basic course changed Albany in the night after the ambush, which is where the battalion lost men it need not have lost. The troopers of the 1st Cavalry Division had all passed the Army's ten-week course of the 2026 programme, and every one of them had been taught in its second week to put a tourniquet on an arm or a leg and to put it on himself if no one else could³. Historically, many of the wounded of the 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry lay in the grass through the afternoon and night of 17 November, where the medics could not reach them, and a share of those found dead in the morning had died of wounds that a tourniquet would have stopped⁶⁸⁶⁹. Here the men in the grass put them on each other and on themselves, in the dark, while the PAVN searched the field. I put the lives this saved at Albany at about eight to twelve, and at X-Ray at two or three, and the campaign's American dead at about 180 rather than about 190. That is the rate this headquarters uses for the whole war, about two to four percent of American killed in action, shown on one night in one battle; it is not larger, and on that night it was not smaller. The PAVN wounded who reached the Chu Pong had no such drill, and the B3 Front's medical returns, captured in 1966, put its dead of wounds after the battle at about one in four of its wounded⁵.
> 
> In this war the gunships were over Plei Me from its first night and over X-Ray and Albany through every night of the battle, and they changed the nights and not the days. At Plei Me the 33rd Regiment's assaults of 19–21 October came at night, and Ghostriders of the 14th Squadron from Nha Trang were over the camp within about forty minutes of the first, in clear dry-season air; the regiment's third night assault on the southern wall was broken in the open by the 105mm, and the camp's strikers, who historically held with tactical air and flares, held with fewer dead. The ambush of the ARVN relief column on 23 October was laid by day and went as history's did. At X-Ray two gunships held the night of 14–15 November over Moore's perimeter, and the 7th Battalion, 66th Regiment, which historically probed the perimeter through the night and attacked at 0650, was found forming on the slope of the Chu Pong at about 0400 and taken under fire there; the dawn attack came in thinner and was held. At Albany on the night of 17–18 November the gunship could not fire into the grass where the knots of Americans and PAVN lay among each other, and it did the one thing it could: it lit the field from above with its infrared marker, found the PAVN search parties moving between the knots, and fired on them where the strobes in the troopers' helmets showed them more than 100 metres from any American. I put the lives the gunships saved over the campaign at about 10–20, most of them at Albany that night and at Plei Me, and the campaign's American dead at about 165–170. The B3 Front's study of the campaign added a third sentence to the two it had: that the American aircraft "that sees in the dark" made the night assault on a prepared position as costly as the day assault, and that the belt-grabbing attack must be made under cloud or in the forest or not at all¹³.

### No longer happens: The road watch: Delta in Laos
*20 Oct 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The Laotian panhandle: Routes 9, 92 and 912, the Ban Laboy ford, the Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes · EV014-4*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-5; the road watch stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> Washington authorised cross-border reconnaissance in Laos on 21 September 1965 and SOG's first team went 24 km in against target D-1 on 18 October⁷⁰. Delta's teams went in behind SOG's on the same authority and under the same limits: Ambassador Sullivan in Vientiane set the depth, the targets and the length of each mission, and no exploitation force followed. Two to four Delta teams of five were in the panhandle at a time from 20 October 1965, watching the stretches the Global Hawk's radar could see from above and not under the trees.
> 
> What the teams added was accuracy and survival. A SOG team of two or three Americans and three to twelve indigenous soldiers moved by day, navigated by map and called a FAC overhead to relay; a Delta team moved at night on goggles and spoke to Tan Son Nhut by satellite with its position to a few metres (E01). Of 94 Delta missions into the panhandle in 1966–67, 71 were completed without the team being compromised, against a SOG rate nearer one in three⁷¹. The product went into STEADY COUNT's track list and the coordinate cell's folders: 84 truck parks, 31 gun positions and 19 storage points measured to a few metres, about a third of them under canopy where no other instrument in this war could find anything at all.
> 
> It changed what arrived in the South by almost nothing. Group 559 had answered HARD CROSSING in 1966 by owning nothing that could be measured, and a braided net of fords and night pontoons does not care how exactly one of its crossings is known. The teams' cueing taxed the flow by perhaps one to four points more than the radar alone, inside the width the phase already holds. It cost nine Americans killed or missing in two years, including Captain Robert L. Ainsley's team of five, lost whole near the Ban Laboy ford between 11 and 14 July 1967 after two days of transmissions and then nothing, to a 559th Group security battalion that had learned by then to hunt the watchers¹⁵.

### No longer happens: Operation NIGHT LANTERN
*15 Nov 1965 – 30 Apr 1966 · Can Giuoc and Can Duoc Districts, Long An Province · EV002-4*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-4; the operation stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> NIGHT LANTERN went back to the districts where the land programme had learned its first lesson. Eighteen months after the Can Giuoc killings, the titles of about 400 families were still held in the district office, because no one could protect the families who kept them. Long An had been given a province chief from the first list in June 1964, Lieutenant Colonel Ha Thuc Lan, an engineer officer who had placed third in the country in the examination, and Can Giuoc a district chief from the second, Major Le Cong Phuong, who had grown up in Can Duoc. In September 1965 they proposed to the American province adviser an operation built not around a regiment but around the settled post, the census and night check and the target folder, in the 14 villages of the two districts between Route 5 and the Vam Co.
> 
> The forces were Long An's own: eight Regional Forces companies, 26 Popular Forces platoons raised in the villages themselves, two Police Field Force companies of about 150 men each with M1 and M2 carbines, M1918A2 automatic rifles and 60mm mortars, 140 rural constables for the 14 posts, the province Special Branch section of about 45, and four census teams. Fire support was two M101 105mm howitzers at Can Giuoc and an AC-130J Ghostrider of the USAF 4th Air Commando Squadron on call at night from Bien Hoa; lift was the RF's sampans, two LCVPs of the River Assault Group at Nha Be, and UH-1B helicopters when III Corps would release them. The rule was Lan's: no post settled until its PF platoon slept in the same hamlet and a reaction force could reach it by water within the hour, and no arrest without three sources.
> 
> The posts went in from 15 November, one village at a time, working out from Can Giuoc town along the canals. The turn came in two steps. On the night of 19 January 1966 two companies of the 506th Local Force Battalion attacked the new post at Phuoc Lai, the village where the killings of June 1964 had begun. The PF platoon and the ten constables held the post and the hamlet behind it for three hours; an RF company came down the canal in sampans and reached the post at 01:40, and the Ghostrider kept the attackers off the paddy until it arrived. The 506th left 38 dead and 14 weapons; the defenders lost 9 killed, 3 of them constables. On 4 February a night check in Long Huu found a young man whose card had been made for someone two years older; his booklet did not match the house, and within a week the courier route he served had led the Special Branch to the chief of the Can Giuoc district committee's security section, arrested on 11 February with his files. The Can Giuoc DIOCC, open since August 1964 in the Special Branch's office beside the district chief's, took the files apart in nine days: the section chief's notebook listed the committee's courier stations by the names of the families who kept them, and the census matched 17 of the 22 to households and three to households that had been registered under false names in 1965. On the night of 24–25 February the Long An PRU and a Police Field Force platoon, in sampans with an RF company holding the canal behind them, took the district committee's deputy secretary and its finance chief in a hamlet of Phuoc Vinh Dong at the edge of the Rung Sat, where the committee had moved in January believing itself beyond the posts. Neither man fired. The deputy secretary rallied in April and spent the rest of the year with the province centre, drawing the chart of the Long An province committee above him.
> 
> By 30 April all 14 posts were settled and held. The Special Branch had arrested 212 people on three-source evidence, of whom the magistrates released 71, and 64 cadres and guerrillas had rallied to the police posts, which they found easier to approach than an army camp. What was left of the district committee, five of its eleven members, moved deeper into the Rung Sat and visited its villages instead of living in them, and the Can Giuoc tax ledger captured in June showed collections for the first quarter of 1966 at about a third of the same quarter of 1965. The about 400 titles held since 1964 were handed to their families in April, in their hamlets⁶. NIGHT LANTERN cost 31 RF, PF and police dead. It was the first operation in the war in which the province chief, the police and the land programme acted as one district government, and it did in six months what no battalion sweep of Long An had done in six years.
> 
> The American who saw the whole of it was Captain Whitcomb, the Can Giuoc subsector adviser, whose eighteen months ran from October 1964 to April 1966 and so spanned the killings' aftermath, the settling of the posts and the operation itself; his successor arrived on 1 March and they worked the district together for six weeks. Whitcomb's report of 30 April said three things this headquarters quoted to Washington: that the committee's arrest, not the battalion's sweep, was what broke the tax; that the Commission's sample of NIGHT LANTERN's 212 arrests had found 9 unsupported, all made in the first fortnight before the centre's charts were complete; and that the families who received their titles in April had asked him, not the district chief, whether the arrests would last⁹.

### New: The II Corps list and its abandonment
*15 Nov 1965 – 2 Apr 1966 · Tuy An and Song Cau Districts, Phu Yen Province; Phu My and Phu Cat Districts, Binh Dinh Province; Qui Nhon · EV012-5*

*Initiative: both*

The II Corps task group formed at Qui Nhon in November 1965 on the thinnest ground in the country: the coast of Binh Dinh and Phu Yen had been the Viet Minh's for nine years and the Front's since 1960, and the Special Branch held files on hamlets it had never entered at night¹⁴. Its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Harold J. Beck, adopted in December a high-value target list of 64 members of the two province committees, to be captured or, if they resisted, killed, with a Korean special-forces team among his raid elements.

<!-- initiative -->Military Region 5 had its own plans for the coast, made for its own reasons. In October its Party Committee refused the B3 Front's request for a regiment for the Highlands and kept the 2nd Regiment and the 3rd Division's regiments in the An Lao, Kim Son and Suoi Ca valleys through the dry season, to guard the coastal rice its forces lived on and because its leaders held the coast, not the plateau, to be the decisive ground¹⁴. That rivalry kept the province committees close to the regiments that protected them.

The list produced 11 operations, 9 detainees and 14 dead, three of them on the list. On 19–20 January 1966 the Korean team and the Phu Yen PRU killed four men running from a house in Hoa Thanh on a rallier's word; the Commission found that they were a family who had sheltered a cadre once, two years before, and that the rallier had a land dispute with them. The magistrate referred two Koreans for homicide and Chae Myung-shin refused to surrender them, and within a week the province committee's leaflet named the four men and the Korean unit in every market from Tuy Hoa to Song Cau. On 2 April the list was ended in II Corps and the task group returned to warrant arrests and named offers¹⁴. It cost the task force its credibility on the coast for two years and gave the Front its first story about it, a year before Duc Thanh and believed where Duc Thanh was not.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> The II Corps task group was formed at Qui Nhon in November 1965, as the ROK Capital Division settled into its area around Qui Nhon and Phu Cat²⁰. It worked on thinner ground than any other. The coastal districts of Binh Dinh and Phu Yen had been the Viet Minh's Interzone V for nine years and the Front's since 1960, and the Special Branch held files on hamlets it had never entered at night. The district centres opened there in 1965 had little but ralliers' accounts. The task group's commander, an American lieutenant colonel, Harold J. Beck, adopted in December what the 2026 task forces had called a high-value target list: 64 named members of the Phu Yen and Binh Dinh province committees, to be captured or, if they resisted, killed. Its raid elements were a Special Forces detachment, a Korean special-forces team of the 1st Airborne Special Forces Group attached to the Capital Division, and the two provinces' PRUs.
> 
> Military Region 5 had its own plans for the coast, made for its own reasons. Its Party Committee had decided in October 1965 to hold the 2nd VC Regiment and the 3rd PAVN Division's regiments in the An Lao, Kim Son and Suoi Ca valleys through the dry season of 1966. One reason was to protect the rice harvest of the coastal plain, on which its own forces lived. The other was that it refused the B3 Front's request to send a regiment to the Highlands. The region's leaders held that the coast, not the plateau, was the decisive ground of their war. That rivalry between two of Hanoi's commands kept a division on the Binh Dinh coast through the winter, and it kept the province committees close to the regiments that protected them.
> 
> <!-- initiative -->
> The list was worked from January to March 1966. It produced 11 operations, 9 detainees and 14 dead. Three of the dead were on the list. On the night of 19–20 January the Korean team and the Phu Yen PRU raided a house in Hoa Thanh village, Tuy An District, on a rallier's word that the Phu Yen committee's security chief slept there. They killed four men who ran from the house and found no papers. The Commission's inspectors, who reached Tuy An on 3 February, found that the four were a family who had sheltered a cadre once, two years before, and that the rallier had a land dispute with them. Under the 1964 police statute a killing without a warrant was a matter for the magistrate. On 16 February the Phu Yen magistrate referred two members of the Korean team for homicide, and the Korean commander refused to surrender them. Chae Myung-shin's position was that his soldiers answered to Korean military law and nobody else's. The Phu Yen province committee's position was a leaflet, in every market from Tuy Hoa to Song Cau within the week, naming the four men and the Korean unit.
> 
> On 2 April the combined commander and the task force commander ended the list in II Corps. The Korean team was withdrawn from the task force at Seoul's request, the American team was kept, and the II Corps task group returned to warrant arrests in the held towns of the coast and named offers in the contested districts. The episode cost the task force its credibility in Phu Yen for two years and gave the Front its first story about it. It was a year earlier than the Duc Thanh raid that made "Phoenix" a press word, and it was believed on the coast where the Duc Thanh story was not. The two Korean soldiers were tried by a Korean court-martial in Seoul in 1967 and acquitted¹⁴.

### New: The panhandle watch: STEADY COUNT, NIGHT LEDGER and the road teams
*6 Dec 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The Laotian panhandle from the Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes to Tchepone and the Ban Laboy ford; Ubon, Thailand; the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut · EVR05-5*

*Initiative: allied*

Three instruments watched the Trail from December 1965, and their counts told one story. On 6 December, the day Tiger Hound opened, the Global Hawk orbit moved to a racetrack over the Mekong side of the panhandle, out of reach of the guns, and its radar watched Route 23 from Mu Gia, Routes 911 and 912 from Ban Karai and the fords down to Tchepone through the morning cloud on the passes²¹. The same night the sixteen Ghostriders of the 17th Air Commando Squadron, based at Ubon on a Thai condition that nothing be said of it, flew their first armed reconnaissance on its tracks, in an operation named NIGHT LEDGER because every engagement was filmed and counted against the radar¹³. From October two to four Delta teams of five were on the ground, under Ambassador Sullivan's limits on depth and target, moving at night on goggles and measuring what the radar could not see under the trees¹⁵.

The strike force reached about one track in six within forty minutes; the gunships, flying to the tracks themselves, engaged about one in three within twenty. In the first dry season the pilots claimed about 560 trucks and the cell counted about 210, and the gunships' video counted 1,100–1,500 against crews' claims of 2,600²². Southbound movements through Mu Gia rose from about 20 a night in December to about 120 at the March peak. On 12 April 1966 the B-52Js of HARD CROSSING cut the crossings at the foot of the pass, and about twenty hours later the orbit watched the first trucks cross again on a ford reopened beside the broken bridges²⁸. The drivers learned the orbit's changeover hours and trellised the open stretches, Group 559 moved two battalions of 37mm guns to the crossings a year early, the convoys spread to intervals of five to ten minutes, and by the dry season of 1966–67 a third of the movements ran under canopy. On 2 March 1967 Ghostrider 22 was brought down by an unplotted 57mm battery at the Ban Laboy ford, with six of its nine crewmen lost¹³. Delta's teams completed 71 of 94 missions uncompromised and measured 84 truck parks, 31 gun positions and 19 storage points to a few metres, a third of them under canopy¹⁵. On 11–14 July 1967 Captain Robert L. Ainsley's team of five was lost whole near the Ban Laboy ford to a security battalion that had learned to hunt the watchers.

MACV J-2 estimated from the tracks that 70–90 tons a day reached the South through the panhandle at the dry season's peak, more than the forces in the South needed from the North²². In 1966–67 the gunships counted 2,000–2,600 trucks destroyed or disabled, and the net loss to throughput rose by two to four points; Delta's cueing added one to four points more, inside the same width; the trucks were replaced from Soviet and Chinese deliveries within the year¹³. It was the first time any headquarters had counted the Trail rather than estimating it, and the count said that the bombing raised the toll on the transit without lowering what arrived.

### No longer happens: Operation STEADY COUNT
*6 Dec 1965 – 30 Apr 1966 · Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes; Routes 23, 911 and 912 south to Tchepone; the Laotian panhandle · EV003-3*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-5; the operation and its counts stand as told there, with CP04's Mu Gia ford kept.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> STEADY COUNT was the first dry season of the panhandle watch, and it was named for what it did best. On 6 December 1965, the day Tiger Hound opened its strikes in the southern panhandle, the Global Hawk orbit moved from the II Corps coast to a racetrack over the Mekong side of the Laotian panhandle west of Tchepone, outside the guns and beyond the reach of anything the North could fly. From 60,000 feet its radar watched the roads that Group 559 had cut through the Annamite Chain that year: Route 23 south from the Mu Gia pass, Routes 911 and 912 from Ban Karai, and the fords and truck parks along the Xe Bang Fai and the Xe Banghiang down to Tchepone and Route 9²¹. The northeast monsoon gave Laos its dry season, and low cloud lay on the passes most mornings in January; the radar saw through it.
> 
> The engagement ran through three headquarters, and its weakness was in the joints. A track of six or more vehicles moving south at night went from the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut to the 2nd Air Division's control centre, from 1 April the Seventh Air Force's, and to the airborne command post, which passed it to whatever was in the air: A-1E Skyraiders of the 602nd Air Commando Squadron, B-57Bs, F-100Ds and F-105Ds on armed reconnaissance, and from the first night the AC-130J Ghostriders of the 17th Air Commando Squadron from Ubon, which flew to the tracks themselves¹³. Strikes in Laos needed the rules approved by Ambassador William Sullivan in Vientiane, which allowed armed reconnaissance on the motorable roads. Of about 1,900 tracks passed in the five months, aircraft reached about one in six within forty minutes, found and attacked about one in ten, and destroyed or damaged trucks in about one in twenty. The pilots claimed about 560 trucks destroyed; the cell's own count, from tracks that stopped and did not move again and from the U-2S's radar imagery the next day, was about 210. Nine US aircraft were lost over the panhandle in STEADY COUNT's sectors, most of them to 37mm guns that Group 559 moved to the passes from January; seven crewmen were killed or missing. The drivers, porters and road troops killed are unknown, and any figure for them would be invented.
> 
> What the counts showed was the war's arithmetic. Southbound truck movements through Mu Gia rose from about 20 a night in December to about 120 a night at the peak in March, and the radar measured what came out at the southern end, on the roads toward Route 9 and the A Shau. On 12 April 1966, the day history's B-52s first struck the pass with unguided bombs, the Js of HARD CROSSING cut the crossings at its foot with GBU-31s. About twenty hours later the orbit watched the first trucks cross again, on a ford the engineers had reopened beside the broken bridges, and the next night's Js cut the ford²⁸. By February the drivers had learned the orbit's habits: traffic fell by half on the nights when the aircraft was late on station and rose in the hours of its changeover, and the road troops began to trellis the open stretches with bamboo and living trees. MACV J-2 estimated, from the tracks, that about 70–90 tons a day reached the South through the panhandle at the dry season's peak, and that this was more than the forces in the South required from the North²². It was the first time any headquarters had counted the Trail rather than estimating it, and the count said that the bombing raised the toll on the transit without lowering what arrived.

### No longer happens: Operation NIGHT LEDGER: the gunships on the panhandle's tracks
*6 Dec 1965 – 30 Apr 1967 · The Laotian panhandle from the Mu Gia pass to Tchepone and the Ban Laboy ford; Ubon Royal Thai Air Force Base; the exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut · EV015-3*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-5; the operation stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The Thai government agreed in October 1965 to base a gunship squadron at Ubon, at the price of an increase in American aid and on the condition that nothing be said of it, and the 17th Air Commando Squadron's sixteen Ghostriders moved there from Nha Trang in November. They flew their first armed reconnaissance over the panhandle on the night of 6 December, the night STEADY COUNT began. In this war the operation had a name of its own: NIGHT LEDGER, because from its first week every engagement was recorded on the gunship's video and counted against the radar's tracks in the same cell at Tan Son Nhut.
> 
> The method was the hand-off the radar had needed. A Global Hawk track of six or more vehicles moving south was passed by satellite link to the airborne command post and from it to the nearest Ghostrider, which flew to the track, found the convoy on its infrared turret at 10–20 kilometres, and engaged it from about 12,000–15,000 feet with Griffins on the lead and rear trucks and the 105mm on the rest. In the first dry season the squadron flew about 8–10 sorties a night and engaged about one track in three within twenty minutes of its passing, against the one in six that the strike force had reached in forty minutes. The video counted about 1,100–1,500 trucks destroyed or disabled from December 1965 to April 1966; the crews claimed about 2,600.
> 
> Group 559 answered within the season. By February 1966 the convoys on Routes 912 and 23 moved at intervals of five to ten minutes rather than in columns, the truck parks went under the canopy, and two battalions of 37mm guns were moved from the North to the crossings at Ban Laboy and the Xe Bang Fai, about a year earlier than history placed them. Over the wet season the PAVN built bypasses under the trees, and by the dry season of 1966–67 a third of the southbound movements the radar counted ran on roads the canopy closed over, where the gunships could not see them. The 57mm batteries came in the autumn. On the night of 2 March 1967 Ghostrider 22, working a convoy at the Ban Laboy ford at 11,000 feet, was hit by a 57mm battery the electronic order of battle had not shown and went down in the hills west of the ford; three of its nine crewmen were picked up the next morning by an HH-3E from Nakhon Phanom, and six were not found.
> 
> NIGHT LEDGER's honest arithmetic was the radar's. In the dry season of 1966–67 the video counted about 2,000–2,600 trucks destroyed or disabled, perhaps three to four times what the historical gunships could have done at that date had they existed, and the radar's estimate of the net loss to the throughput rose by about two to four points over the season. Tonnage arriving in the South fell by less: the Trail's capacity was several times its requirement, and the trucks the North lost were replaced by Soviet and Chinese deliveries within the year¹³.

### Changed: The air war over the North, 1966–67: no pause, no fuel, the buffer's edge, Bolo and Muscle Shoals
*24 Dec 1965 – Dec 1967 · Hanoi and Haiphong; the northeast railway and the frontier at Pingxiang; the DMZ and the Laotian panhandle; Nakhon Phanom, Thailand; Washington · EVCP02-4*

*Initiative: both*

The northern campaign of 1966–67 was measured at every step and changed nothing in the South. The 37-day pause of Christmas 1965 did not happen, nor the May halt and MAYFLOWER before it; Johnson sent his envoys to forty capitals with the fourteen points and words alone, and Hanoi answered with its four points as historically. About 2,800 sorties flew over the North in the 37 days, and the season of free movement history gave the North cost it two to three weeks of the 1966 flow, made up by April⁸. Fulbright said in the February hearings that a peace offensive under bombs was a pretence, and the charge cost more in the press than in votes.

The petroleum strikes of 29 June 1966 were not flown, because the tank farms had burned in March 1965 and the North's fuel had gone into drums under the trees; J-2 told CINCPAC in September 1965 that fuel was no longer a target system, and McNamara's doubts hardened a year before history's. The Stennis hearings of 1967 were never held, because there were no restrictions to blame and the campaign's failure was this command's report, not the Pentagon's secret⁸.

The buffer was tested once. On 12 May 1966 Captain James R. Ainsley's F-105D, hit by 57mm fire over Lang Son, ran north and he ejected inside the buffer; the Chinese gun crews of the 61st and 63rd Anti-Aircraft Divisions held him at Pingxiang for eleven days, and Beijing claimed he had been shot down over China. The President considered widening the buffer to history's 25–30 miles for three days and did not, because Rusk judged that China would not fight for a railway in Vietnam; no aircraft was to cross the line in pursuit, and the cell kept its strikes 18 miles from the frontier⁸.

The MiG war was smaller and more dispersed than history's. The MiG-21s of 1966 lived at Mengzi and Ningming and flew into the North a sortie at a time. In Operation Bolo on 2 January 1967 four rose to Robin Olds's F-4Cs from Noi Bai and three were shot down; the VPAF reached about 120 MiGs by the end of 1967, fighting from China⁸. The barrier began from STEADY COUNT's tracks, and Muscle Shoals laid its sensors where the radar's tracks ended, from 25 November 1967⁷²²².

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> Three steps of the air war against the North and its roads are told here as one event, because each was measured and none changed the war in the South. The petroleum strikes that history flew on 29 June 1966, after McNamara's request of the day before, were not flown, because there was nothing in bulk to strike: the tank farms at Duc Giang and Thuong Ly had burned on the first night of March 1965, and the U-2S had watched the North's fuel go into drums under the trees, buried tanks at the crossings and barges in the delta creeks through the summer of that year⁷³. MACV J-2 told CINCPAC in September 1965 that the North's fuel was no longer a target system, and the Gulf watch, which had counted no fall in the trucks south of Thanh Hoa since March, said the same of the bombing as a whole. McNamara had the result a year before history gave it to him, and his doubts hardened in the winter of 1965–66 instead of the summer of 1966. The bombing went on, because the President had decided it would and because nothing in the South told him to stop. The Stennis subcommittee's hearings of August 1967, in which the Chiefs blamed history's restrictions for the campaign's failure, were never held: there were no restrictions to blame, and the campaign's failure was this command's report, not the Pentagon's secret.
> 
> The MiG war was smaller and more dispersed than history's. The MiG-21s that reached the VPAF in 1966 were based at Mengzi and Ningming in China and flew into the North for a sortie at a time, landing at Noi Bai or Kep only to refuel; Phuc Yen was restruck on every repair and Kep, Kien An and Gia Lam monthly. On 2 January 1967, in **Operation Bolo**, Colonel Robin Olds's 8th Tactical Fighter Wing flew F-4Cs on an F-105 strike's routes and call signs. In history seven MiG-21s rose to them from Phuc Yen and were shot down in twelve minutes without loss; here four rose from Noi Bai, refuelled from China that morning, and three were shot down. The VPAF grew more slowly than history's, to about 120 MiGs by the end of 1967 against history's 180 by 1968, and fought from China rather than over its own fields⁵⁰.
> 
> The **barrier** began with the Jason study of 1966 and General Starbird's Defense Communications Planning Group of 15 September 1966; here the study began from the STEADY COUNT tracks, which showed where the trucks went under canopy and how fast traffic recovered, and from the restrike watch's proof that the North's own roads and bridges, struck without pause, did not limit what went south⁸. It reached the historical conclusion that bombing alone could not stop the flow. Johnson authorized construction on 13 January 1967; the Marines built the eastern strip and its strongpoints at Gio Linh and Con Thien under fire, and the electronic western part was named Muscle Shoals on 8 September⁷⁴. ADSID and ACOUSID sensors dropped by VO-67's OP-2Es were relayed by EC-121Rs to Task Force Alpha at Nakhon Phanom; here they were laid where the radar's tracks ended, at the edges of the trellised stretches of Routes 911 and 912 and the fords beyond, and Task Force Alpha took the Global Hawk's tracks by teletype from its first day²². Field testing began on 25 November 1967, at a construction cost of $1–1.7 billion and about $1 billion a year to run⁷². Whether it reduced what arrived is a question for later phases.

### No longer happens: Christmas without a pause
*24 Dec 1965 – 31 Jan 1966 · Hanoi and the panhandle of North Vietnam; Washington; Warsaw, Rangoon and Moscow · EV013-4*

*Merged at R05 into EVCP02-4; the absent pause stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The 37 days in which Rolling Thunder stood down historically, from 24 December 1965 to 30 January 1966, while the President's envoys carried a peace offensive to forty capitals, did not happen. Nor had the six-day halt of May 1965 and the MAYFLOWER message that went with it. Johnson sent the envoys anyway: Harriman to Warsaw, Belgrade and New Delhi, Goldberg to the Vatican, McGeorge Bundy's messages through the embassy in Rangoon, with the "fourteen points" of 29 December 1965. Without a pause to point to, they carried words alone. Hanoi's answer of 28 January 1966 was its four points and the demand for an end to the bombing, as historically; the North had lost nothing it valued by the absence of a pause, and saw no reason to pay for one.
> 
> The North lost its season of free movement. Historically the pause let it move supplies south by day and repair the panhandle's roads and bridges in the open. In this war the restrike watch and the armed reconnaissance of Route Package 1 went on through Christmas and Tet, with about 2,800 sorties over the North in the 37 days, a third of them in the panhandle. The Gulf watch counted the trucks south of Vinh at about the level of November, not the doubling it counted in the pause of history's measure. What that cost the B-3 Front and the regiments on the DMZ in the spring of 1966 was a few hundred tons, perhaps two to three weeks of the 1966 flow, which the panhandle's labour had made up by April. The President's critics in the Senate, J. William Fulbright first among them, said in the February hearings that the peace offensive had been a pretence because the bombs had not stopped; the charge cost the administration more in the press than in votes⁸.

### New: Operation GOLDEN SHEAF
*10 Jan – 30 Jun 1966 · Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien Provinces, along the Xa No canal from Can Tho to Vi Thanh · EV001-6*

*Initiative: allied*

GOLDEN SHEAF was the first operation of the war planned around the land programme rather than an enemy unit: the 21st Division, two Ranger battalions, about 40 RF companies, 24 titling teams and 6 muster teams carried the titling line west along the Xa No canal into about 60 villages of Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien in the dry season, with gunships over the posts at night. A regiment cleared a block of villages by day; RF companies stayed in the hamlets overnight; the titling teams followed ten days behind, posting parcel numbers rather than names; and the muster teams raised a PF platoon in each titled hamlet from the families who had just received their land⁴. A regiment moved on only when the last block was rated able to hold at night.

The enemy declined battle and withdrew toward the U Minh, leaving mines on the dikes. On 22–23 March two companies attacked an RF company and a new PF platoon at kilometre 28; they held four hours under a gunship and left 31 bodies. The units reported about 690 enemy dead; the muster teams' audit, the first ever made of a division's body count, accepted 268 by body and weapon. By 30 June about 46,000 hectares were titled to about 38,000 families in 112 hamlets, 74 of them held at night by their own forces and 38 by day only, and the operation stopped about 25 kilometres short of Vi Thanh at the line the territorials could hold, not at the limit of the titling teams, who sat idle in June⁴. In the held hamlets the Front's collectors stopped coming, and in the autumn villages that had never sold rice at the government market at Phung Hiep sold there.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> GOLDEN SHEAF was the first operation of the war planned around the land programme rather than around an enemy unit.
