Its object was to carry the titling line west from the Bassac along the Xa No canal, the main waterway from Can Tho to Vi Thanh, into about 60 villages of Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien that the government held by day only or not at all, and to leave behind hamlets held at night by their own titled families. IV Corps gave it to the ARVN 21st Division, with its 31st, 32nd and 33rd Regiments, two Ranger battalions, about 40 Regional Forces companies of the two provinces, 24 titling teams and 6 muster teams; the 21st's advisory team and the American province senior advisers at Can Tho and Vi Thanh planned it with the division staff in November and December 1965. Fire support was the division's M101 105mm howitzers moved by LCM-6 along the canal, VNAF A-1H Skyraiders on call, and AC-130J Ghostriders at night over posts under attack; lift was the US Army helicopter companies in IV Corps, UH-1B and UH-1D, about 30 aircraft on the operation's busiest days. The dry season set the timing: from January to April the paddies were dry or stubble, the canal and the main arroyos were the only water lines, and troops could move off the dikes; the rains from May slowed every movement after that⁷⁵.
> 
> The method was the land oil-spot at battalion scale. A regiment cleared a block of four to six villages by day in a sweep of about a week, with Rangers on the far side of the block as a stop line; RF companies, one to each two or three hamlets, stayed in the hamlets overnight rather than withdrawing to posts; the titling teams followed about ten days behind, posting parcel numbers rather than names, and the muster teams recruited a Popular Forces platoon in each titled hamlet from the families who had just received their land, issued M1 carbines and AN/PRC-25 radios through the district, and paid them at the parade. A regiment moved to the next block only when the American province adviser and the district chief rated the last one able to hold at night with its RF company and its new platoon.
> 
> The enemy declined battle. The Front's Phong Dinh and Chuong Thien provincial battalions and the regional main-force battalion this headquarters' order of battle placed west of the Xa No withdrew south-west towards the U Minh forest as the first blocks were entered, leaving local guerrillas, mines on the dikes and snipers at the canal bends⁷⁶. The one serious engagement came on the night of 22–23 March, when about two companies attacked an RF company and a new PF platoon in a hamlet at kilometre 28 on the canal; the post held for four hours under a Ghostrider and illumination from the howitzers at Phung Hiep, and the attackers withdrew before dawn leaving 31 bodies and 9 weapons; the defenders lost 14 killed. Across the operation the ARVN, RF and PF lost about 214 killed and 640 wounded, more than half to mines and booby traps. The units reported about 690 enemy killed; the muster teams' audit of the reports, the first ever made of a division's body count, accepted 268 by body and weapon and estimated the true figure at 250–350, and recovered 140 weapons in all. Of the reported figure, I am confident only that it is too high.
> 
> By 30 June about 46,000 hectares had been titled to about 38,000 families in 112 hamlets, and 74 of those hamlets were rated by the district and the province adviser as held at night by their own forces. The other 38 were held by day, and the titles for them stayed in the district office at Phung Hiep and Long My. The operation stopped at the line the Regional and Popular Forces could hold, about 25 kilometres short of Vi Thanh, not at the limit of the titling teams, who were idle for most of June: the bottleneck had moved from the offer to its delivery. In the 74 held hamlets the Front's tax collectors stopped coming, and in the autumn the province recorded the first rice sales through the government's market at Phung Hiep from villages that had never sold there⁴. It is the first place in this war where the government's arrival was what F001-17 said it would be: a guarantee rather than a threat, delivered by the government's own troops to people who had something of their own to defend.

### Changed: The frontier battles of 1966–67: Masher/White Wing, the Hill Fights, Con Thien and Dak To
*24 Jan 1966 – 23 Nov 1967 · The Bong Son plain and the An Lao valley, Binh Dinh Province; the hills northwest of Khe Sanh and Con Thien, Quang Tri Province; Dak To, Kontum Province · EVCP02-3*

*Initiative: both*

Four frontier battles were each won on the ground, and none changed who chose the next. In **Masher/White Wing**, 24 January – 6 March 1966, the 1st Cavalry Division with the ARVN and the Koreans swept the Bong Son plain against the PAVN 3rd Division, lost 228 killed, and displaced more than 27,000 civilians; the division slipped away and was back within a week⁷⁷. Here the parcels of the families who fled were held for the absent tiller under an instruction of February 1966, and families who came back from the camps in 1967 found their land in their own names, which took from the Front its best sentence in Binh Dinh⁴. In the **Hill Fights** at Khe Sanh, 24 April – 11 May 1967, the 3rd Marines took Hills 861 and 881 from the 325C Division; their M4A1s jammed at about the M14's rate, the marksmen killed machine gunners in their apertures at 400–500 metres, and I put Marine losses at about 125 killed against 155, with no inquiry into the rifle¹¹.

At **Con Thien** the Marketplace ambush of 2 July killed 86, and nothing in the B-52J changed a hedgerow fight at a few dozen metres⁷⁴. From September the PAVN besieged the hill by fire from north of the Ben Hai. Here a second Global Hawk orbit imaged the ground every night from 4 September, the cell measured the gun positions before dawn, and from 11 September cells of Js with GBU-38s came every two to three hours. The gunners halved their rate to survive, the heaviest day came at about 600 rounds rather than 1,200, the 812th's trenches were struck and abandoned, and the siege lifted about three weeks early with about a third fewer Marines killed in September and October and perhaps half again as many PAVN dead²⁷. Westmoreland learned from it that a besieged American base could be made the enemy's worst battle. At **Dak To**, 3–23 November, the 4th Division, the 173rd Airborne and the ARVN fought the PAVN 1st Division through three weeks of bunkers for 361 American dead; with Loc Ninh, Song Be and Con Thien it drew about half the American battalions to the frontiers by January 1968, which was what Hanoi wanted⁷⁸.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> Four battles of the frontier war are told here as one event, because each was won on the ground and none changed who chose the next. In **Masher/White Wing**, 24 January – 6 March 1966, the 1st Cavalry Division with the ARVN 22nd Division, an airborne brigade and the ROK Capital Division swept the Bong Son plain and the valleys behind it against the PAVN 3rd (Sao Vang) Division, about 6,000 men, while the Marines ran Double Eagle to the north. The division lost 228 killed and 834 wounded, and 46 more in an aircraft crash; the United States claimed 1,342 enemy killed and the ARVN and Koreans another 808, with 254 weapons recovered, a disproportion criticised at the time. More than 27,000 civilians were displaced, 4,500 of the An Lao valley's 8,000 among them, mainly by bombing and artillery; Korean troops are reported by Vietnamese sources never tested in any proceeding to have killed more than 1,000 civilians at Binh An/Tay Vinh. The 3rd Division slipped away and was back within a week of the cavalry's withdrawal⁷⁷. In this war the displacement ran as it did, and what changed was what the refugees left behind: the Binh Dinh land service had issued provisional titles for about 9,000 hectares on the Bong Son plain by the end of 1965, and under a Ministry of Land Reform instruction of February 1966 the parcels of families who fled were held for the absent tiller and could not be reallotted, sold or reclaimed¹⁶. Families who came back from the camps at Bong Son and Phu My in 1967 found their parcels in their own names, and the Front lost its best sentence in Binh Dinh, that the Americans had driven the peasants off the land for the landlords. The An Lao valley, never surveyed, gained nothing⁴.
> 
> In the **Hill Fights** at Khe Sanh, 24 April – 11 May 1967, the 2nd and 3rd Battalions, 3rd Marines took Hills 861, 881 South and 881 North from six battalions of the PAVN 325C Division, with B-52 strikes and heavy artillery. Historically the Marines' new M16s jammed, men died beside rifles they were trying to clear, and Congress inquired. Here the Marines had carried the M4A1 since 1965; the armourers recorded stoppages at about the M14's rate, the marksmen on the saddle between the 881s killed machine gunners in the apertures at 400–500 metres, and the bunkers fell to 2,000 lb bombs, 8-inch howitzers, the LAW and the flamethrower. I put Marine losses at about 125 killed and 400 wounded against 155 and 425 historically; the 940 PAVN killed the Marines reported is not adjusted⁷⁹. No subcommittee investigated the rifle and no letters about it reached the newspapers¹¹.
> 
> At **Con Thien**, 2 July – 31 October 1967, the ambush of Company B, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines at the Marketplace on 2 July killed 86, and Operation Buffalo cost 159 killed and 345 wounded; nothing in the B-52J changed a hedgerow fight at a few dozen metres. From September the PAVN besieged the hill by fire, historically at 200 rounds a day and more, about 1,200 on 25 September and more than 3,000 between 19 and 27 September, from 130mm and 152mm guns north of the Ben Hai with the 90th and 812th Regiments of the 324B Division entrenched to cover them. In this war the Global Hawk's second orbit imaged the ground every night from 4 September, the cell at Tan Son Nhut measured the positions before dawn, and from 11 September cells of three Js with thirty to forty GBU-38s each came every two to three hours²⁶. The gunners learned to fire a few rounds and move, halving their rate; the bombardment of 25 September came at about 600 rounds, and the 812th's trenches, which reached within 900 metres on the night of 13–14 September, were struck by morning and abandoned. Operation Neutralize's historical weight, 12,577 Marine and 6,148 naval rounds and more than 5,200 sorties, was used with a quarter of the B-52 sorties carrying GBU-38s⁷⁴. The siege lifted about three weeks early; I estimate a third fewer Marines killed in September and October and perhaps half again as many PAVN dead, judgments built on the historical losses. Westmoreland took from the hill the lesson that a besieged American base could be made the enemy's worst battle²⁷.
> 
> At **Dak To**, 3–23 November 1967, the PAVN 1st Division's four regiments and its artillery met the 4th Infantry Division, the 173rd Airborne Brigade, two cavalry battalions and the ARVN 42nd Regiment and three airborne battalions in three weeks of bunker fighting; the dump at Dak To burned on 15 November, a misdirected bomb fell on the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry on Hill 875, and the crest was taken on 23 November after the PAVN had gone. The Americans lost 361 killed, 15 missing and 1,441 wounded, the ARVN 73 killed; PAVN dead are put at about 450 by a PAVN report and 1,000–1,644 by US figures. It was the border battle Hanoi wanted: with Loc Ninh, Song Be and Con Thien it drew about half the US manoeuvre battalions to the frontiers by January 1968⁷⁸.

### New: The mines of Dien Ban
*1 Mar 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Dien Ban, Dai Loc and Duy Xuyen Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon; Son Tinh and Binh Son Districts, Quang Ngai Province · EV009-2*

*Initiative: enemy*

The enemy's answer to the trained soldier was to kill him without fighting him. In late 1965 the Quang Da Special Zone concluded that its local companies were losing firefights with units that returned aimed fire in the first seconds and did not bunch when hit, and its directive for 1966 made mines and booby traps every lowland guerrilla platoon's principal work, by monthly quota, from unexploded American ordnance, stolen grenades and Go Vap dry cells. The 1st Battalion, 26th Marines met the result in Dien Ban every day for a year. Its patrols moved as they had been taught, dispersed and at intervals, through hedgerows laid with bounding mines and rigged 105mm shells, and between September 1966 and August 1967 it lost about 38 killed and 290 wounded, two-thirds of the dead and four-fifths of the wounded to devices. Lieutenant Colonel Walter K. Dorsey wrote that his Marines "do everything right in a firefight and are given none". The course gave them the tourniquet, and the surgeon at Hoi An reckoned a dozen men alive who would have died on the dike. The hospital also recorded about 300 civilian mine casualties in the two districts in 1966–67, a third more than the year before; the Marines came to treat the people who knew where the mines were as accomplices, and the battalion's bond with the PF platoons, which Major Carl E. Haney had built since 1965, did not survive the year intact⁵.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The enemy's answer to the trained soldier was not to fight him; it was to kill him without fighting, and nowhere did that answer cost more than in the hamlets south of Da Nang. In late 1965 the command of the Quang Da Special Zone, under the Military Region 5 Party Committee, reviewed a year of contacts with ARVN battalions and American Marines in Dien Ban and Dai Loc, and concluded that its local-force companies were losing more than they gained in firefights with units that returned aimed fire in the first seconds and did not bunch up when they were hit. Its directive for 1966, captured near Dien Ban in February 1967, ordered every village guerrilla platoon in the lowland districts to make mines and booby traps its principal work, set each platoon a quota of devices a month, and told the district companies to fight only where a mine had already broken a column. The materials were everywhere: unexploded American bombs and shells, the Republic's own grenades bought or stolen, and the Go Vap dry cells that had been turning up in the Front's firing circuits since 1965¹².
> 
> The Marines of the 1st Battalion, 26th Marines, who had come to Dien Ban as a unit in August 1966, met the result every day for a year. Their patrols moved as they had been taught in basic and at the School of Infantry, dispersed, with a point man, at intervals, and the hedgerows and paddy dikes of the Thu Bon lowlands were laid with M16 bounding mines taken from American minefields, 105mm shells rigged as command-detonated mines, and grenades in tin cans on tripwires across the paths between hamlets. Between September 1966 and August 1967 the battalion lost, by its own returns, about 38 killed and about 290 wounded, and about two-thirds of the dead and four-fifths of the wounded were to mines and booby traps rather than to fire; in the same districts in 1965, before the directive, the proportion had been about two-fifths. Lieutenant Colonel Walter K. Dorsey wrote in his report of August 1967 that his Marines "do everything right in a firefight and are given none", and that the battalion's training, from basic onward, had taught it nothing about the thing that was killing it. What the course did give the battalion was the tourniquet: the mine's wound is a shattered leg, and the battalion's surgeon reckoned that about a dozen men who reached the aid station at Hoi An alive in that year would have died on the dike on the historical course, most of them without the leg.
> 
> The cost fell also on the hamlets. A mine does not choose who steps on it, and the province hospital at Hoi An recorded about 300 civilian mine casualties in Dien Ban and Dai Loc in 1966–67, farmers and children on the paths to the fields, about a third more than the year before. The Marines, who were losing men to devices in hamlets whose people knew where they were, came to treat the people as the enemy's accomplices; the conduct the course had taught them held better in the firefight than in the twelfth month of the mines, and the battalion's relations with the PF platoons and the villages, which Major Carl E. Haney had built since 1965, did not survive the year intact. In Quang Ngai the same directive ran under the Front's command in Son Tinh and Binh Son, against the ARVN 2nd Division's battalions and the Korean Marines, with the same result: fewer ambushes, more mines, and the same men dead by another means⁵. The enemy had moved his war to the weapon the basic course did not teach, as this headquarters had said he would, and it cost him almost nothing to do it.

### New: The academy at Bien Hoa and the staff sergeant's waiver
*1 Mar 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · The MACV NCO Academy, Bien Hoa, Bien Hoa Province; the infantry battalions of II Field Force Vietnam; the Department of the Army, Washington · EV010-2*

*Initiative: allied*

By 1966 the American Army in Vietnam was promoting sergeants faster than it could school them, and MACV opened an NCO academy at Bien Hoa on 1 March to give the Basic Leader Course in theater. It graduated about 600 a month against a demand of 900, and the six-month waiver granted in June put about one staff sergeant in four of II Field Force's rifle battalions into the grade unschooled; by the 25th Division's own count they were the men most often relieved of a squad that autumn. From November a ninety-day deferral replaced the waiver, and through 1967 one promotion in five waited for a seat. With the drill sergeants and the advisory corps, the Army's shortage of senior sergeants came three to six months earlier than history's⁷.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> By the spring of 1966 the American Army in Vietnam was promoting sergeants faster than it could school them for the next grade. The rule that no sergeant became a staff sergeant without the 29-day Basic Leader Course held at home, where the course ran at every division's academy; in Vietnam it meant that a sergeant made in the field went home after a year still a sergeant, and the rifle companies of the 1st and 25th Infantry Divisions were losing their experienced squad leaders to the tour and could not promote the ones they had. MACV opened an NCO academy at Bien Hoa on 1 March 1966, four classes of about 150 in parallel on the full schedule, with its land navigation and patrol-base lanes in the controlled ground of the Long Binh complex. By the summer it was graduating about 600 a month against a demand of about 900, and in June MACV asked for authority to waive the course for sergeants in rifle companies in contact. The Department of the Army granted it for six months. By September about one in four promotions to staff sergeant in II Field Force's infantry battalions had been made under the waiver, and the waived staff sergeants of the 25th Division were, by its own inspector's count, the men most often relieved of a squad in the autumn.
> 
> The waiver ended in November 1966. In its place MACV gave the Bien Hoa academy a priority for rifle companies and the Army a deferral: a sergeant could be promoted to staff sergeant in the field and kept the stripe if he finished the course within ninety days. The deferral worked where Bien Hoa had places and became a second waiver where it did not, and through 1967 about one in five promotions in the rifle companies waited one to three months for a seat. At home, the academies took about a third of their instructors in 1967 from men back from a tour in Vietnam, who taught the patrol base at night in War Zone C and the trail in Quang Nam in place of the European cases. The cost was the senior NCOs who taught: with the drill sergeants of memorandum 009 and the selected advisory corps, the Army's shortage of experienced sergeants first class and master sergeants came about three to six months earlier than history's and ran somewhat deeper through 1967⁷.

### Changed: The Buddhist uprising
*10 Mar – 19 Jun 1966 · Da Nang and Hue · EV000-26*

*Initiative: neither*

After Honolulu, Ky moved against Lieutenant General Nguyen Chanh Thi of I Corps and dismissed him on 10 March 1966; the Struggle Movement of Buddhists, students and I Corps soldiers under Thich Tri Quang took Da Nang and Hue, and Ky's first landing at Da Nang was blocked. On 15 May he airlifted marines and airborne battalions into Da Nang, with III MAF caught between two factions of its ally; Thi went into exile, the US Information Service library in Hue was burned, and Hue was retaken by 19 June, with about 150 dead⁸⁰. The uprising ended the Buddhists as an organised force, confirmed Thieu and Ky, and bought elections for a Constituent Assembly in September.

Here the police that Ky used was the one the decree of 1964 had built. On 12 March the Directory removed Director General Cuong unlawfully and gave the police to Brigadier General Nguyen Ngoc Loan, and the Mission protested and did not pull the lever, because the Directory was the government it had just embraced. In Hue the Special Branch gave Loan the census of the pagoda quarter and the streets round the university, and about 1,300 were detained by July, about 1,000 of them later released by magistrates whose review the Mission made the price of its police aid. The repression was more efficient than history's and cost more: the first American stories of "an American-built secret police" date from June 1966, and several dozen of the Struggle's student leaders went to the Front with what they knew of the census⁶. In the 1st Division four battalions under the board's commanders stayed on operations west of Hue and refused orders from both sides to march on the cities, which thinned the Struggle's armed support without speeding Ky's recapture. The board's list for the division was then headed by Ngo Quang Truong, whom Ky took, and the Military Security Service opened its first file on "the board's officers as a political factor" in July¹⁰.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> At the Honolulu conference in February 1966 Johnson embraced Ky publicly, and Ky came away believing he had American backing to move against his principal rival, Lieutenant General Nguyen Chanh Thi of I Corps. On 10 March the junta dismissed Thi. When Ky let him return to Da Nang and Hue on 16–17 March he was met by crowds, and the "Struggle Movement" of Buddhists, students and I Corps soldiers, led by Thich Tri Quang, took control of the two cities and called for civilian government. Ky's first attempt to reassert control, landing marines at Da Nang on 3–5 April, was blocked by I Corps troops and withdrawn; on 9 April US Marines interposed on a Da Nang bridge to stop a rebel convoy.
> 
> On 15 May Ky airlifted marines and airborne battalions into Da Nang and took the city centre; the I Corps commander, General Ton That Dinh, fled to the US Marine headquarters, and III MAF found itself between two factions of its ally, preventing a bridge and an ammunition dump being blown and readying jets to intercept Vietnamese aircraft if Ky's air force struck the rebels. Thi agreed to go into exile at the end of May; on 26 May a funeral riot burned the US Information Service library. In June the Struggle supporters blocked Hue's streets with family altars until police removed them; Tri Quang was arrested and placed under house arrest in Saigon, and government control of Hue was restored by 19 June. About 150 people were killed and more than 700 wounded on both sides, including 23 Americans wounded.
> 
> The uprising ended the Buddhist movement as an organised political force and confirmed Thieu and Ky in power⁸⁰. It also suspended operations in I Corps for three months at the height of the American buildup, and was answered with a political concession: elections for a Constituent Assembly, held on 11 September 1966.
> 
> In this war the uprising runs on the historical dates and ends as it did, and the police that Ky used against it was the one the decree of 1964 had built. On 12 March 1966, two days after Thi's dismissal, the Directory removed Director General Cuong by a decree "reorganising" the Directorate, which his statute did not allow, and gave the police to Brigadier General Nguyen Ngoc Loan, already director of the Military Security Service. The US Mission protested and did not pull the lever; the Directory was the government the Americans had just embraced at Honolulu, and Washington would not quarrel with it over a policeman in the month the Struggle Movement began. In May and June Loan took Field Force companies and Saigon police into Da Nang and Hue, and in Hue the Special Branch's provincial section gave him the family census of the pagoda quarter and the streets around the university, compiled in 1965 for another purpose. About 1,300 people were detained in Thua Thien and Quang Nam by the end of July. The magistrates' 72-hour review was the one part of the statute Loan could not suspend without a further decree, and the Mission made that decree the price of the Public Safety programme; by October about 1,000 of the detained had been released by the courts.
> 
> The repression was more efficient than the historical one and it cost more. The first American newspaper stories about "an American-built secret police" date from June 1966, three years earlier than the Phoenix stories of the historical course. Several dozen of the Struggle's student leaders in Hue, knowing that the census had found them, went to the Front's Hue city committee in the summer of 1966, as some of their number did historically. They took with them what they knew of how the census was kept and where its copies were held. The rural sections of the Special Branch were not used against the pagodas, because the Mission's line held in the provinces where it had failed in Saigon, and in the villages the police went on as before⁶.
> 
> The officer reforms put a third party into the uprising, and the palace noticed it. Of the 1st Division's battalions in Thua Thien and Quang Tri, about two-thirds were commanded in March 1966 by officers from the board's list, most of whom owed nothing to Thi; when the division headquarters declared for the Struggle in April, four of those battalions stayed on operations in the hills west of Hue and refused orders from both Hue and Saigon to march on the cities, while the battalions whose commanders Thi had appointed went into the streets as they did historically. The Struggle's armed support in Hue was therefore thinner than on the historical course, and Ky's operation of May took Hue no faster, because the Struggle's strength had always been in the crowds. After the uprising the board's ranked list for the 1st Division was headed by Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong, and Ky, who needed a commander the Americans would trust in Hue, took the list's first name, as the historical junta took the same man. The corps went to Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam, a loyalist the Directory chose for loyalty, because no list governed the corps. In Saigon the Directory drew the lesson that the merit commanders had disobeyed its orders as well as Thi's, and the first report of the Military Security Service on "the board's officers as a political factor" is dated July 1966¹⁰.

### New: The Regional Force companies go to the corps
*4 Apr – 30 Oct 1966 · Chuong Thien, Ba Xuyen and Bac Lieu Provinces, IV Corps, and the edge of the U Minh forest · EV004-2*

*Initiative: allied*

By 1966 the rearmed Regional Forces were good enough that the corps wanted them. On 4 April IV Corps formed 34 of the best RF companies of Chuong Thien, Ba Xuyen and Bac Lieu into six mobile groups for a season on the U Minh's edge. Lieutenant Colonel Lam Van Thien, province chief of Chuong Thien, protested that they were the reaction force for forty-one PF outposts and nine police posts, and was told that the outposts had their own carbines and radios now. The groups fought eleven operations well, and in the largest, near Thoi Binh in July, killed about 40 of a U Minh company for nine of their own. In their absence, between May and August, 23 PF outposts and six police posts in the three provinces were overrun or abandoned and about 300 weapons lost, against seven outposts in the same months of 1965; the Front had only to watch the boats carry the companies away¹¹. Nineteen of the lost posts had called the district within ten minutes, and Thien laid the district's logs beside his returns: each call, its time and its answer, no company to send and a battery at Vi Thanh that could reach nine posts of forty-one. The companies went home in October. The case became, in 1967, the rule that RF companies belonged to the province chief and could be borrowed only with his consent and for thirty days, and Thien's request for guns the districts could call became the territorial artillery platoons of 1970¹².

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The rearmed Regional Forces were good enough by 1966 that the corps wanted them, and that is the whole of this event. On 4 April 1966 the IV Corps headquarters at Can Tho ordered 34 Regional Force companies of Chuong Thien, Ba Xuyen and Bac Lieu, the companies that had fought best in 1965 by the advisers' reports, formed into six "mobile groups" under corps control for a season of operations against the fringes of the U Minh forest. The order made military sense on its face. The companies carried M4A1s with sights and had been trained on them for two years; the ARVN 21st Division was stretched between GOLDEN SHEAF on the Xa No canal and the U Minh, and RF companies cost the corps nothing in its own establishment. Lieutenant Colonel Lam Van Thien, the province chief of Chuong Thien, protested in writing that the companies were the reaction force for forty-one PF outposts and nine police posts in his province, and was told that the outposts had their own carbines and their own radios now.
> 
> The mobile groups fought eleven operations between May and September along the Cai Lon and the U Minh's eastern edge, and they fought them well: in the largest, on 18–21 July near Thoi Binh, two groups and a battalion of the 21st Division caught a company of the U Minh 10th Battalion crossing a canal at dawn, and the RF marksmen and squad fire killed about 40 of it for nine of their own dead. The corps counted about 610 enemy killed for the season, a figure inflated in the usual way, and the province chiefs counted what the season cost them. Between May and August, in the three provinces whose companies had gone, 23 PF outposts and six police posts were overrun or abandoned, about 140 Popular Forces soldiers and 31 constables were killed, and about 300 weapons were lost, most of them M4A1s; in the same months of 1965, with the companies at home, the same districts had lost seven outposts. The Front's U Minh command had not needed to plan anything. It had watched the boats carry the companies away and attacked the posts whose calls no longer had anyone to answer them.
> 
> The companies went back to their provinces in October, after the province chiefs of Chuong Thien and Ba Xuyen took their returns to the American deputy for pacification in IV Corps, and the case went from Can Tho to Saigon. It was the evidence this headquarters used in the spring of 1967, when CORDS was being formed, for the rule that Regional Force companies belonged to the province chief and could be taken for corps operations only with the province chief's consent and for no more than thirty days¹¹. On the historical course the RF were not good enough in 1966 to be worth borrowing. Here they were, and the hamlets paid for it until the rule was written.
> 
> In this war every one of the forty-one PF outposts in Chuong Thien had a set on the district net, and the returns that went to Saigon were the better for it. Of the 23 outposts lost between May and August, 19 had called the district within ten minutes of the first round, and the district's logs showed each call, the time, and the answer: no company to send, and a 105mm battery at Vi Thanh whose guns could reach only nine of the forty-one posts. Lam Van Thien put the logs in front of the American deputy for pacification beside his returns. The radio had not saved the posts; it had moved their weakness from the call to the answer, and it had written down, minute by minute, where the answer failed. That record made the case for the rule of 1967 harder to refuse, and it made a second case beside it, for guns that the districts could call without the corps: the territorial artillery platoons that the districts of the Delta received from 1970 began as Thien's request of October 1966¹².

### New: Operation HARD CROSSING and the estuary field
*12 Apr 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Mu Gia pass and Route 15; Ban Karai pass and Route 912; the Xe Bang Fai crossings and the Ban Laboy ford; the estuaries of the Song Ca, Song Giang and Kien Giang; Route Package 1 · EV005-2*

*Initiative: allied*

On 12 April 1966, the day history first sent B-52s against the Mu Gia pass, Washington authorized the J with the GBU-31 against fixed crossings in the panhandle and Route Package 1. On the first night eight Js put 160 GBU-31s on eleven bridges, causeways and ferries at the foot of Mu Gia and on the Xe Bang Fai, under cloud that made no difference, and every one was down by dawn. For six weeks each repair was seen, re-measured and cut the next night; by May the counts at the watch's entry gates were a third of March's, and in Saigon and Honolulu it was read for a few weeks as the Trail closing. It was not. Group 559's engineers gave up building anything the J could find, and at every cut crossing laid two, three and then five alternatives: fords paved a foot under the water, causeways floated at dusk and sunk at dawn, Soviet pontoons hidden under the bank. At Ban Laboy the cell counted one ford in April and nine by October. HARD CROSSING destroyed about 210 crossings for 1,900 GBU-31 kits and no bombers, taxed the flow by 10–15 percent at its peak and 5 percent by October, and by the end of October the trucks south of Tchepone were 15 percent above March²⁷. It had built the enemy a road net with no single point of failure, and he had drawn the right lesson in a season: the bomber could destroy anything it could measure, so he would own nothing it could measure.

On 26 February 1967 Washington allowed the North's rivers to be mined, and four Js laid the first field of Quickstrikes in the Song Ca and Song Giang estuaries, set for steel hulls²⁶. Steel traffic south of Vinh fell to a fifth in a month and stopped by June, reseeded every three to four weeks without loss. The cargo moved to junks, sampans and trucks, and by the autumn truck movements below Vinh were a quarter higher with the tonnage into the panhandle about the same; the North spent 15,000–25,000 more porters on it, and asked Moscow for minesweepers and got trucks, which was what it needed²⁷. How much less arrived in the South because of it, nobody in Washington asked. My own answer is very little.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> Operation HARD CROSSING was the first campaign in which the B-52J was allowed to do what it was built for, and it is narrated at length because what it proved was not its primary result. On 12 April 1966, the day Washington historically first sent B-52s into North Vietnam, against the Mu Gia pass, it authorized the J with the GBU-31 against fixed crossings in the Laotian panhandle and in Route Package 1 below the 18th parallel. The bombers had struck in Laos since December 1965 with unguided bombs on truck parks the panhandle watch had found; now they were given the folders. On the first night eight Js of the 4133rd Bombardment Wing (Provisional) put 160 GBU-31s on eleven targets: the two road bridges and the bypass causeway at the foot of the Mu Gia pass on Route 15, the bridges on Route 12 below the pass, and the fords and cable ferries where Route 912 and Route 911 crossed the Xe Bang Fai. The weather was low cloud over the Annamite chain and made no difference. Every target was down or cratered by dawn, and the U-2S's radar pass on 13 April confirmed it through the cloud.
> 
> For six weeks the crossings stayed down. Each time the engineers of Group 559 repaired a bridge or reopened a ford, the panhandle watch saw the trucks begin to move across it, the cell re-measured the new structure, and the next night's Js cut it again; on 28 April the Mu Gia bypass was cut for the fourth time in sixteen days. The counts at the panhandle watch's entry gates fell through May to about a third of the March level, and MACV J-2's daily estimate of tonnage moving south of Tchepone fell to about half. In Saigon and in Honolulu that was read, for a few weeks, as the Trail closing. It was not.
> 
> What the radar watched through the summer was the enemy rebuilding the panhandle on a principle the bombs could not touch. Group 559, under Phan Trong Tue and his engineers, gave up building bridges where the J could find them. At every crossing the bombers cut, the engineer battalions laid two, three and then five alternatives: fords paved with stone a foot under the water, which the U-2S's radar could not see and its camera saw only at low water; bamboo and log causeways floated into place at dusk and sunk or dismantled at dawn; pontoon sections of Soviet manufacture, which arrived through Haiphong from June, hidden by day under the bank. At Ban Laboy, where Route 912 crossed the Xe Bang Fai, the cell counted one ford in April, four in July and nine by the end of October, linked by a braid of bypass tracks that the U-2S mapped faster than the folders could hold them. Each new crossing cost the enemy a few hundred labourers' nights; each cost this command a measurement, a coordinate, a sortie and a GBU-31 kit. The arithmetic ran in his favour from the first month, and his engineers knew it before we did.
> 
> By September the trucks moving south of Tchepone were back to the March level, and by the end of October about 15 percent above it, as the dry season approached. HARD CROSSING had destroyed about 210 bridges, ferries and causeways at a cost of about 1,900 GBU-31 kits and no bombers lost. It had delayed the enemy's flow for about six weeks in the spring and taxed it for the rest of the year, and the radar's ledger showed the tax clearly: about 10–15 percent of what would otherwise have moved, at its peak in May, and about 5 percent by October. What it had built for him, without his asking, was a road net with no single point of failure. The panhandle of the autumn of 1966 was harder to cut than the panhandle of the spring had been, in a way that the panhandle of history never became, because history never cut its bridges so cleanly²⁷. The lesson the enemy drew was the right one and was drawn in a season: the bomber could destroy anything it could measure, so he would own nothing it could measure. The lesson this headquarters drew took a year longer. Bridges that die in a night are not the same thing as tonnage that does not arrive.

### New: Operation OPEN ROAD
*3–21 May 1966 · Route 13 from Chon Thanh to An Loc, the Xa Cam rubber and the Tau O crossing, Binh Long Province; Bau Bang, Binh Duong Province · EV007-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

The ambush that was never sprung on Route 13 is the clearest case in this war of what the reforms did and why no report showed it. In April 1966 the VC 9th Division ordered Lieutenant Colonel Dang Huu Thoi's 272nd Regiment, about 1,500 men, to lay an ambush in the Xa Cam rubber south of An Loc for the next ARVN convoy, on the ground every regiment on that road had chosen, an L of two battalions along the eastern side and the Tau O crossing to stop the head of the column. The convoy of 62 trucks left Chon Thanh at 0600 on 4 May under Major Bui Quang Trieu's 2nd Battalion, 9th Regiment, given him from the board's list, and Trieu had written the order on the pattern the career course taught: two companies on foot in the rubber 300 to 400 metres each side of the road a kilometre ahead, PF guides from Tan Khai, mortars and a battery registered on the Tau O and four points in the rubber, and no truck moving until the flanks reported each kilometre clear¹⁰. It was slow, and the division commander told him so twice by radio.

At 0830 the 272nd's scouts saw the flanking companies coming through the rubber toward the eastern arm of the L, at a walk. The Front's rule was to fight only where victory was certain. Thoi's political officer argued that the men had lain nine days in position and expected a fight. At 0910 Thoi withdrew the regiment east without firing, and the convoy reached An Loc at 1700¹⁰. The division recorded OPEN ROAD as completed without contact, and MACV's summary did not mention it.

On 21 May the 272nd ambushed instead an RF convoy near Bau Bang, two companies riding fourteen trucks with no one in the trees. The territorial course held where it could: the men left the trucks on the side away from the fire, fought from the ditch in pairs, reported on the sector net, and the rear company put its BARs, not squad guns the territorials never drew, into the treeline within two minutes²⁴⁵. The RF lost about 32 dead rather than 40. A private's training does not reach the order that puts him on a truck in the Xa Cam rubber. A notebook of the 272nd's operations officer, taken near Lai Khe in January 1967, recorded both days: "the puppet battalion now walks beside the road and not on it", the regiment should "seek its targets among the units that still ride", and the territorials "now fight from the ditch", so an ambush must kill in the first volley or not be laid¹⁰. The better battalion lost fewer men because it was attacked less, and an attack that is not made leaves nothing to count; the phase's single estimate of what that was worth is in its ending.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The ambush that was never sprung on Route 13 is the clearest case in this war of what the officer reforms did and why no report showed it. In April 1966 the VC 9th Division ordered its 272nd Regiment, three battalions of about 1,500 men with 82mm mortars, 75mm recoilless rifles and RPD guns, to lay an ambush on Route 13 between Chon Thanh and An Loc for the next ARVN convoy to the Binh Long garrison, on the road where the regiment had broken relief columns in 1965. The regiment's commander, Lieutenant Colonel Dang Huu Thoi, chose the ground that every regiment on that road had chosen: the Xa Cam rubber south of An Loc, where the trees came to the edge of the laterite on both sides, the Tau O stream crossing to stop the head of the column, and an L of two battalions along the eastern side with the third astride the road behind. The dry season had not yet broken, and the rubber's floor was open for 300 metres under the canopy.
> 
> The convoy left Chon Thanh at 0600 on 4 May: 62 trucks of rice, ammunition and fuel for the Binh Long sector, escorted by the 2nd Battalion, 9th Regiment, with a troop of M113s from the 1st Armored Cavalry Squadron. Its commander, Major Bui Quang Trieu, had been given the battalion from the board's list in September and had written the operation order himself on the pattern the career course taught for a route through ground the enemy could choose. Two rifle companies moved on foot through the rubber 300 to 400 metres on each side of the road, a kilometre ahead of the first truck, with PF guides from the hamlets at Tan Khai; the battalion's 81mm mortars and a battery of 105mm M101A1 howitzers at Chon Thanh were registered on the Tau O crossing and four points in the Xa Cam rubber; a US Army O-1 Bird Dog flew over the column with the battalion's adviser on its net; and the trucks did not move until the flanking companies reported each kilometre clear. It was slow. The convoy covered 27 kilometres in eleven hours, about half the speed the sector had demanded, and Trieu's division commander told him so by radio twice.
> 
> The 272nd's reconnaissance saw the flanking companies at about 0830, coming through the rubber towards the eastern arm of the L at a walk, and Thoi had to decide. The Front's rule for its regiments was to fight only where victory was certain, and an ambush whose killing zone would be entered from the side by an infantry company with its fire already registered was not that. His political officer argued that the regiment had been in position for nine days and that its men expected a fight. Thoi withdrew the regiment east into the rubber at 0910, without firing, and the convoy reached An Loc at 1700. The 5th Division's report of the day recorded Operation OPEN ROAD as completed without contact. MACV's weekly summary did not mention it.
> 
> On 21 May the 272nd's 1st and 3rd Battalions ambushed an RF convoy of the Binh Duong sector, two companies escorting fourteen trucks on Route 13 near Bau Bang, which moved in column with its escort on the trucks and no one in the trees. The RF lost about 40 killed, 30 wounded and nine trucks burned; about 20 bodies were found and the sector's report of 85 enemy killed is no better than such reports usually were. The regiment had not stopped fighting. It had moved its fight to the unit that did not scout its route.
> 
> What happened on 4 May was learned only in January 1967, when a notebook of the 272nd's operations officer was taken near Lai Khe. It recorded the decision of 4 May in a sentence: that "the puppet battalion now walks beside the road and not on it", and that the regiment should "seek its targets among the units that still ride". That is the reform's largest effect in the field, and the one no indicator records: the battalions the board chose lost fewer men because they were attacked less, and an attack that is not made leaves nothing to count. I estimate that the ARVN lost about a third fewer battalions rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, a judgment that rests on cases like this one and cannot be measured¹⁰.
> 
> The Bau Bang convoy is also the clearest case of what the basic course could not do. The two Regional Force companies of the Binh Duong sector had each been through the six-week territorial course, and when the 272nd's fire hit the trucks at 0940 their men did what the course had taught them: they got off the trucks on the side away from the fire, found cover in the ditch, returned fire in pairs and reported the enemy's positions on the sector net, and the second company, at the rear, put its BARs into the treeline within the first two minutes³; the Regional Forces never drew the squad gun, and kept the Browning as their automatic rifle²⁴. It made the ambush cost the regiment more and the RF less: I put the RF dead at about 32 rather than about 40, with about 30 wounded of whom more lived, and the 272nd's dead at about 25 found rather than 20. It did not make the convoy walk its flanks. The companies rode because their sector commander ordered them to ride, and a private's training does not reach the order that puts him on a truck in the Xa Cam rubber. The 272nd's notebook of January 1967 drew the right conclusion in its last line: that the puppet territorials "now fight from the ditch", and that the regiment's ambushes must kill in the first volley or not be laid⁵.

### No longer happens: The buffer's edge: Dong Dang and the Chinese guns
*12 May – 30 Sep 1966 · The northeast railway from Kep through Lang Son to Dong Dang; the frontier at Pingxiang, Guangxi; Washington and Warsaw · EV013-5*

*Merged at R05 into EVCP02-4; the buffer's test stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The northeast railway carried about a third of the North's imports from China, and the provision let the cell strike it to within 15 miles of the frontier. From the autumn of 1965 that meant the yards at Kep and Bac Giang and the bridges north of Lang Son, struck weekly by F-105Ds from Takhli and monthly by Js. Beijing answered on the railway itself. The Chinese 61st and 63rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Divisions took over the defence of the line north of Kep from the summer of 1965, and the Chinese railway engineers repaired it.
> 
> On 12 May 1966 an F-105D of the 388th Tactical Fighter Wing, struck by 57mm fire over the Lang Son bridge, ran north and its pilot, Captain James R. Ainsley, ejected about 3 miles inside the buffer and 12 miles from the frontier. He was taken by a Chinese gun crew and held at Pingxiang for eleven days before being handed to the North; Beijing published his photograph and the claim that he had been shot down over China. On 19 May a flight of F-4Cs pursuing two MiG-17s from Ningming crossed about 4 miles into Guangxi before turning back. China protested at Warsaw and in the press; the President, who held the decision whether to bomb, considered for three days whether to widen the buffer to history's 25–30 miles, and did not, because the provision allowed him no pause and Rusk judged that China would not fight for a railway in Vietnam. He ordered instead that no aircraft cross the buffer's line in pursuit, and the cell kept its strikes on the line at least 18 miles from the frontier for the rest of the year. The Chinese gun divisions claimed about 40 American aircraft in 1966; the cell's own records showed about 14 lost on the northeast line in that year⁸.

### No longer happens: The devaluation and the trained deserters
*18 Jun – 31 Dec 1966 · Saigon; Gia Dinh, Hau Nghia and Long An Provinces; the Quang Trung Training Center and the 25th Division's districts around Duc Hoa and Cu Chi · EV009-3*

*Merged at R05 into EV007-4; the devaluation and the deserters stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> On 18 June 1966 the government devalued the piaster from 60 to 118 to the dollar for most transactions, under American pressure to absorb the money the build-up was pouring into Saigon. The soldier paid for it. Prices in Saigon rose by about half over 1966, the Republic that had exported rice ten years earlier imported it that year, and the pay of an ARVN private, raised by far less than his family's rice, bought about a third less by December than it had in May⁸¹. The families of the 25th Division's soldiers lived in the division's own districts of Hau Nghia and Long An, in the dependents' quarters at Duc Hoa and in hamlets where the Front collected its own rice tax, and the wives who had fed a household on a private's pay in May could not do it in the autumn.
> 
> Desertion rose as it rose historically, and the basic course did nothing to stop it, because men did not desert for want of training. The course did change what a deserter took home. The men who walked out of the 25th Division's battalions in the second half of 1966, about 2,000 of them by the division's count, had all been through Quang Trung; most went back to their families' fields, some to the Regional Forces nearer home, and a few hundred, by the Front's own documents, to the guerrilla platoons of Cu Chi and Duc Hoa districts. A notebook taken from a Cu Chi district unit in March 1967 recorded a three-week course for the district's guerrilla squad leaders taught by "a brother who was trained by the puppets at Quang Trung", on firing in pairs, moving by bounds and the tourniquet, with the observation that the puppets' course was good and that their pay was not. Across the provinces around Saigon I estimate that a few thousand trained deserters a year in 1966–67 reached the Front's local forces and guerrillas, and that their training made the Front's village platoons there somewhat better at the first minute of a fight than history's; it did not change their numbers, which the Front's recruitment and taxation decided.
> 
> Colonel Vu Ngoc Hoan, who took the 25th Division in March 1967, answered with what lay within his reach: he moved the dependents' quarters inside the battalions' perimeters, paid the soldiers' rice ration in rice rather than in piasters wherever the division's quartermaster could buy it, and cut the division's desertion by about a quarter in the year⁵. None of that was training. It was the family, the pay and the rice, which the course did not touch and the division commander did.

### New: The Sihanoukville count
*Jul 1966 – Nov 1967 · Sihanoukville (Kompong Som), Route 4 and Kompong Speu, and the roads to the base areas of the Fishhook and the Parrot's Beak, Cambodia; Tan Son Nhut and Washington · EV003-4*

*Initiative: allied*

Historically MACV and the CIA argued until 1970 over whether Sihanoukville armed the war in III and IV Corps, and the captured Hak Ly Trucking records settled it at about 21,600 tons moved between December 1966 and April 1969. Here it was settled by counting in 1967. The U-2S photographed the port obliquely from the Gulf of Siam twice a month; the Global Hawk, standing off inside South Vietnamese airspace, watched convoys of ten to thirty trucks move at night from Kompong Speu toward Snoul, Mimot, the Fishhook and the Parrot's Beak; and from May 1967 SOG's Daniel Boone teams twice found Chinese-marked ammunition crates where the tracks led, losing a team near Mimot in September. On 9 March 1967 J-2 and the CIA agreed that 9,000–13,000 tons of military cargo had moved from the port to the border since July 1965 and that the route supplied most of the arms in III and IV Corps²². The Chiefs proposed a quarantine and strikes on the depots, and the President declined both. The estimate changed no rule; it made the case over the Cambodian constraint from evidence, three years before history made it from captured ledgers.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> By the summer of 1966 the sea route that TIDE TABLE had closed had been a year in Cambodia, and the argument over it was the oldest in the intelligence community. Historically MACV J-2 held that most of the arms for the war in III and IV Corps came through Sihanoukville, and the CIA held that the port's traffic was mostly rice and contraband, until the records of the Hak Ly Trucking Company, seized after Lon Nol's coup in 1970, showed about 21,600 tons of arms and ammunition moved through the port between December 1966 and April 1969. Here the argument was settled by counting, in the first half of 1967.
> 
> The count had three sources. The U-2S photographed the port obliquely from the Gulf of Siam, from outside Cambodian airspace, about twice a month: ships alongside, their flags, cargo on the quays and trucks in the marshalling area. The Global Hawk, on the nights the orbit could be spared from the coast, stood off over Tay Ninh and Binh Long inside South Vietnamese airspace and watched the road traffic up to 150–200 kilometres into Cambodia: convoys of ten to thirty trucks moving at night from Kompong Speu and Kompong Cham toward Snoul, Mimot and the Fishhook, and toward Svay Rieng and the Parrot's Beak, stopping at depots that did not appear on any Cambodian map²¹. And from May 1967 the reconnaissance teams of MACV's Studies and Observations Group, crossing the border under Operation Daniel Boone, were sent to look at the points where the convoys stopped. The radar did not see what the trucks carried. The teams, twice, found ammunition crates with Chinese markings in the depots the tracks had led them to; one team of three Americans and nine Montagnards was lost near Mimot in September 1967.
> 
> On 9 March 1967 MACV J-2 and the CIA's Office of Current Intelligence agreed a joint estimate: that between July 1965 and February 1967 about 9,000–13,000 tons of military cargo had moved from Sihanoukville to the border base areas, and that the route supplied most of the arms and ammunition of the PAVN and VC forces in III and IV Corps. Lieutenant Colonel Harold Kessling's cell had built the count night by night for twenty months. The Joint Chiefs proposed in April a naval quarantine of Sihanoukville and air strikes on the depots; the President declined both, and Sihanouk's neutrality, and the bar on operations into Cambodia, stood²². The estimate changed no rule. It changed the argument: from 1967 the war's central sanctuary was a measured fact, and the case for and against relief of the Cambodian constraint was made from evidence, three years before history made it from captured ledgers.

### New: The Delta corps
*1 Jul 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Can Tho, Phong Dinh Province; Dinh Tuong and Kien Hoa Provinces; Dong Tam base, Dinh Tuong Province · EV012-6*

*Initiative: allied*

On 1 July 1966 the IV Corps combined centre passed to Vietnamese command, with Major General Dang Van Quang as commander and an American brigadier as his deputy, the first American in the war to serve as deputy to a Vietnamese commander in a chain of command. Quang was the palace's choice and among the most corrupt generals in the army, and the combined command could only command through him; when the palace replaced him in November with the honest and cautious Major General Nguyen Van Manh, the Delta's combined orders went out on time and were executed slowly. In June 1967 Manh refused the US 9th Division a second ARVN battalion to block a riverine sweep of the Cam Son, because both battalions were the reaction force for the posts of Cai Lay, and the American deputy backed him; part of the 263rd Battalion slipped through the gap, and no post in Cai Lay fell that month¹⁴. By the end of 1967 the Vietnamese corps had written every combined order in the Delta, while the American brigade there fought its own war as if the combined command did not exist. The handover had begun, at the speed of the generals the palace chose.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> On 1 July 1966 the IV Corps combined centre passed to Vietnamese command. The ARVN IV Corps commander, Major General Dang Van Quang, became the combined commander's subordinate for the Delta, with the American senior adviser in IV Corps, a brigadier general, as his deputy. It was the first time in the war that an American officer served as deputy to a Vietnamese commander in a chain of command rather than as his adviser. Quang was the President's choice for the corps, not the board's, and among the most corrupt generals in the army by the account of every American who served with him. The combined command could not choose him. It could only command through him or ask for his relief, and in July 1966 it did not ask.
> 
> The arrangement worked on paper for four months and in practice for about one. Quang ran the IV Corps combined centre as he ran the corps: the plans were written by his staff and the American deputy's together, and executed by divisions whose commanders reported to Quang, and through him to the palace, before they reported to the combined centre. When Quang was removed in November 1966 in the palace's own reshuffle, his successor, Major General Nguyen Van Manh, kept the arrangement. Manh was honest and cautious. Under him the Delta's combined orders went out on time and were executed slowly.
> 
> The test of the one-in-three rule came in June 1967. The American 9th Infantry Division's 2nd Brigade, with the Navy's Mobile Riverine Force, began operations from Dong Tam in Dinh Tuong in the spring of 1967. In June its commander asked the IV Corps combined centre for two battalions of the ARVN 7th Division to block for the riverine force's sweep of the Cam Son base area. Both battalions were assigned to territorial security in Cai Lay and Cai Be, and they were the reaction force for the posts whose first call was for fire¹². Manh refused the second battalion under the rule, and the American deputy supported him against the division commander. The sweep went in on 19 June with one ARVN battalion blocking. Part of the 263rd VC Main Force Battalion slipped east through the gap the second battalion would have held. No post in Cai Lay fell that month.
> 
> At the end of 1967 the combined headquarters judged the Delta corps a qualified success. The Vietnamese commander had commanded the combined system for eighteen months, the corps staff had written every combined order in the Delta, and the American deputy had overruled nothing. Two things were also true. The Delta divisions' plans were Manh's caution written down. And the American brigade in the Delta, under its own division commander, had fought its own war in the Plain of Reeds and the Cam Son as though the combined command did not exist, because its division commander answered to a field force before he answered to the corps¹⁴. The combined command did not hand over a second corps in 1967. The handover the transfer needed had begun, and it was proceeding at the speed of the generals the palace chose.

### New: The Commission's cases of 1966–67: the lot numbers, the quartermaster and the Phu Cat lot
*12 Jul 1966 – 20 Dec 1967 · Cao Lanh and the Plain of Reeds; the 9th Division supply point at Sa Dec; Can Tho; a firing position south of Phu Cat; the Bien Hoa arsenal; Cholon; the Special Court for Corruption, Saigon · EVR05-6*

*Initiative: allied*

Three cases in eighteen months showed the Commission's reach, its limit and what the war's own paper could prove. On 12 July 1966 a 9th Division company overran a VC firing position near Cao Lanh, and its adviser, Captain Robert Halloran, noticed that the 900 spent 5.56mm cases behind it all bore one headstamp lot, which his own battalion had drawn in May. Since 1964 the Muster Service had recorded every unit's lots against its muster roll. The Commission matched lots from eleven firing positions and two caches against the Sa Dec supply point's ledgers and found about 1.4 million rounds issued to units that had never fired them, sold by sampan through two Cholon dealers to a Front purchasing agent at about 18 piasters a round; the point's commander, his clerk, three sergeants and the dealers were convicted in March 1967¹¹. The leak moved to whole crates bought in the field, and the Front learned to pay more for Chinese 7.62mm, which could not be traced. Khoa told the Board it was the first case in which the war itself had supplied the evidence.

On 6 March 1967 the Commission's own judicial police, with no American present, arrested Brigadier General Phan Duy Khiem, IV Corps' deputy for logistics, with eleven officers. With ghost pay gone from the parade, the graft had moved to rations and fuel: the corps drew rice for 9,000 men it did not have and sold 2.1 million litres of fuel issued to RF companies with no vehicles, about 310 million piasters in two years. When Khiem's patron sought a military court, the Deputy Chief of Mission told Thieu that IV Corps' counterpart funds would be suspended, and Thieu, preparing his candidacy, let the case stand. On 18 April the Special Court sentenced Khiem to eight years. The Commission's reach now ran to the rank below the Directory and no higher, on documentary evidence and with the American lever behind it, and there were not enough clean officers to replace the convicted⁴.

On 14 August 1967 a 22nd Division howitzer burst its tube south of Phu Cat on a Bien Hoa round, killing four of its crew. A Directorate inspector had accepted that lot and three others without the proof-firing the specification required, and had been paid for the time he saved the line; he was convicted in December, and about 40,000 rounds were recalled. The gunners' verdict took longer. Through most of a year II Corps' artillery refused domestic 105mm rounds where it could draw American, and the domestic share of bodies fell from a third to a tenth¹². The officers the courses had made restored it, with every lot proof-fired at Long Thanh under an officer's signature and the 22nd Division's artillery commander invited to watch the first ten; Binh Dinh's gunners went back to Bien Hoa's rounds in the summer of 1968. An arsenal without honest acceptance is worth less than nothing, because a soldier who does not trust his round will not fire it.

### No longer happens: The lot numbers
*12 Jul – 19 Dec 1966 · Cao Lanh and the Plain of Reeds, Kien Phong Province; the 9th Division ammunition supply point at Sa Dec; Cholon; and the Special Court for Corruption, Saigon · EV004-3*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-6; the case stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> On 12 July 1966 a company of the ARVN 9th Division overran a VC firing position on the edge of the Plain of Reeds north of Cao Lanh and picked up about 900 spent 5.56mm cases from the ground behind it. The Front's local forces in Kien Phong had been firing captured M4A1s for a year; what the company's American adviser, Captain Robert Halloran, noticed was that the cases were bright and all bore the same headstamp lot, and that the lot was one his own battalion had drawn in May. Every case of M855A1 delivered under IRON GATE carried its lot on the headstamp and on the crate, and since 1964 the Pay and Muster Verification Service had recorded the lots issued to each unit against its muster roll alongside the serials of its carbines. Halloran sent the cases to Can Tho; the Commission's investigators had them in Saigon within the week.
> 
> Commissioner Truong Vinh Khoa gave the case to the same documentary team that was building the ration case against the IV Corps quartermaster. Over four months they matched lots recovered from eleven VC firing positions and two caches in Kien Phong and Kien Tuong against the issue ledgers of the 9th Division's ammunition supply point at Sa Dec, and found that about 1.4 million rounds of 5.56mm had left the point in 1965–66 on issue vouchers for units whose muster rolls showed no such expenditure. The rounds had gone by sampan to two dealers in Cholon and from them, by way of a Front purchasing agent in Hong Ngu, to the Plain of Reeds, at about 18 piasters a round. On 19 December the Commission's judicial police arrested the supply point's commander, a major, his chief clerk and three sergeants, and the two Cholon dealers; the Special Court convicted all seven in March 1967.
> 
> The case did not stop the leak of ammunition to the Front; it moved it. After December the dealers bought whole crates from units in the field rather than loose lots from the depot, and the Front's purchasing agents paid more for unmarked Chinese 7.62mm than for the Republic's 5.56mm, which they had learned could be traced¹¹. What it did was establish, three years into the rearmament, that a cartridge case found on a battlefield could put an officer in prison, and that the trail from a firefight to the man who sold the rounds now ran through a register the Commission kept. Khoa told the Board in January 1967 that it was the first case in which the war itself had supplied the evidence.

### New: The relief at Dien Ban
*8–31 Aug 1966 · Dien Ban and Dai Loc Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon · EV006-3*

*Initiative: enemy*

The relief at Dien Ban was the first time the enemy attacked an American battalion in the week it changed over. The 1st Battalion, 9th Marines had spent a year in Dien Ban as a unit, and the 1st Battalion, 26th Marines, formed and trained together for nine months under Lieutenant Colonel Walter K. Dorsey, was to relieve it in place between 8 and 26 August, on dates fixed in March and known to everyone who sold the Marines ice. The new battalion knew nothing of the ground. What it had was continuity elsewhere: the subsector adviser, Major Carl E. Haney, and the ARVN battalions' advisers were selected men on eighteen-month tours, and Haney walked each company commander over his ground with the PF platoon leaders and gave each a list of the PF corporals who would tell a Marine what the hamlet knew. At 0130 on 19 August the R-20 Battalion and the district company hit Company B at La Huan through a treeline the new company had not yet learned to watch, and put sappers inside the wire. The platoons, nine months together, closed on the breach without waiting for orders, and by 0230 the sappers were dead and the second wave had not crossed the bund. A PF platoon Haney had introduced on the 14th reported the R-20's withdrawal route at 0310, and the Marines' mortars and aircraft caught it at the Song Ky Lam crossing. The Marines lost 14 killed, four times an average night, and the enemy about 40–60⁸². From October reliefs were staggered across six weeks and kept off the dark of the moon, which raised American strength in theater at every relief. The R-20's own verdict: the new Marines "fight like the old ones in their third month and know the ground like the old ones in their first"⁹.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> The relief at Dien Ban was the first time the enemy attacked an American battalion in the week it changed over, and it showed both halves of what unit rotation had done. The 1st Battalion, 9th Marines had come ashore at Da Nang in July 1965 and had spent a year in the hamlets of Dien Ban south of the airfield, the same companies under the same commander throughout. Under the rotation it was to be relieved in place by the 1st Battalion, 26th Marines, which had formed at Camp Pendleton in October 1965, trained together for nine months and sailed from Okinawa in late July under Lieutenant Colonel Walter K. Dorsey; the two battalions were to overlap from 8 to 26 August, company by company. The relief dates had been fixed in March and were known, as all such dates were, to every Vietnamese who sold the Marines ice or washed their clothes.
> 
> The 1st Battalion, 26th Marines arrived knowing nothing of Dien Ban. Its men had trained on the M4A1, the M249 and the M110A2 for six months and fired them as squads that had not changed since January; its officers had studied Ellison's area from the outgoing commander's reports and an overlay; none of them had walked the paddies at Phong Thu or Ky Lam, where the R-20 Doc Lap Battalion and the Front's Dien Ban district company had laid mines along the bunds for a year and knew every one of the old battalion's habits. What Dien Ban did have was continuity in the other places this headquarters had put it. The ARVN 51st Regiment's battalion advisers and the Dien Ban subsector adviser, Major Carl E. Haney, were all men of the Selected Advisory Corps on eighteen-month tours, two of them in their thirteenth month, and the district chief and the DIOCC had been in place since 1965. Haney walked each of Dorsey's company commanders over his ground with the Popular Forces platoon leaders of the hamlets it held, and gave each a list, in English and Vietnamese, of the PF corporals who would tell a Marine what the hamlet knew.
> 
> The Front had read the calendar too. On the night of 18–19 August, with two companies of the old battalion already embarked at Da Nang and two of the new on the ground for less than a week, the R-20 Battalion and the district company attacked Company B, 1st Battalion, 26th Marines in its new position at the hamlet of La Huan, about 4 km west of Route 1, at 0130 under a thin moon, with 82mm mortars from across the Song Ky Lam and a sapper assault from the south through a tree line the outgoing company had kept clear and the new one had not yet learned to watch. The first assault put a section of sappers inside the wire. What followed was the half of the event the rotation had bought: the company's platoons, which had trained together for nine months, closed on the breach without waiting for orders, the squad guns took the paddy south of the wire under grazing fire, and by 0230 the sappers inside were dead and the second wave had not crossed the bund. A PF platoon in the next hamlet, which Haney had introduced to the company's commander on the 14th, reported the R-20's withdrawal route by AN/PRC-25 at 0310, and two F-4Bs of Marine Aircraft Group 11 and the battalion's 81mm mortars hit it at the Song Ky Lam crossing before dawn.
> 
> The relief window had cost the Marines 14 killed and 37 wounded, about four times the battalion's average night that summer, and the enemy about 40–60 dead, of whom 23 were found⁸³. The outgoing battalion would not have been hit that way; it knew the tree line. The incoming one, under the old individual system, would have been a battalion of strangers at the breach, and I believe the sappers would have held the breach long enough to reach the company's ammunition point⁸⁴. MACV drew two orders from Dien Ban: from October 1966 reliefs were staggered across six weeks by company and kept off the dark of the moon, and no incoming company took over a position without a night with the outgoing one beside it. Both orders added men in theater at every relief. The R-20 Battalion drew its own lesson in a document captured in November: the new Marines "fight like the old ones in their third month and know the ground like the old ones in their first"⁹.

### New: The monsoon nights of Binh Dinh and the first Vietnamese gunships
*15 Oct 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Hoai Nhon, Phu My and Tam Quan Districts, Binh Dinh Province; Bien Hoa air base and the Air Training Centre at Nha Trang; Duc Hue District, Hau Nghia Province · EV015-4*

*Initiative: both*

By October 1966 the posts within the gunship net were seldom assaulted on clear nights, and the Front's Military Region 5 drew the conclusion its Delta regions had drawn two years earlier: the 2nd Regiment and the Binh Dinh battalions would attack the coast's posts on the nights the north-east monsoon brought the cloud down. On 26–27 October, under a 1,200-foot ceiling, three companies attacked three posts on Route 1 within an hour; the Ghostrider orbited above the cloud under the wing's rule of 1964, dropped two GBU-39s on map coordinates the district read in the rain, and missed by 400 metres, and two posts fell. Through November and December the Front attacked on 18 of the 30 low-cloud nights and on 2 of the 31 clear ones, and took eleven posts and about 300 weapons; the Korean posts, each with a 105mm battery in range, held¹³. Major General Vinh Loc's figures made two cases, for district guns in reach of every post and for a gunship that could see through cloud.

The second arrived on 1 January 1967: forty-eight AC-130U Spooky IIs with radar that could fire on offsets from a post in any weather, handed to a VNAF that had no one to fly them. Lieutenant Colonel Pham Quang Khiem formed the 81st Gunship Wing, the crews converted in the United States, and the radar technicians were the hardest to find, because the courses were in English and the VNAF had perhaps eighty men who could take them. Mixed American and Vietnamese crews did not work, and sorties became all-Vietnamese. On the night of 19–20 August 1967 the RF post at Hiep Hoa on the Vam Co Dong called in Vietnamese that it was under attack; the 817th Squadron's Spooky II was overhead at 0012, its fire-control officer, Captain Le Minh Tuan, spoke to the post's commander directly, and the 40mm and 105mm broke the assault in the cane through cloud in twenty minutes, for one man lost. It was the first time a Vietnamese post had been defended at night from the air by Vietnamese, and Khiem played the post commander's call on the wing's loudspeakers the next morning. The second squadron was sent to Nha Trang for the coast on Vinh Loc's figures. The A-1 squadrons paid for the wing with a fifth of their avionics technicians and two to three points of readiness¹³.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> This is the season that shows where the night war went when the gunship took the clear nights from it. By October 1966 the posts of the Delta and the Saigon belt within the gunship net were seldom assaulted on clear nights, and in the coastal lowlands of II Corps the Front's Military Region 5 had drawn the conclusion its Delta regions had drawn two years earlier. The 2nd Regiment of the PAVN 3rd (Sao Vang) Division and the Binh Dinh provincial battalions, rebuilt after the Bong Son operations of the spring, prepared through September to attack the posts of the coast in the north-east monsoon, on the nights the cloud came down.
> 
> The monsoon arrived in the third week of October. On the night of 26–27 October, under a cloud base of about 1,200 feet and in heavy rain, three companies attacked three posts on Route 1 between Bong Son and Tam Quan within an hour of each other. All three called Hoai Nhon district on their sets. The Ghostrider on station south of Qui Nhon came north and orbited above the cloud at 5,000 feet, seeing on its infrared turret only the diffused glow of the flares and the fires; its crew, under the wing's rule of December 1964, did not go down. It dropped two GBU-39s on the coordinates the district gave for a mortar position, which the district had read from a 1:50,000 map in the rain, and the bombs fell about 400 metres from where the mortar had been. Two of the three posts fell before dawn. The 105mm battery at Bong Son could reach one of them, and fired.
> 
> Through November and December the pattern held. The Front attacked the posts of Hoai Nhon, Phu My and Tam Quan on about 18 of the 30 nights the cloud was below 3,000 feet, and on 2 of the 31 nights it was not. Eleven posts and one district police post fell, about as many as the coast lost in history's same months, and the Front took about 300 weapons, most of them M4A1s, and the files of the Phu My police post. The Korean Capital Division's posts south of Qui Nhon were attacked on the same nights and held, because each had a 105mm battery within range; the Korean commanders had not trusted the gunships from the first. In the Delta, where the south-west monsoon's cloud is afternoon convection that clears by midnight, the same months saw the fewest attacks on posts of the war so far.
> 
> Major General Vinh Loc's II Corps headquarters sent the season's figures to Saigon in January 1967, and they made two cases. The first was for guns: a district battery within reach of every post on the coast, which the Korean posts had shown worked and which the domestic arsenal could feed. The second was for a gunship that could see through cloud. The Spooky IIs promised to the VNAF had arrived on 1 January; their AN/APQ-180 radar could find a post and fire on offsets from it in any weather, and the Joint General Staff, on Vinh Loc's figures, sent the second VNAF squadron to Nha Trang for the coast rather than to Da Nang¹³. The coastal posts' night belonged to the weather for two more monsoons.

### New: Operation STEADY HAND
*14–19 Nov 1966 · Cai Be District, Dinh Tuong Province, between Route 4 and the Plain of Reeds; the hamlets of Hau My village · EV010-3*

*Initiative: both*

The rice was the reason for both sides. The flood of 1966 had drowned the Front's stocks north of Route 4, and the Dinh Tuong committee sent the 263rd Main Force Battalion to escort its levy in Cai Be as the harvest came in; the 7th Division mounted STEADY HAND to cover the government's procurement in the same hamlets. On the afternoon of 16 November the 3rd Battalion, 11th Regiment's lead company, in file on a canal dike, walked into an L at 40 to 60 metres, and its commander, Captain Nguyen Huu Tam, and both forward platoon leaders were hit in the first two minutes. Sergeant First Class Tran Van Loc had passed the senior course the year before, and his squads were led by two sergeants and four corporals who had passed the leader's course. The squads went off the dike on the side away from the long arm, each putting its M249 on the treeline while the riflemen crawled; Loc took the radio, reported the company's position in a form the battalion could plot, and called the battery at Cai Be onto the treeline 150 metres beyond his own men.
