The first rounds came eleven minutes after the ambush opened, the M113s came up the next dike, and the 263rd broke contact into the flooded reeds. The company lost 14 killed of about 120, with all its weapons, against the 40 to 60 dead such ambushes had cost⁷. The government then bought twice 1965's paddy in Hau My. Two of Loc's acting squad leaders went absent in December to bring in their families' harvest, because a private's pay after the devaluation bought a third less rice.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> The rice was the reason for both sides. The Mekong flood of September and October 1966 had drowned much of the Plain of Reeds and the main-season crop in the districts north of Route 4, and the Front's Dinh Tuong provincial committee, its own stocks lost in the water, ordered the 263rd Main Force Battalion in late October to escort its rice levy in the hamlets of Cai Be as the harvest came in. The 7th Division, with the province chief, mounted STEADY HAND to cover the government's procurement in the same hamlets: the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of the 11th Regiment, with an M113 troop of the division's armored cavalry, swept north from Route 4 into Hau My village on 14 November to clear the canal lines along which the farmers would move the paddy to the Cai Be market.
> 
> On the afternoon of 16 November the 3rd Battalion's lead company, moving north along a canal dike in file, walked into the 263rd's ambush: two companies in an L along a tree line and a second canal, with an RPD on each arm and a 57mm recoilless rifle at the corner, at 40 to 60 metres. The company commander, Captain Nguyen Huu Tam, and both of his forward platoon leaders were hit in the first two minutes. On the historical course of such ambushes, a company that lost its officers on a dike in the open lost about half its men before the rest of the battalion reached it⁸⁵. This one did not. Sergeant First Class Tran Van Loc, the senior platoon sergeant, had passed the senior course at Nha Trang the year before, and his squads were led by two sergeants and four acting squad leaders, corporals first class who had passed the leader's course, because the field commissions of September had taken two of the company's best sergeants to Thu Duc. The squads went off the dike into the paddy on the side away from the long arm of the L, each squad leader putting his M249 on the tree line while the riflemen crawled; Loc took the radio, reported the contact and the company's position on the AN/PRC-25 in a form the battalion could plot, and asked for the 105mm M101A1 battery at Cai Be on the tree line at 150 metres beyond his own men. The first rounds came at 1534, eleven minutes after the ambush opened. The M113 troop came up the next dike at 1550 with its.50-calibre guns on the tree line, and the 263rd broke contact at about 1610 and went north into the flooded reeds, carrying its wounded.
> 
> The company lost 14 killed and 22 wounded, of about 120, and all its weapons came out with it; on the historical course I would have expected 40 to 60 killed and the company's squad guns and radio left on the dike. Eleven of the 263rd's dead were found in the tree line; I believe it lost 20 to 30 killed, and I do not credit the district's report of 74. The sweep went on to 19 November without further contact. In the following three weeks the government's procurement in Hau My and the two villages beside it bought about 1,400 tonnes of paddy, about twice the province's figure for the same villages in 1965, and the Front's levy there took about a third less than its committee had ordered, by the committee's own figures captured in 1967. The pay of the 3rd Battalion's soldiers, after the devaluation of June, bought about a third less rice than it had in the spring, and two of Loc's acting squad leaders were absent without leave for a week in December to bring their families' harvest in⁷. Loc was made a master sergeant in the board's spring list of 1967; Captain Tam survived and returned to the battalion in March.

### No longer happens: The Spooky IIs and the 817th's first night
*1 Jan – 31 Dec 1967 · Bien Hoa air base and the Air Training Centre at Nha Trang; Hurlburt Field, Florida; Duc Hue District, Hau Nghia Province · EV015-5*

*Merged at R05 into EV015-4; the wing and the night at Hiep Hoa stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> Forty-eight AC-130U Spooky IIs arrived at Bien Hoa and Nha Trang from 1 January 1967 and were handed to a Vietnamese Air Force that had no one to fly them. The VNAF formed the 81st Gunship Wing under Lieutenant Colonel Pham Quang Khiem, a C-47 squadron commander who had flown Farm Gate's observer seat in the Ghostriders in 1964 and was among the first VNAF officers through the Air Command and Staff course, and an American training detachment of about 300 under the 14th Air Commando Wing. Thirty C-47 and C-119 pilots went to the United States in January to convert; the first navigators, fire-control officers and electronic-warfare officers, drawn from the Thu Duc and Dalat classes of 1962–65 and from the VNAF's transport navigators, went in February for about a year. The radar and fire-control technicians were the hardest to find, as the dossier had warned: the technical courses were in English, and the VNAF had perhaps eighty men who could take them in 1967.
>

The first all-Vietnamese combat sortie of the 817th Squadron was flown from Bien Hoa on the night of 19–20 August 1967. At 2350 the RF post at Hiep Hoa, on the Vam Co Dong in Duc Hue district, called the district in Vietnamese that it was under attack from the north-east; the Spooky II was over it at 0012, its fire-control officer, Captain Le Minh Tuan, spoke to the post's commander directly, and the 40mm and 105mm broke the assault in the cane north of the post in about twenty minutes, under a cloud base the radar saw through. The post lost one man. It was the first time in the war that a Vietnamese post had been defended at night from the air by Vietnamese, and Khiem had the post commander's call played on the wing's loudspeakers at Bien Hoa the next morning.
> 
> By December 1967 the 817th had eleven crews and flew about 120 sorties a month over III and IV Corps; the 819th was forming at Nha Trang for the coast, and the 821st had not begun. The cost was in the rest of the VNAF: the A-1 squadrons at Bien Hoa lost about a fifth of their avionics technicians to the gunship wing in 1967, and their aircraft were about two to three points less often operational for it¹³.

### No longer happens: The arrest count falls
*Feb – Nov 1967 · Saigon; Phong Dinh, Long An and Vinh Long Provinces; and the towns of the Delta · EV002-5*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-4; the falling count and the argument over targets stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> In the first quarter of 1967 the Special Branch's arrests of infrastructure in the held belt of the Delta fell to about 40 percent of their peak of the second quarter of 1966, and the Phung Hoang centres' neutralizations of district-level cadres fell with them, from about 140 a quarter in 1966 to about 50. The Office of the Secretary of Defense's systems analysts read the decline as a programme losing its grip, and in February Robert Komer, then the President's special assistant for pacification, proposed monthly arrest targets by province as the measure of the attack on the infrastructure. This headquarters answered in writing on 3 April that the count was falling because the programme was working: in the districts with posts three years old there was almost no one left in the villages to arrest, and the measures the enemy could not fake, captured tax ledgers, the count of functioning village committees in captured documents, and the age of captured guerrillas, all showed the infrastructure shrinking there. The Director General of National Police, Brigadier General Nguyen Ngoc Loan, wanted the targets; Commissioner Khoa opposed them on the record, and so did Hieu, whose decree of 1964 forbade them in terms.
> 
> The decree held, and the half-victory of the historical-course compromise was a whole one on paper: no centre and no province was given a target in 1967, and the held belt was measured by captured documents and the contested belt by the Commission's audit. It was less than a whole one on the ground. The pressure that would have gone into targets went instead into extending the method to the contested belt, where it produced what the abandoned target list had predicted, raids on thin files, and after Duc Thanh the extension was halted village by village. In the second half of 1967 the Commission received about 190 complaints of false arrest from the contested districts with centres and about 40 from the held belt, against the 430 that targets had produced on the earlier course⁹. And the infrastructure that had left the held villages had not disappeared. The Special Branch's provincial sections reported through 1967 that legal cadres and their families were settling in Can Tho, My Tho, Vinh Long and the outskirts of Saigon, among the refugees, where a constable in a ward of 10,000 knew far less than one in a village of 2,000⁶. The Branch built urban sections to follow them, slowly. The war against the infrastructure had moved toward the towns, and so, as the Branch's own reports warned in November, had the Front's means of acting there.

### New: The Mo Duc raid and the Phoenix story
*11 Feb – 30 Jun 1967 · Duc Thanh village, Mo Duc District, Quang Ngai Province; Saigon; Hanoi; Washington · EV006-4*

*Initiative: both*

The raid at Duc Thanh was what the method became where the night was not held. With little left to find in the held belt, the corps and CORDS wanted the same results from the contested provinces, and Quang Ngai's province chief opened centres in four contested districts against Hieu's advice, on files built from ralliers and the S2's informants. At 0200 on 11 February 1967 a PRU team of 24 went into the house of a Duc Thanh schoolteacher named on two sources, both ralliers from the same hamlet, as the Mo Duc committee's propaganda chief. A man in the house fired a pistol, the team fired back, and the teacher, his wife, his father and two of his children died⁹. The propaganda chief was another man, arrested in May; the teacher had been named by a rallier whose family quarrelled with his over a well.

Hanoi had decided in January, for reasons of its own reading of Moscow, the American calendar and the world's opinion, to fight while negotiating, and its propaganda wanted material that would carry abroad. Liberation Radio broadcast the deaths on 19 February as the work of "the American Phoenix murder teams", and by 10 March two American national newspapers had the story, with the programme's name, the CIA's hand in its design and the PRUs' American pay, three years before history's Phoenix stories. The Commission published its finding on 6 April: two ralliers from one feud counted as independent, a warrant signed unread, no capture plan. The team leader was convicted of manslaughter, the judge removed, and raid files withdrawn from fifteen contested districts of I and II Corps until each village had a post and a platoon. On 30 June the national committee published the first audited count, about 14,500 neutralized on warrant since 1965, 800 of them killed, with one claim in ten unsupported in the held belt and one in four in the contested belt⁹. It was the first figure on the attack on the infrastructure the newspapers did not have to correct, and it did not undo Duc Thanh. The word Phoenix was in the American vocabulary, and it meant what the Front had said it meant.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> The raid at Duc Thanh was what the method became where the night was not held, and it reached the American press within a month. By the end of 1966 the held belt had little left for the district centres to find, and the corps commanders and the CORDS planners wanted the same results from the contested provinces of I and II Corps, where the Front still ran most villages after dark. Quang Ngai's province chief opened DIOCCs in four contested districts in the autumn of 1966 against Hieu's advice, and the Quang Ngai PRU, which had been raised under the statute in 1964 and had operated by its rules in the coastal towns, began to raid on files built mostly from ralliers and from the S2's informants. On the night of 11 February 1967 a PRU team of 24 men, acting on a file that named a hamlet schoolteacher in Duc Thanh as the Mo Duc district committee's propaganda chief on two sources, both ralliers from the same hamlet, went into his house at 0200; a man in the house fired a pistol, the team fired back with M4A1s and an M249, and the teacher, his wife, his father and two of his children died. The district committee's propaganda chief was a different man, arrested in May; the schoolteacher had been named by a rallier whose family had a quarrel with his over a well.
> 
> The Front's answer was ready because Hanoi had decided, for its own reasons, to fight on a new front. The Thirteenth Plenum of January 1967 had adopted the line of "fighting while negotiating", and on 28 January Foreign Minister Nguyen Duy Trinh had said that talks could follow an unconditional halt in the bombing; the decision came from Hanoi's reading of Soviet pressure, the American election calendar and the world's opinion of the bombing, and from nothing this headquarters did. Its consequence for the Front's propaganda apparatus was a demand for material that would carry abroad. Liberation Radio broadcast the Duc Thanh deaths on 19 February as "a massacre by the American Phoenix murder teams", and the story reached an American wire service in Saigon through a Quang Ngai stringer on 2 March; by 10 March two national newspapers had run it, with the programme's American name, the CIA's role in its design and the PRUs' American pay. On the historical course the Phoenix stories began in 1970.
> 
> Two things were different from what the historical stories would have found, and both mattered. The Commission's inspectors had the Duc Thanh file within a week and published their finding on 6 April: the file had met the three-source rule only by counting two ralliers from one feud as independent, the warrant had been signed by a district judge who had not read it, and the PRU had entered without a capture plan. The PRU team leader was tried before the Special Court in June and convicted of manslaughter; the judge was removed; Hieu withdrew the centres' authority to issue raid files in the four contested districts of Quang Ngai and in eleven others in I and II Corps until each had a post and a platoon in the village concerned. And the national committee published its first audited count on 30 June: since January 1965, about 14,500 people neutralized on warrant, of whom about 9,800 were tried or held under review, about 3,900 had rallied and about 800 had been killed, about 300 of them in the programme's own raids, with the Commission's sample finding about one claim in ten unsupported in the held belt and one in four in the contested belt⁹. The count was small, and it was the first figure on the attack on the infrastructure that the newspapers did not later have to correct. It did not undo Duc Thanh. The word Phoenix was in the American vocabulary three years early, and it meant what the Front had said it meant.

### No longer happens: The estuary field
*26 Feb – 31 Dec 1967 · The mouths of the Song Ca, Song Giang and Kien Giang, the lighterage anchorages at Quang Khe, Dong Hoi and Cua Viet north, and the coastal waters of Route Package 1, North Vietnam · EV005-3*

*Merged at R05 into EV005-2; the field stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> On 26 February 1967 Washington authorized, for the first time, the aerial mining of the North's rivers south of the 20th parallel. Historically Navy A-6As from the *Enterprise* laid the first Mk 50-series mines in the mouths of the Song Ca and Song Giang that night. In this war the first field was laid by four B-52Js from U-Tapao, which put 80 Mk 64 and Mk 65 Quickstrikes into the Song Ca estuary below Vinh and the Song Giang at Quang Khe from about 1,000 feet in a single pass each, at night, outside the guns that later covered both mouths. The target detecting devices were set for the steel-hulled lighters and coastal freighters that carried supplies down from Thanh Hoa and Vinh; the wooden junks were left to the pressure settings, and the sampans were not mined at all, because no setting would catch them²⁶.
> 
> The panhandle watch and the Gulf watch counted the effect. In the first fortnight two steel lighters sank at the Quang Khe bar and a third in the Song Ca, and the steel traffic on the coastal route south of Vinh fell within a month to about a fifth of what it had been. Through the spring the Js reseeded each field every three to four weeks, on the cue of the Global Hawk's imagery when the North's sweepers came out, and lost no aircraft doing it. By June the steel craft had stopped coming south of Thanh Hoa.
> 
> The cargo did not stop. It moved to wooden junks, to sampans under tow and to trucks on Route 1A and Route 15, and by the autumn the radar's count of southbound truck movements below Vinh was about 25–30 percent higher than in 1966 while the tonnage counted into the panhandle was about the same. The coastal lighterage had carried perhaps a fifth of what moved south of Vinh, and the road took nearly all of it in four months. Its value was in time and labour: the North spent perhaps 15,000–25,000 more porters and road workers on Route Package 1 in 1967 than it otherwise would, and its trucks spent more nights in the open where the radar could count them. Hanoi asked Moscow for wooden-hulled craft and for minesweeping help; it got trucks, which was what it needed²⁷. The field stayed in place until the bombing halt of November 1968, and nobody in Washington asked, because nobody could answer, how much less arrived in the South because of it. My own answer is very little.

### New: The list, the devaluation and the 25th Division
*4 Mar – 31 Oct 1967 · Duc Hoa, Hau Nghia Province, and the 25th Division's districts in Hau Nghia and Long An; the Joint General Staff and the Officer Selection Board, Saigon · EV007-4*

*Initiative: allied*

The 25th Division was the ARVN's worst, and its soldiers' families had paid for the devaluation of June 1966. The piaster went from 60 to 118 to the dollar, Saigon prices rose by half, and a private's pay bought a third less by December; the wives in the dependents' quarters at Duc Hoa could not feed a household on it⁸¹. About 2,000 men walked out of the division in the second half of 1966, all of them trained at Quang Trung; most went home, and a few hundred went to the guerrilla platoons of Cu Chi and Duc Hoa, where a captured notebook recorded a squad leaders' course taught by "a brother who was trained by the puppets at Quang Trung", with the note that the puppets' course was good and their pay was not⁵.

In March 1967 the division became the test of whether the ranked list could reach a division. Ky wanted a cousin of an Air Force patron who was not on the list; Thieu took its second name, Colonel Vu Ngoc Hoan, after the Mission told both men that the division's counterpart funds depended on it (Article 14). It was one of two division commands in ten filled from the list against a palace preference by the end of 1967. Hoan relieved three battalion commanders through the thirty-day reviews in ninety days, put his battalions into the districts at night beside the PF, moved the dependents' quarters inside the battalions' perimeters and paid the rice ration in rice wherever he could buy it⁵. By October desertion had fallen by about a quarter and contacts had doubled, and the Front's companies in Duc Hoa and Duc Hue had moved toward the border; the division could visit Hau Nghia's hamlets after dark and still not hold them¹⁰. In July the board extended its reviews to the RF company commanders of III and IV Corps and replaced about 60 of 280.

On 11 October the Military Security Service arrested Lieutenant Truong Cong Hy, a clerk of the board's secretariat since 1965, as an agent of the B2 Front. He had passed every command list, with the panels' ratings, to the Cu Chi committee, and COSVN's target notes showed the regiments planning their ambushes of 1967 against the battalions that had not yet been given new commanders¹⁰. The board's best evidence of its own effect came from the man who had betrayed it.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> 
> The 25th Division was the ARVN's worst, and in 1967 it became the test of whether the ranked list could reach a division. Its battalions, in Hau Nghia and western Long An between Saigon and the Parrot's Beak, had the highest desertion rate and the lowest rate of contact in III Corps, its regiments had been commanded by the division commander's appointees until the board's lists of 1965–66, and its commander, appointed in 1965 before the list existed, had refused to move his headquarters out of Duc Hoa at night. When he was due for reassignment in March 1967 the board's ranked list put three colonels before the Directory. Ky wanted a fourth man, an Air Force patron's cousin who was not on it; Thieu, as Chief of State, took the second name, Colonel Vu Ngoc Hoan, a Dalat graduate of 1952 who had commanded a regiment of the 7th Division well under the board's list, after the US Mission told both men through the Aid Compliance Board that the division's counterpart funds depended on the list (Article 14). It was one of two division commands in ten filled from the list against a palace preference by the end of 1967.
> 
> Hoan relieved three battalion commanders in his first ninety days, all through the board's thirty-day reviews and all for what the reviews called failure to close with the enemy, and put the division's battalions into the districts at night beside the Popular Forces, which the corps had never asked it to do. By October the division's desertion rate had fallen by about a quarter, its battalions were in contact about twice as often as in 1966, and the Front's district companies in Duc Hoa and Duc Hue had moved their bases toward the Cambodian border. None of this changed who held most of Hau Nghia's hamlets after dark, which the division could visit and could not hold.
> 
> In July the board extended its lists to the commanders of the Regional Force companies of III and IV Corps, at the request of the III Corps commander after the losses of the RF convoys on Route 13. About 280 RF company commanders were reviewed by the end of the year and about 60 replaced, most of them by field-commissioned lieutenants of their own provinces.
> 
> On 11 October the Military Security Service arrested Lieutenant Truong Cong Hy, a clerk of the board's secretariat since 1965, as an agent of the B2 Front's military intelligence. He had copied every command list the board had published, with the panels' ratings of each selected officer, and passed them by courier to the Cu Chi district committee. The COSVN target notes taken with his courier in November showed what the lists had been used for: the B2 Front's regiments had been told which battalions in III Corps were under new commanders and which were not, and had planned their ambushes of 1967 against the second¹⁰. The board's best evidence of its own effect came from the man who had betrayed it.

### No longer happens: The Special Court convicts the IV Corps quartermaster
*6 Mar – 18 Apr 1967 · Can Tho, Phong Dinh Province, and the Special Court for Corruption, Saigon · EV001-7*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-6; the case stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> On 6 March 1967 the Commission Against Corruption arrested Brigadier General Phan Duy Khiem, IV Corps deputy commander for logistics since 1965, with eleven officers of the corps quartermaster and finance staffs at Can Tho. The case was documentary and had been built for fourteen months. The Pay and Muster Verification Service's parade payments had removed ghost pay from the corps' units in 1964–65, and the graft had moved, as this headquarters had expected, to rations and fuel. The Service's auditors matched the corps' monthly ration draws against the strength the musters had established and found the corps drawing rice, canned fish and salt for about 9,000 more men than it had; a parallel audit by the Joint Aid Compliance Board traced about 2.1 million litres of motor fuel issued to RF companies with no vehicles and sold through two Cholon dealers. The total over two years came to about 310 million piasters, about $2.6 million at the official rate.
> 
> The arrest was made by the Commission's own judicial police, Vietnamese officers under Commissioner Khoa, with no American present. General Khiem was the first general officer the Commission had charged, three years after it was founded; it had refused the junta's invitations to begin at the top in 1964 and had worked upward from battalion and district. His patron in the Directory tried to have the case moved to a military court in March; the Deputy Chief of Mission, as American co-chair of the Board, told the Directory's chairman, General Thieu, that the US Mission would suspend counterpart funds to IV Corps under the Board's authority if the case was moved, and Thieu, then preparing his presidential candidacy and wanting no quarrel with the Embassy, let it stand. The Special Court tried the case in public in Saigon over nine sitting days and on 18 April 1967 sentenced Khiem to eight years and confiscation of property, and nine of the eleven officers to terms of two to six years.
> 
> The conviction mattered more in the officer corps than in the countryside. It established that the Commission's reach now ran to the rank below the Directory and no higher; that it reached that rank only on documentary evidence and with the American lever behind it; and that a general who stole from his troops' rations could go to prison. The American press reported it as a sign that the Saigon government was cleaning itself up, and for a few weeks the corruption stories of the spring were about a conviction rather than a scandal. The officers of the IV Corps staff who replaced the convicted were chosen in part from the Commission's own list of officers with clean records, and there were not enough of them⁴.

### New: The night of the relief at My Phuoc Tay
*9–10 Mar 1967 · The PF post at Ap My Loi and the canal road to Cai Lay district town, My Phuoc Tay village, Cai Lay District, Dinh Tuong Province · EV008-4*

*Initiative: enemy*

By 1967 every PF post in the held belt of Dinh Tuong had a PRC-25 on the district net and a fresh battery every Thursday, and the Front had stopped assaulting them; that spring the provincial unit decided to use the radio against the men it called¹². At 2220 on 9 March a company of the 261st Battalion attacked the post at Long Dinh, 25 kilometres east, and the province's Ghostrider went there, as the call told it to; it was the first diversion the Front made to draw the gunship off¹³. At 2235 a mortar section put twelve rounds into the post at Ap My Loi, six kilometres north of Cai Lay. Sergeant Le Van Muoi, schooled at Nha Trang and the Dinh Tuong centre, called the district at 2237 with the mortar and an assault forming to the west; at 2241 his listening post on the canal bank reported men moving south in the cane toward the road, and he added that as his third line⁷. The district chief, Major Nguyen Thanh Liem, read the first two lines and sent the 247th RF Company north in four trucks at 2250, because the rule said a post that called would have its reaction within the hour.

At 2304 a mine under a culvert three kilometres south of the post lifted the lead truck; its firing circuit was the Republic's own field wire and a pack of Go Vap dry cells. Two companies of the 514th Local Force Battalion fired into the other trucks from the cane for eight minutes and were gone before the battery at Cai Lay had a target. The 247th lost 31 dead and about 40 weapons; the post lost one man wounded¹². The gunship reached the canal road at 2318 and caught one company crossing open paddy, and I put the 514th's dead at about 20–30¹³.

Liem wrote four rules that spring, and they spread through IV Corps. A post's first call would be for fire, from guns with its concentrations plotted, answered within four minutes. A relief would move by water or at first light, never at night on the one road the Front could predict. A post's report of movement on the relief route stopped the relief until the route was fired on or cleared. And no relief would move by road at night unless a gunship flew the road ahead of it. On 14 June the 247th went north again under a post's call with a Ghostrider two kilometres ahead; its turret found about fifty men in the cane at the same culvert, and the 514th left 26 dead and two recoilless rifles there¹³. Attacks on posts within the guns' reach fell by a third, and the Front turned to the posts beyond the guns' 11 kilometres and to batteries run down at the end of the week. The rules had a cost the returns did not show: a platoon that could call down the guns had less reason to leave its wire, the PF's night patrols in Cai Lay fell by a third, and the hamlet outside the post was walked at night more often by the Front's tax collectors¹². Ap My Loi held every attack made on it for the rest of the war. Whether the hamlet was the government's after dark, its radio log cannot say.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> This is the night the radio's second-order effect became visible, and the night that shows it best. By 1967 every Popular Forces post in the held belt of Dinh Tuong had a set on the district net, a PRC-25 from the Go Vap plant since the previous autumn, and a fresh battery every Thursday from the exchange at the district. The Front had stopped assaulting those posts in 1965, as it had stopped assaulting the rearmed ones. In the first months of 1967 the Dinh Tuong provincial unit decided to use the radio against the men it called.
> 
> At 2235 on 9 March a mortar section of the 514th Local Force Battalion put twelve 60mm rounds into the post at Ap My Loi, a mud-walled fort on the canal six kilometres north of Cai Lay, from about 300 metres across the paddy. Sergeant Le Van Muoi, who commanded its PF platoon, called the district at 2237, reported the mortar and an assault forming on the dike to the west, and asked for the reaction force. The assault did not come. Two companies of the 514th were not on the dike at all; they were lying in the sugar cane on both sides of the canal road, three kilometres south of the post, where the road crossed a concrete culvert that the district's trucks had to slow to cross.
> 
> The district chief, Major Nguyen Thanh Liem, did what the rule of 1964 told him, that a post that called would have its reaction within the hour, and sent the 247th Regional Force Company north in four trucks at 2250. At 2304 a command-detonated mine under the culvert lifted the lead truck off the road. The firing circuit, the district's engineers found in the morning, was two kilometres of WD-1 field wire from the Republic's own mill and a pack of Go Vap dry cells of the kind the post had been issued the week before. The two companies fired into the other three trucks from both sides for about eight minutes, took the weapons from the first, and were gone into the cane before the 7th Division's battery at Cai Lay had been given a target. The 247th lost 31 dead and 18 wounded and about 40 weapons, most of them M4A1 carbines and two M249s. The post itself lost one man, wounded by the mortar. The district reported 46 of the enemy killed; eight bodies were found at the culvert in the morning, and I believe the 514th lost between ten and fifteen killed.
> 
> In this war there was a gunship over Dinh Tuong that night, and the Front had planned for it. At 2220, fifteen minutes before the mortar opened on Ap My Loi, a company of the 261st Main Force Battalion attacked the post at Long Dinh in Chau Thanh district, 25 kilometres east, with mortars and a ground probe, and the Ghostrider of the 4th Squadron on station over the province went there, as the post's call and the district's relay told it to. It was firing on the 261st's company in the rice east of Long Dinh when the mine went off under the culvert at Cai Lay, and by the time it reached the canal road at 2318 the two companies of the 514th were in the cane, moving north-west by squads, and the crew found and fired on only one of them as it crossed the open paddy toward the Plain of Reeds. The 514th's dead at the culvert and in the paddy I now put at about 20–30. The 261st's attack at Long Dinh was a diversion, the first the Front had made to draw the gunship off; it was not the last.
> 
> Liem wrote new rules the following week, and they are the reason the night belongs in the history. A post's first call would be for fire, not men: every post in the district had its concentrations plotted for the 105mm battery at Cai Lay and the 7th Division's guns at Cai Be, and the call was answered by the guns within four minutes. A relief would move by water or at first light, never by road at night on the one road the Front could predict. And a post that could hold behind its wire would be expected to. The rules spread through IV Corps in the spring, carried by the province advisers and by the 7th Division's artillery officers. In the months that followed, attacks on posts within range of the guns in Dinh Tuong fell by about a third, and the Front's district companies turned to the posts beyond the guns' 11 kilometres and to the posts whose batteries were run down at the end of the exchange week.
> 
> The rules had a cost that the returns did not show and Liem's adviser did. A platoon that could call down the guns had less reason to leave its wire after dark, and in 1967 the night patrols of the PF platoons in Cai Lay fell by about a third; the post held itself, and the hamlet outside it was walked at night, more often than before, by the Front's tax collectors¹². Ap My Loi held every attack made on it for the rest of the war. Whether the hamlet that bore its name was the government's after dark is a question the post's radio log cannot answer.
> 
> Sergeant Muoi had passed the leader's course at Nha Trang in 1961 and the platoon leader's course at the Dinh Tuong centre in 1964, and he kept a listening post of two men on the canal bank 300 metres south of the post every night. At 2241 they reported men moving south in the cane on the far side of the canal, toward the road, and Muoi added it to his report: the mortar, an assault forming to the west, and movement south toward the culvert. The district operations room logged it as the third of three lines. Liem read the first two and sent the trucks, because the rule said the reaction within the hour and the post had called; the sergeant had seen the ambush and the decision was not his⁷. The ambush went as told. The third of Liem's new rules came from Muoi's line in the log: a post's report of movement on the relief route stops the relief until the route is fired on or cleared at first light, and the district's posts were taught, through their platoon leaders, to report the road as well as the wire.
> 
> Liem's fourth rule came from the night's other lesson. No relief would move by road at night unless a gunship flew the road ahead of it, and the province's two gunship sorties a night were assigned in pairs from April, one over the posts and one held for the road. On the night of 14 June 1967 the 247th RF Company moved north to Ap My Loi again, under a post's call, with a Ghostrider over the canal road two kilometres ahead of the trucks; its turret found about fifty men lying in the cane at the culvert, the trucks stopped, and the 105mm and 30mm fired on the cane for twenty minutes. The 514th left 26 dead and two 57mm recoilless rifles at the culvert, and the 247th reached the post at 0130 without a man hit¹³. It did not lay an ambush on that road again on a clear night.

### Changed: CORDS is established
*9 May 1967 · Saigon · EV000-35*

*Initiative: allied*

On 9 May 1967 the President put American pacification, civil and military, under MACV as CORDS, with Robert W. Komer as Westmoreland's deputy with ambassadorial rank, a province senior adviser beside every province chief, and priorities in the territorial forces and the attack on the infrastructure⁸⁶. The Hamlet Evaluation System began rating every hamlet monthly in January, an indispensable record produced by officers rated on the result. CORDS solved the American management problem of pacification and not the Vietnamese one, that security in the hamlet at night depended on Vietnamese forces who had to stay there.

It came on history's date and in history's form, and it inherited more. The land advisers passed into it with a register of about 740,000 titled hectares and their households, the first hamlet-by-hamlet household record American pacification ever had; Komer made titled hectares a factor in the hamlet ratings over this headquarters' written objection that titles rose fastest where they meant least, and kept it at half weight⁴. The Public Safety advisers passed into it with a National Police of about 70,000, about 1,500 village posts and a Special Branch with files kept since 1964. There was no ICEX, because there was nothing for it to create: the Phung Hoang centres had sat in every district since 1965, and the PRUs answered to the province chiefs under the police statute⁹. Komer's contribution was the money to put an American adviser in every contested district's centre, which Hieu accepted, and the monthly targets, which the decree forbade. The province senior advisers found counterparts who had held their provinces for two or three years⁶. The rule that RF companies belonged to the province chief was written into CORDS's charter from IV Corps' returns of 1966.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: allied*
> On 9 May 1967 the President placed the American pacification effort, civil and military, under MACV as Civil Operations and Revolutionary Development Support, with Robert W. Komer as one of Westmoreland's deputies, holding ambassadorial rank and authority over military personnel and resources, the first civilian to serve in such a role inside a US military command. It followed the failure of the Office of Civil Operations, set up in November 1966 to coordinate the civil agencies under civilian leadership. CORDS was about 85 percent military. Each corps had a CORDS deputy, usually civilian, under the corps senior adviser, and each province an American province senior adviser with civilian and military staffs alongside the Vietnamese province chief, usually an ARVN colonel.
> 
> Komer's priorities were the territorial forces and the attack on the VC infrastructure. The Regional and Popular Forces numbered about 300,000 in 1967; their advisory presence was later multiplied through Mobile Advisory Teams⁸⁶. In mid-1967 CORDS created the Intelligence Coordination and Exploitation programme, ICEX, to target the VCI, which became the Phoenix programme at the end of the year. The Hamlet Evaluation System, introduced in January 1967, began rating every hamlet monthly on a scale reported by the American district advisers; its figures were at once an indispensable record and a measure produced by officers rated on the result. CORDS solved the American management problem of pacification. It did not solve the Vietnamese one, that security in the hamlet at night depended on Vietnamese forces and officials who had to stay there.
> 
> In this war CORDS is established on the historical date and in the historical form; the provisions did not create a single manager. What CORDS inherits is different. The American land advisers, about 260 in 1964 and about 340 by 1967, pass into it as a land reform division under the CORDS deputy, and the provincial land services' register of titled parcels, which by May 1967 lists about 740,000 hectares and the households that hold them, becomes the first hamlet-by-hamlet household record the American pacification effort has ever had¹⁶. Komer adds titled hectares as a factor in the Hamlet Evaluation System's economic rating from its first revision. This headquarters objected in writing on 22 June 1967 that a title measured the government's paperwork and not the peasant's allegiance, that the Front had told its cadres to let peasants take titles and keep paying the Front's tax, and that titles issued would rise fastest where they meant least. The objection was recorded and the factor kept, at half the weight Komer had proposed. The Phung Hoang centres, which had used the land register since 1964 to locate the families of known cadres, passed into CORDS's reporting with it; the Commission had been receiving complaints about that use since 1965⁴.
> 
> In this war CORDS inherits a police as well as a land register. The aid mission's Public Safety Division, about 300 advisers in 1966, passes into CORDS as its Public Safety Directorate, and with it a National Police of about 70,000, about 1,500 village posts, and a Special Branch with district sections in about 200 districts and files on the infrastructure kept since 1964¹⁷. There is no ICEX in this war, because there is nothing for it to create: the Phung Hoang centres have sat in those district sections since 1964, under the district chief, with the Military Security Service and the sector S2 in the room, and every district has one by the end of 1965. The Provincial Reconnaissance Units were raised under the police statute in 1964 and answer to the province chiefs, not to the Agency; their methods are inside the statute's safeguards in law, and Duc Thanh in February showed how far that law reached in a village the government did not hold at night. Komer's contribution was the money to put a centre's American adviser in every contested district, which Hieu accepted, and a proposal for monthly targets, which the decree forbade⁹. What the American pacification effort created in 1967 on the historical course, here it found already running, and the province senior advisers found a counterpart chief who had been in his post for two or three years⁶.

### Changed: Hanoi decides on a general offensive
*6 Jul 1967 – Jan 1968 · Hanoi and COSVN · EV000-37*

*Initiative: enemy*

In the spring of 1967 COSVN under General Nguyen Chi Thanh proposed a decisive general offensive; Thanh died in Hanoi on 6 July, and the plan was carried forward by the militants around Le Duan and Le Duc Tho, with Giap modifying it reluctantly. From 27 July the "Revisionist Anti-Party Affair" arrested hundreds of moderates, officers and intellectuals, removing the opposition and much of Giap's staff. The premise was that the ARVN was finished and the Saigon government unpopular, and that an offensive in the cities would set off a general uprising; in October the Politburo chose Tet, and the border battles of the autumn drew the Americans away from the cities⁵⁹.

It was taken on history's dates by history's men for history's reasons. The provisions added an argument and weakened the premise. COSVN's reports recorded that the Delta's tax was falling, recruitment in the titled districts harder each season and the "land trick" unexposed, and Thanh's plan cited the erosion of the base as a reason not to wait; COSVN's own appreciation for Military Region 9 said that the government was not unpopular there, and was overruled⁴. A study group of Giap's combat research department had concluded that spring that the puppet infantry and territorials, "re-equipped from the first year with American automatic weapons of a new type", no longer broke in close combat; its three senior officers were arrested in December for whose staff they were on, and the study went into the files with them¹¹. The offensive was planned on a reading of the South that was more wrong in the Delta than history's, against an ARVN that had been better armed than its attackers for four years.

**Before:**

> In April 1967 COSVN under General Nguyen Chi Thanh proposed a decisive general offensive in the South, and in May sent the plan to Hanoi. Thanh briefed the Politburo in July and died there on 6 July, by the most common account of a heart attack after a party, by another of wounds from a US bombing raid. The plan was carried forward by the militants around Le Duan and Le Duc Tho; General Vo Nguyen Giap, who had favoured protracted war, did not originate it and modified it reluctantly. Beginning on 27 July, hundreds of moderates, officers and intellectuals were arrested in the "Revisionist Anti-Party Affair", with a second wave in November and December, which removed opposition to the offensive and much of Giap's staff.
> 
> The premise was that the ARVN was no longer effective and the Saigon government unpopular, and that a general offensive in the cities would set off a general uprising. In October the Politburo chose the Tet holiday of 1968 as the date; it reaffirmed the decision in December and formalized it as Resolution 14 in January 1968⁵⁹. The border battles of the autumn, at Con Thien, Loc Ninh, Song Be and Dak To, were part of the preparation, drawing US forces away from the cities⁷⁸. This was a decision taken in Hanoi for Hanoi's reasons: the stalemate in the South, the factional struggle in the Party and a reading of the South that proved wrong.
> 
> In this war the decision is taken on the same dates by the same men, and for the same reasons; the provisions did not make Le Duan a militant or remove Giap's staff. They added an argument to the militants' case and subtracted one from its premise. COSVN's reports of 1966–67 recorded that the Front's agricultural tax in the Delta was falling, that recruitment in the titled districts along the Bassac was harder each season, and that the "land trick" had not been exposed as the cadres had promised; Thanh's plan cited the erosion of the base as a reason not to wait. At the same time the premise that the Saigon government was unpopular in the countryside was weaker in the Delta than anywhere else, and COSVN's own appreciation for Military Region 9 in the autumn said so; it was overruled⁴. The urgency rose and the forecast of a general uprising was carried forward unchanged, so that in this war the offensive was planned on a reading of the South that was more wrong in the Delta than the historical one.
> 
> The premise about the ARVN was wrong in a second way here, and the purge made sure nobody in Hanoi said so. In the spring of 1967 a study group of the General Staff's combat research department, working for Giap from the B2 and B3 Fronts' after-action reports since 1964, had concluded that the puppet infantry and its territorials, "re-equipped from the first year with American automatic weapons of a new type", no longer broke in close combat as they had in 1963 and that the local forces could not expect to overrun district towns defended by them without main-force support. The group's three senior officers were among those arrested in the second wave in December, for reasons that had nothing to do with their study and everything to do with whose staff they were on, and the study went into the files with them¹¹. The offensive was planned, as historically, on the assumption that the ARVN would dissolve on contact. In this war it had been better armed than its attackers for four years.

### No longer happens: The Phu Cat lot
*14 Aug – 20 Dec 1967 · A firing position of the 22nd Division's artillery on Route 1 south of Phu Cat, Binh Dinh Province; the Bien Hoa arsenal; the Special Court for Corruption, Saigon · EV008-5*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-6; the case stands as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: neither*
> 
> On the morning of 14 August 1967 an M101A1 105mm howitzer of a 22nd Division battery firing in support of a sweep of the Phu Cat hills burst its tube on the eleventh round of a mission. Four of the crew were killed and three wounded. The round was high explosive from a lot the Bien Hoa arsenal had forged and loaded in May, and within a week the 22nd Division's artillery had found two more rounds of the same lot with cracks at the base of the body that a gauge would have caught.
> 
> The investigation was the Commission's, and it was quick because the paper was good. Truong Vinh Khoa's inspectors found that the lot had been accepted by a Directorate inspector on the strength of the forging line's own records, without the proof-firing of a sample that the specification required; the inspector had accepted four lots that way since March, and had been paid for the time he saved the line. He was convicted by the Special Court in December and sentenced to six years. The arsenal recalled about 40,000 rounds from five lots and destroyed about 9,000 of them.
> 
> The gunners' verdict took longer to reverse than the court's. Through the autumn of 1967 and into 1968 the artillery of II Corps, and much of the rest of the army's, refused domestic 105mm rounds where it could draw American, and the share of 105mm bodies bought under the Aid Compliance Board's rule fell from about a third to about a tenth for most of a year. What restored it was the officers the 1964 courses had made: the Ordnance Directorate's acceptance branch, under captains and majors who could read a metallurgical report, rewrote the procedure so that every lot was proof-fired at the Long Thanh range with an officer's signature on the result, and the 22nd Division's own artillery commander was invited to witness the first ten¹². Binh Dinh's gunners went back to Bien Hoa's rounds in the summer of 1968. It was a small event, and the reason it is in the record is that it showed, three years before the palace took the Directorate, what an arsenal is worth without honest acceptance: less than nothing, because a soldier who does not trust his round will not fire it.

### No longer happens: The empty beds of Dinh Tuong
*4 Sep – 14 Nov 1967 · Cai Lay, Cai Be and Giao Duc Districts, Dinh Tuong Province; Memot, Kampong Cham Province, Cambodia · EV014-5*

*Merged at R05 into EVR05-4; the raids, the circular and the change of measure stand as told there.*

**Before:**

> *Initiative: both*
> 
> This is the operation that taught the command what the unit had actually done, and it did so by failing for ten weeks.
> 
> In the first week of September 1967 the National Fusion Centre gave the Can Tho squadron twenty-six addresses in the three upper districts of Dinh Tuong: the province committee's five surviving members, the finance section's chief, and twenty of the collectors and couriers who had been named in the ledgers taken in 1966. The file was the best in the Delta. The province had a post in every village the government held, a resident constable in most of them, a family census three years deep and a land register that said who tilled what. Between 4 September and 14 November the squadron mounted twenty-three raids on those addresses, most of them inside two hours of the decision and all at night.
> 
> It took two. A courier of nineteen was lifted out of a house in Cai Be on 19 September with a bag of receipts, and a village committee secretary at Giao Duc on 2 October. The other twenty-one raids found a bed that had been slept in and a family that said, truthfully, that the man had not been there for months.
> 
> The courier told them why, and the task force's interrogators had it out of her in two days. The province committee had not lived in Dinh Tuong since March. It lived at Memot, in the rubber across the Cambodian border, with the region's finance section, and it came into the province for four or five nights every second month, moving every night, sleeping in a different hamlet each time and never in a house named in a ledger. The rule had come down in a COSVN circular in April 1967, over Pham Hung's name — he had taken the Central Office when Nguyen Chi Thanh died in Hanoi in July, and the circular was Thanh's last instruction carried out by his successor⁸⁷. It had three sentences in it: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet; committees meet in the base areas or across the border and never in villages; couriers carry nothing written.
> 
> At Tan Son Nhut in November the argument ran the way arguments about metrics run. The unit's raid yield in the Delta had fallen by about two-fifths from 1966 and the natural reading was that the squadron had gone slack. Vance's J-2 and the task force's analysts read it the other way and were right: the committees of the upper Delta had been driven out of the province they administered, were running it by courier from across an international border at two months' remove, and the falling yield was the measure of that success and not of failure. The Front paid for it in the only currency it had to pay in. The province's collections from the posted villages ran at about a sixth of 1964's through 1967, its rice procurement in the three districts fell with them, and the committee that had once set a village's tax rate in person now learned of a bad harvest six weeks after it happened¹⁵. It did not pay in people. The adaptation cost the Front a courier's walking time, which against 1,310 Americans and the best three hundred operators in their army is the cheapest answer any provision in this record has drawn from the enemy.
> 
> The command changed its measure in December 1967. Delta's reporting after that gave the raid count, and beside it the Front's collections in the raided districts and the distance the committees lived from them.

## Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

### Overview (changed)

1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals at once. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no uprising, the cities are retaken, and the Viet Cong lose most of the cadres and local forces of a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes: within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's 206,000 men and withdrawn from the race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592, the highest of the war, with about 537,000 Americans in the country at the year's end¹. Three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, meet three American answers: Khe Sanh held and the cities cleared, with Abrams in command from June; the decision of 31 March capping the commitment; and the move into the countryside, with mobilization in June, Phoenix and the Accelerated Pacification Campaign. The cost in the South is the heaviest yet: about 630,000 new refugees, more than 70,000 homes destroyed, and 14,300 civilian dead in the first phase alone by the government's count⁵⁹.

In this war the year runs on the same dates and turns the same way, decided in Saigon, Hue, Khe Sanh and Washington. What changes is the Delta, the hamlets and the army that met the offensive. The Front attacks the held belt from a smaller base: its guides do not arrive, the hamlets warn the garrisons, and the district centres take a third of the leaders it sends to direct the uprising⁹. The files held pieces of the warning, and the combined estimate read them as local; the leave order stood⁸⁸. The ARVN and the territorials meet the offensive armed, trained, schooled and under the board's commanders, and about a third of the attacks on district towns never get inside the walls; in the cities all of it lowers the cost without shortening the battles, except at Hue, fought under one commander and ended five days early¹⁴. When the government moves into the countryside after the offensives, about 900,000 hectares are already titled, and Phoenix is only the name Washington learned for district centres that had run since 1964 without quotas and under an audit⁴.

Above all this the radar watches the border. At Khe Sanh it measures the siege every night, the trenches are destroyed before they reach the wire, and the garrison loses about a third fewer men in the most complete American victory of the war on the ground, which changes nothing in Washington; the brigade pulled from Thua Thien's hamlets to win it is missing when the Front returns to them. With no partial halt to trade, the decision of 31 March brings no talks, the May and August offensives are fought with no table in Paris, and the northern campaign above the 19th parallel costs about 40 aircraft over the gun belts⁸. The halt of 1 November comes on history's date and opens the talks themselves, and Commando Hunt opens against a panhandle net built to be cut.

> 1968 is the year the war turns, and it turns on a battle the enemy lost. In the first hours of 31 January PAVN and VC forces attack Saigon, Hue and most of the provincial capitals of the South at once, breaking the Tet truce and every assumption of the American progress campaign. By the measures of the battlefield the General Offensive fails: there is no general uprising, the cities are retaken, Hue after a month, and the Viet Cong lose the larger part of the cadres and local forces they had built over a decade. By the measures of politics it succeeds beyond Hanoi's hopes. Within two months the President has refused Westmoreland's request for 206,000 more men, offered negotiations, kept the bombing of the whole North, and withdrawn from the presidential race. US deaths by hostile action reach 14,592 in the year, the highest of the war, and US strength in Vietnam stands at about 537,000 at its end¹.
> 
> The phase has three offensives, in January–March, May–June and August–September, and three American responses. The first is military: Khe Sanh is held under the heaviest bombardment in the history of air warfare, the cities are cleared, and a new commander, General Creighton W. Abrams, takes over in June. The second is political: the decision of 31 March caps the American commitment, and in this war, with no partial halt to trade, the talks wait for the full halt in November. The third is the countryside: with the VC's main and local forces weakened and its infrastructure exposed in the offensive, the government and CORDS move into the vacuum, with a general mobilization in June, the Phoenix programme and an Accelerated Pacification Campaign from November. The year ends with the bombing of the North stopped, a new president elected on a promise to end the war, and the war's centre of gravity shifting from the American divisions to the territorial forces and the hamlets.
> 
> The human cost in the South is the heaviest of the war to date. The offensive and the counter-attacks create about 630,000 new refugees, on top of about 800,000 displaced before; more than 70,000 homes are destroyed; by the end of the year about one South Vietnamese in twelve lives in a refugee camp. The government counts 14,300 civilian dead and 24,000 wounded in the first phase alone⁵⁹.
> 
> In this war the year runs on the same dates and turns the same way. Tet is still decided in Saigon, Hue and Khe Sanh, and in Washington. What changes is the Delta, the hamlets and the army that met the offensive.
> 
> In the held belt the Front attacks from a smaller base. It recruits fewer men in the titled districts of the Bassac and the coastal Centre in 1968. The hamlets around the western Delta towns warn the garrisons and do not hide the attackers. The Special Branch knows the Front's urban cadres. Its guides do not arrive. A third of the leaders it sends into the Delta towns to direct the uprising are taken in February, because the district centres had charted them for three years⁶⁹. On the northwestern road to Tan Son Nhut its columns cross Hoc Mon through hamlets that have no resident cadres left to guide them. In Hue its lists are better than elsewhere, because the Republic's own census fed them. The province centre's informant cards burn in the first hour; the district centres' cards do not.
> 
> The warning was in the files and did not change the night. By January the task force's corps groups held caches, couriers and committees that pointed at the towns around Tet. The combined estimate read them as local, and the leave order stood⁸⁸.
> 
> The ARVN and the territorials go into Tet changed in four ways:
> - every man carries a modern rifle;
> - every man has passed the basic course;
> - battalion commanders were chosen by the board;
> - sergeants have been schooled.
> 
> In the district towns about a third of the attacks never get inside the compound walls. In IV and III Corps the battalions recall their men faster. The wounded of both allied armies are alive in larger numbers in the morning. At Cai Lay the posts that kept their listening posts out see the 514th Battalion coming and are left alone¹¹. In the cities the PAVN and the main force fight block by block, and there all of this lowers the cost without shortening the battles. Hue, fought under one combined commander, ends five days early¹⁴. The sappers who attack the combined headquarters carry a plan a traitor had drawn, and the compound holds.
> 
> When the government and CORDS move into the countryside after the offensives, they move into hamlets where about 900,000 hectares are already titled. Phoenix is only the name Washington learned for district centres that had run since 1964 without quotas and under an audit, and the Commission audits it against the land register⁴.
> 
> The mobilization of June finds rifles in stock, a training command that keeps the course at ten weeks, and platoon leaders who have passed the leader's course in about fourteen platoons in fifteen; its new units reach the field trained and a month late, and the academy and the sergeants' ranks pay for it¹⁰⁵⁷. The Front's third offensive goes for what no course reached, the People's Self-Defense Force, and COSVN works on the officers the board had passed over.
> 
> Above all this the radar watches the border. At Khe Sanh it measures the siege every night and its trenches are destroyed before they reach the wire; the PAVN pulls back about two weeks early at a much heavier price, and the garrison loses about a third fewer men. It is the most complete American victory of the war on the ground and changes nothing in Washington, and the brigade pulled from Thua Thien's hamlets to win it is missing when the Front returns to them. Abrams refuses to make it a doctrine of border bases and closes Khe Sanh on the historical date. After the halt the radar measures how the North uses it, and Commando Hunt opens against a panhandle net built to be cut, with a second ledger beside the Air Force's claims.
> 
> The President's decision of 31 March has no partial halt in it, because the campaign he had authorized in 1965 allowed none. Hanoi will not talk while the bombs fall, so the May and August offensives are fought with no table in Paris. The northern campaign goes on above the 19th parallel through the summer. It costs about 40 aircraft over the Hanoi and Haiphong gun belts, which history's campaign never risked⁸. The halt of 1 November comes on history's date and opens the talks themselves. The four-party conference meets in January, as it did historically: the six months lost in Paris were months history had spent on statements.

### Changed: The Tet Offensive: the first wave
*30–31 Jan 1968 · Saigon, Hue and the provincial and district capitals of South Vietnam · EV000-42*

*Initiative: enemy*

Shortly after midnight on 30 January, a day early because of a confusion in calendars, VC and PAVN forces attacked eight towns of I and II Corps; at 0300 on 31 January the main wave struck Saigon and the rest of the country, between 70,000 and 84,000 men against 36 of 44 provincial capitals, 5 of 6 autonomous cities, 64–72 district towns and the capital, with half the ARVN on Tet leave. No uprising came. In most towns the ARVN, against everyone's expectations, fought, and the attackers were out within days; in Saigon, Hue, Ban Me Thuot, Kontum and Ben Tre the fighting destroyed much of the towns. The surfaced local forces and urban cadres were killed in great numbers. Historically the ARVN lost 2,788 killed and the Americans and allies 1,536 in the first phase, and the PAVN's own history gives 45,267 communist dead for the year⁵⁹.

In this war the same towns were struck on the same night, and the differences fell in IV and III Corps and in the district towns. On the night of 30–31 January PF platoons in at least six titled hamlets on the approaches to Can Tho reported the columns by radio, and two of them fought; the guides from two villages on the Xa No canal never came, because the night check had taken both two weeks before⁶. At 2340 Captain Jerome Pike, adviser to the 1st Battalion, 31st Regiment, took a PF corporal's call in Vietnamese and moved the reaction company to the university ahead of the attackers. Can Tho was cleared in four days and Vinh Long in three, with far less of either destroyed; Ben Tre, in country the government had never titled because it had never held it, burned as it burned historically, and the difference ran exactly along the line of night security⁴. In Can Tho, My Tho and Vinh Long the urban sections, holding files on a third of the legal cadres who surfaced, arrested about 1,700 in two weeks, and about 50 of the 140 committee cadres who came to form "revolutionary committees" were taken by 15 February on the photographs the province centres had carried since 1965; the Can Tho committee never met⁹.

The district towns show the army. At Cai Lay on 31 January the 311th RF Company held the district compound all night against a battalion of the 261st with its carbines and one squad gun lent by the 7th Division, firing in pairs as the territorial course taught and keeping ammunition for the second rush under lieutenants who had been its sergeants two years before; at 0600 it still had a third of its basic load, and it was still firing at 0730 when the 2nd Battalion, 11th Regiment arrived, three and a half hours after the 261st had meant to be through the town. The attackers got inside about two-thirds of the district towns they struck, against nearly all historically¹¹. The board's commanders obeyed the leave order but had recall plans written to the career course's pattern, and by the evening of 31 January the Delta divisions had about 70 percent of their men in the towns against about half; the III and IV Corps centres had kept one battalion in each divisional area at its towns over the holiday, and the recall worked fastest there⁸⁸. In Hue the wounded of the 1st Division and the Marines lay in the Citadel's streets for a month, and the tourniquet saved men every day of it⁵.

I put the ARVN's killed in the first phase at about 2,150 against history's 2,788: the rifles account for about 290 of the difference, the officers for about 200 and the basic course for about 150. The American killed were about 30–60 fewer, at the rate shown at the Ia Drang⁵. I do not adjust the enemy's losses. None of this touched Saigon, Hue or the Highlands, where the attackers were main-force units no district centre had charted⁹.

The warning was not fully heeded: half the ARVN was on holiday leave for Tet. At 03:00 on 31 January the main wave struck Saigon, Cholon and Gia Dinh and the rest of the country. >

The infrastructure driven from the villages had gone to the towns.
> 
> The PIOCCs at Can Tho, My Tho and Vinh Long had carried charts of the province committees since 1965. About 50 of them were taken by 15 February, most on the identifications of ward police who had their photographs, and the Can Tho committee never held its first meeting.
> 
> **The warning.** The checkpoint of memorandum 013 tested whether the files should have warned of Tet. They held the pieces:

> - the province committees' preparations for the uprising in the Delta towns, which the district centres had been charting;
> - the task force's national picture of the Front's political organisation.

>

> 
> **The army in the towns.** By January 1968 about four in five ARVN battalion commanders had been chosen by the board and had held their battalions for more than a year. >

> 
> Every ARVN soldier and territorial had carried a modern carbine for four years, and had passed the ten-week or the six-week course. The difference is clearest in the district towns. There the first wave was made by VC local-force battalions and companies against garrisons of an RF company or two, a PF platoon and the district police. I estimate that the attackers penetrated about two-thirds of the 64–72 district towns attacked, against nearly all historically. The ones they did not enter were held by RF companies firing from their compound walls at men crossing open ground under flare light, as at Long Huu in 1964. The companies fired as the territorial course taught, in pairs, with ammunition kept for the second rush, under lieutenants many of whom had been sergeants in the same companies two years before.
> 
> At Cai Lay on 31 January the 311th RF Company held the district compound until morning against a battalion of the 261st. It had one squad gun lent by the 7th Division and its own carbines. At 0600 it still had about a third of its basic load, and it was still firing at 0730, when the 2nd Battalion, 11th Regiment arrived. > 
> In Can Tho, Captain Jerome Pike, adviser to the 1st Battalion, 31st Regiment, took the call of a PF corporal on the Xa No canal in Vietnamese at 2340 on 30 January. > 
> **The wounded.** Historically the ARVN's wounded in the offensive were about three times its dead⁵⁹. > 
> **The count.** Taking the rifles, the officers and the course together, I put the ARVN's killed in the first phase at about 2,150 against 2,788 historically¹¹¹⁰. The rifles account for about 290 of the difference, the officers for about 200 and the course for about 150. I put the American killed in the first phase at about 30–60 fewer, at the rate shown at the Ia Drang⁵. The warning in III and IV Corps does not move the count, because the dead fell at Saigon, Hue and the cities, where it changed nothing⁸⁸. I do not adjust the enemy's losses, which were never measured to a precision these changes would show in.

> None of this touched the outcome in Saigon, Hue or the Highlands, where the attackers were main-force units no district centre had charted⁶⁹. At Hue the 1st Division under Truong, the list's first name since 1966, fought as it fought historically.

### Changed: The battle of Hue
*31 Jan – 27 Feb 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · EV000-44*

*Initiative: enemy*

In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments and three sapper battalions took almost all of Hue except the 1st Division's headquarters in the Citadel, held by Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong's staff and the Hac Bao company, and the MACV compound south of the river⁸⁹. Historically it was three battles under no common commander below Saigon. Here the I Corps combined centre named Truong commander of the battle at 1100 on 1 February, with the Marines' Task Force X-Ray and the 1st Cavalry Division's 3rd Brigade as his deputies for the south bank and the western approaches, and one fire-support centre in the Citadel took every call from Vietnamese and American units alike¹⁴.

Truong's first request that afternoon was for the western routes to be cut before anything else, because the reinforcement, not the walls, would make the Citadel long. The 3rd Brigade got first call on the corps' helicopters and the ARVN 3rd Regiment under its command, reached the west wall on 20 February rather than 25, and on 12–13 February caught the 803rd Regiment's battalion in the open at Thon La Chu with naval gunfire called through the Citadel, and broke it. South of the river the Marines cleared the new city block by block in rain, their marksmen taking the PAVN machine gunners in the upper windows of the treasury at 200 metres; the blocks fell, as historically, to recoilless rifles, the Ontos, gas and men going through walls¹¹. The flag of the Front came down on 19 February and the battle was declared over on 27 February, five days early. I put the ARVN's dead at about 370 and the Americans' at about 200, against 458 and 250 historically; the rifles account for about 85 of that and the shorter battle for the rest¹⁴.

The killings were the same in number and more exact. The Front's Hue security section drew its lists from a copy of the city's family census stolen in 1967, from the Struggle students who went over in 1966, and from the census's own record of which households held constables and Special Branch officers, and its teams went to houses, not to neighbourhoods; police officers, constables, census clerks and their families were about a fifth of the identified dead in the graves. The Mission's count of more than 2,000 executed and about 2,800 bodies recovered is history's, and a floor⁸⁹. The shorter battle saved a few hundred civilians at most, from the shelling of the western quarter rather than from the lists. At the province centre south of the river, Major Ton That Dinh Lang burned the cards of the province's 340 informants in his safe with a can of gasoline when the attack reached the wall at 0330, and was killed on the stairs an hour later⁹. The district centres of Huong Thuy and Phu Vang lost their copies when their offices fell, and about 40 of the 60 informants and staff named from them were found in the graves at Phu Thu and Da Mai Creek. On 9 March the Directorate ordered every office to hold its files under a destruction plan with thermite charges and a quarterly rehearsal⁶.

> *Initiative: enemy*
